note: Per-country resource entries shown in the record popup, grouped into collapsible categories with a count each. Every entry is a record with its own description and source link, tagged by lens, so they can be toggled and indexed like anything else on the map. Written per country because the answer differs per country; the guides carry the explanation, these carry the resources. Categories marked scope=release are only shown on release and biosafety-decision records and in the country box, because a consultation window is about a decision being made — on a clinic or a company record it is noise. The rest are shown everywhere, because testing, complaining and certification apply whatever the reader is looking at.

test.d: Lateral flow strips, the same format as a pregnancy test. Crush tissue or seed in water, dip, read in five to ten minutes. Sold to anyone, a few pounds each, in packs. Strips are trait-specific, so know which trait to look for before buying.
Strips plus the extraction kits that go with them, sold internationally — which matters because the trait to test for differs by region.
Sells in small quantities with published prices, which makes it the most usable of the three for someone testing a handful of samples rather than a lorry.

The largest food and feed testing network in the world, with laboratories in more than 60 countries and the default commercial route for a confirmatory DNA test. A strip result tells you what to do next; this is what an enforcement body acts on.

test.n: GMOMETHODS — the EU database of validated detection methods, and the ENGL laboratory network
test.d: IF YOU ARE COMMISSIONING A TEST, THIS IS WHERE THE METHOD COMES FROM. An application to authorise a GM food or feed in the EU MUST INCLUDE A METHOD FOR DETECTING, IDENTIFYING AND QUANTIFYING IT, and the EU Reference Laboratory (EURL GMFF, hosted by the Joint Research Centre) validates that method for sensitivity, specificity, accuracy and reliability. The validated methods are then PUBLISHED FREE in the GMOMETHODS database, searchable by EVENT, UNIQUE IDENTIFIER, SPECIES, APPLICANT and technique. So for most authorised events anywhere in the world there is a published, peer-validated PCR method a laboratory can be asked to run — and the unique identifier this map keeps telling readers to write down is the key to finding it. The JRC also publishes decision tools, GMO-MATRIX and EVENT-FINDER. Behind it sits the EUROPEAN NETWORK OF GMO LABORATORIES (ENGL), the national enforcement laboratories of every EU country PLUS NORWAY, SWITZERLAND AND TURKEY. THE HONEST LIMIT: detecting UNAUTHORISED GMOs relies on screening that only indicates presence and needs confirmation by other approaches; and the EURL and ENGL's own report of 26 March 2019 addresses the difficulty of detecting organisms made by NEW MUTAGENESIS TECHNIQUES — gene-edited plants may leave nothing a method can target. Work on GM animals and microorganisms is still in progress.

decides.d: Every party to the Cartagena Protocol must name a contact for biosafety, and the list is public. For most of the world it is the only named biosafety contact that exists, and it holds the decisions filed for that country.

decides.n: Comité Sahélien des Pesticides (CILSS) — regional pesticide registration
decides.d: In the Sahel the pesticide decision is largely REGIONAL rather than national. The Comité Sahélien des Pesticides, under CILSS, examines dossiers and registers products for its member states at once, so what may lawfully be sold in a member country is often decided by the committee rather than by that country's own directorate. A reader trying to find out whether a product is authorised, or to object to one, should check the regional register as well as the national one. Shown only for the member states.

decides.n: Biosafety Clearing-House — what a country profile holds
decides.d: Referenced by 135 rows in this box. A country profile on the Clearing-House holds the national focal point and competent authorities the country has notified, its national biosafety law where filed, and the decisions it has submitted under Article 20. It is a country's OWN FILINGS, so a thin profile means the country has filed little — not that it decides little. Filing is a treaty obligation without a sanction for missing it.

notice.d: Parties file their decisions here, and for most first imports for release a public consultation is required beforehand. For countries with no notice venue of their own, this is the only place an application becomes visible in advance.

Where a gazette is the announcement venue, this forum lists the official journals of the EU and EFTA states with links to their online editions. It does not cover the rest of the world, and for most of the gazette rows on this map the print edition remains authoritative.

notice.n: Cartagena Clearing-House — the decision even when the gazette is not online
notice.d: A gazette is authoritative and often unreachable: Ethiopia's is sold in Addis Ababa, Namibia's has no online archive. But a party to the Cartagena Protocol files its decisions to the Clearing-House regardless, so the substance of what was authorised is usually readable there even where the official announcement is not. The date of gazette publication still governs when a measure takes effect.

notice.n: Finding your country's official gazette — Guide to Law Online and the Michigan gazettes directory
notice.d: THE FILE'S EXISTING GAZETTE ROW COVERS THE EU AND EFTA ONLY; this is the route everywhere else. In most countries A LAW ENTERS INTO FORCE ON THE DATE OF PUBLICATION IN THE OFFICIAL GAZETTE, and in civil law jurisdictions the gazette is often the SOLE SOURCE of the authoritative text until codes are updated — which is why an authorisation, a ban or a quarantine order may exist nowhere else. Two free directories find it: the LAW LIBRARY OF CONGRESS GUIDE TO LAW ONLINE, which lists legal resources online for every country with gazette details under the Legislative and Legal Guides sections; and GOVERNMENT GAZETTES ONLINE, a University of Michigan project giving DIRECT LINKS plus the language, publication frequency, time coverage and content of each — covering around sixty countries including Algeria, Burkina Faso, Congo, Djibouti, Kenya, Saint Lucia, Sri Lanka and Uruguay. For machine translation of texts in other languages, GLOBAL REGULATION. TWO LIMITS: the Library of Congress FOREIGN OFFICIAL GAZETTES (FOG) database IS NO LONGER UPDATED, and its own Foreign Legal Gazettes Guide covered only about HALF of the 240 jurisdictions it collects for as of early 2024. Where a gazette is unreachable, the Cartagena Clearing-House row in this box is the fallback.

certify.d: The global umbrella for organic standards, which exclude engineered material by definition in every member scheme. Use it to find the certifier operating where you are: a positive test costs an operator the certification and the price premium immediately, without a hearing.

Certifies biodynamic production in more than 60 countries to a standard stricter than organic, including on seed: varieties bred by methods it rejects cannot be used at all. Where no national organic body exists, an international certifier still operates.

A certifier's own website will always say it is accredited; only the accreditor's register says whether that is still true. IOAS publishes the organic certification bodies it accredits, worldwide. Check a certificate against this before relying on it, and note that the EU, the US and several other jurisdictions run their own control-body lists as well — a body may be on one and not another. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

certify.n: EU list of recognised control bodies for organic imports
certify.d: The Commission publishes the control bodies and control authorities recognised for organic production in third countries, each with a code of the form XX-BIO-NNN that appears on the product label. If a label carries such a code, this is where to check the body behind it is still listed — recognition has been withdrawn before, most visibly over fraudulent certification of raw Indian cotton. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

certify.n: PGS global map — participatory guarantee systems
certify.d: Where a country's organic certification runs through participatory guarantee rather than a third-party auditor, this is where to find it: an IFOAM and FAO register searchable by country and product. It matters for this map because a PGS sets its own standard through its members, so what 'organic' excludes in a given initiative is decided locally rather than by a national regulation.

legal.n: Center for Food Safety — legal programme
legal.d: Has brought most of the significant US litigation in this field, including the cases that vacated approvals for engineered alfalfa and sugar beet pending fuller environmental review. Takes information from the public and publishes model ordinance text for local measures.

Files formal objections to EU approvals and requests internal review of Commission decisions — a specific legal mechanism most people do not know exists. Its published objections are the template for anyone drafting one.

Environmental lawyers who litigate on process rather than on the technology: whether an assessment was adequate, whether a consultation was real, whether access to documents was refused lawfully. That is the ground on which these cases are usually won.

legal.n: Public Patent Foundation — OSGATA v. Monsanto
legal.d: Brought the case in which organic and conventional growers sought protection from patent claims over seed that arrived on their land without them planting it. The court declined jurisdiction on the strength of a binding commitment not to sue over trace presence, which is now the operative assurance.

The largest farmers' organisation in the world, 200 million smallholders across 81 countries, and the origin of the term food sovereignty. It supports members facing seed law and land disputes and has regional secretariats on every inhabited continent, so there is one within reach almost anywhere.

Researches and publishes on seed laws, land deals and corporate concentration, and works with local organisations rather than in one jurisdiction. Its published analysis of a country's seed law is often the only independent account of it in any language a reader here can use.

Follows the Cartagena Protocol negotiations and publishes briefings for delegations from developing countries. Where a national law was drafted from a template, this is usually where the counter-analysis of that template was written.

Connects environmental lawyers in more than 70 countries and supplies scientific and legal support to local counsel free of charge. It is the practical answer for someone with a case and no lawyer who knows this subject: the local lawyer exists, and ELAW is what backs them.

legal.n: Access Initiative — finding your rights to information and participation
legal.d: Documents, country by country, what rights of access to environmental information, participation and justice actually exist in law. Worth reading before writing anything, because the answer differs enormously and is rarely obvious.

legal.n: ITPGRFA — the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture
legal.d: The treaty that recognises FARMERS' RIGHTS — Article 9 — including the protection of traditional knowledge, the right to participate in benefit-sharing from plant genetic resources, and the right to participate in national decisions about their use. It also states that nothing in the article limits farmers' rights to save, use, exchange and sell farm-saved seed, subject to national law. Each party names a national focal point, listed here. Two limits worth knowing: implementation is left to national law, so what Article 9 means in practice is decided domestically; and the treaty's multilateral system covers a listed set of crops rather than everything. Useful where a seed-law or variety-rights argument needs an international peg. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

legal.n: Stockholm Convention — persistent organic pollutants, national focal points
legal.d: Parties designate a national focal point and an official contact point, both listed here, and each prepares a National Implementation Plan setting out how it will eliminate or restrict the listed chemicals. Several of the pesticides this map's contamination records involve are listed under it. Where a national pesticide register is thin or unpublished, a country's implementation plan is often the fuller public document, and it is filed with the convention rather than with the ministry.

legal.n: UNDROP — UN Declaration on the Rights of Peasants and Other People Working in Rural Areas
legal.d: Adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2018 and named by only one row in this file until now, though it is the instrument several of the organisations here actually use. It recognises peasants' RIGHT TO SEEDS — including the right to save, use, exchange and sell farm-saved seed, to keep traditional knowledge, to participate in decisions on plant genetic resources, and to protection against loss of that knowledge — alongside rights to land, water and a healthy environment, and the right to PARTICIPATE IN DECISION-MAKING on matters affecting them. Two things to know before relying on it: it is a DECLARATION, not a treaty, so it binds nobody directly and works through domestic adoption and argument; and the OHCHR collects submissions on its implementation, which means a national account of how a government is or is not honouring it can be filed and read. Cameroon's RADD has used it that way — see this file's Cameroon entry.

open.d: US notices with a comment window, searchable and subscribable by email. Thirty to sixty days, and a comment filed inside it must be addressed in the decision. Subscribe rather than check: thirty days is short if you hear on day twenty-eight.

Every European assessment is published in full with the panel's reasoning and opened for comment, typically for thirty days. The document states what was assessed, which makes it possible to comment on what was not.

Australia publishes each application, the risk assessment plan and the proposed field sites, then invites comment for around thirty days. Knowing the sites before the decision is what makes a local objection possible.

open.n: Biosafety Clearing-House — what your country has filed
open.d: Every party must file its decisions here, and for most first imports intended for release a consultation is required beforehand. For a country with no notice venue of its own this is the only place an application becomes visible in advance — and it is also where to check what a neighbour has decided about the same organism. What a country profile actually holds: the national focal point and competent authorities the country has notified, its national biosafety law where filed, and the decisions it has submitted under Article 20. It is a country's OWN FILINGS, so a thin profile means the country has filed little — not that it decides little. Filing is a treaty obligation without a sanction for missing it.

open.n: Cartagena Protocol — the right to be consulted
open.d: Article 23 obliges every party to consult the public in decisions about living modified organisms and to make the results available, while protecting confidential information. Where a country runs no consultation at all, this is the obligation it is not meeting, and citing it by article is more use than an objection with no footing.

open.n: UN Environment Programme — national biosafety frameworks
open.d: UNEP helped most countries write their biosafety framework, and the resulting documents — which set out who decides and how the public is involved — are published. For a country whose own ministry publishes nothing, this is often where the procedure is actually written down. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

records.n: WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform
records.d: Searches every national trial register at once, so a gene or cell therapy trial registered in one country is findable from another. For a patient, this is where to check whether a treatment being offered is a registered trial at all — an unregistered one is a warning in itself.
The largest single register, and it carries results as well as protocols. Search by condition and by intervention; the sponsor field is what ties a trial to the company entries on this map.

No government publishes a register of high-containment laboratories. This research project is the only global account of where they are, and the source of the 118 on this map — including the ones still under construction, which is when a community can still ask about them.

records.n: Tracing the company behind a trial, a facility or a release — OpenCorporates and the GLEIF LEI
records.d: A SPONSOR NAME ON A TRIAL, AN APPLICANT ON A RELEASE PERMIT OR AN OPERATOR OF A FACILITY IS OFTEN A SUBSIDIARY, and this map's industry entries are only useful if the parent can be found. OPENCORPORATES draws from NATIONAL BUSINESS REGISTRIES IN AROUND 145 JURISDICTIONS — over 220 million companies and 300 million officers, PROVENANCED TO THE OFFICIAL SOURCE — giving current status, NAMED DIRECTORS and industry codes. GLEIF's LEGAL ENTITY IDENTIFIER database is the complement and is FREE: its LEVEL 2 DATA answers WHO OWNS WHOM, publishing the LEI of an entity's DIRECT AND ULTIMATE PARENT alongside the child record, and the reverse. The two are mapped to each other, and an LEI record also carries the HOME-REGISTRY NUMBER AND REGISTERING AUTHORITY, which is what lets you cross to the national register itself. TWO LIMITS: only entities that have obtained an LEI appear in the ownership layer, and a child may report an EXCEPTION where it has no parent, opts out for exceptional reasons, or its parents hold no LEI — so an absent parent is not proof of independence. Just over half the global LEI population is linked to OpenCorporates.

treaty.d: Any member of the public may bring a communication against a party government — no fee, no lawyer, no nationality test, and no need to have exhausted the courts first in every case. It examines whether a state gave the public information, participation and access to justice on environmental decisions, which is exactly what a refused consultation is. It moves slowly, it works in public, and governments would rather it did not exist. 47 parties, mostly Europe and Central Asia.

treaty.n: Escazú Agreement — Latin America and the Caribbean
treaty.d: The regional counterpart to Aarhus, and the only environmental treaty anywhere with an article obliging states to protect environmental defenders. It guarantees access to environmental information and participation in decisions, which reaches biosafety decisions directly.

treaty.n: Cartagena Protocol Article 23 — the right to be consulted
treaty.d: Every party must consult the public on decisions about living modified organisms and make the results available. Where a country runs no consultation at all, this is the obligation it is not meeting — and citing it by article, in writing, is more use than an objection with no footing.

treaty.n: Nagoya–Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol — who pays
treaty.d: Sets out response measures where a living modified organism causes damage to biodiversity. Ask in writing which provision applies and who would pay; the answer, or its absence, is the useful document. Only about 55 countries have ratified, so whether it applies where you are is itself worth establishing.

an_inspect.n: USDA APHIS — animal welfare complaints and inspection reports
an_inspect.d: Takes complaints about licensed and registered facilities from anyone, and publishes the resulting inspection reports including the failures found. A complaint can therefore produce a public document about a facility that otherwise publishes nothing.

an_inspect.n: Animal welfare inspection — the general route
an_inspect.d: Most countries license animal research through an agriculture, health or home affairs ministry and inspect on a schedule. Whether the public may complain, and whether reports are published, varies enormously — the two questions worth asking first.

an_inspect.n: The Animal Welfare Body inside the institution, and the WOAH animal welfare focal point
an_inspect.d: Two routes exist almost everywhere even where no public register does. FIRST, INSIDE THE INSTITUTION. Under EU DIRECTIVE 2010/63/EU — followed closely in Switzerland, the UK and Norway too — every authorised establishment MUST HAVE AN ANIMAL WELFARE BODY, comprising at least one person with practical knowledge of animal care and husbandry, ONE SCIENTIFIC MEMBER, AND A DESIGNATED VETERINARIAN. It advises on acquisition, care, housing and use, applies the 3Rs, KEEPS TRACK OF HOW PROJECTS AFFECT THE ANIMALS, and advises on project applications — so an internal record exists of what is being done and at what severity, and a NON-TECHNICAL PROJECT SUMMARY is published for each authorised project. National competent authorities grant authorisation and INSPECT breeders, suppliers and research establishments, and each Member State has a NATIONAL COMMITTEE for the protection of animals used for scientific purposes. SECOND, INTERNATIONALLY. Each of WOAH's 182 member countries nominates a NATIONAL FOCAL POINT FOR ANIMAL WELFARE, alongside focal points for veterinary laboratories and wildlife. Where no national body is named in this box, that focal point is a real named official who can be asked who licenses and who inspects. Note WOAH's animal welfare standards, unlike its health standards, DO NOT FALL UNDER THE WTO SPS AGREEMENT, so they carry no trade enforcement.

an_inspect.n: AAALAC International — the accredited-organisations directory, and what accreditation is and is not
an_inspect.d: WHERE NO GOVERNMENT PUBLISHES A LIST OF ANIMAL FACILITIES, THIS ONE IS PUBLIC AND SEARCHABLE. AAALAC International, a private non-profit founded 1965, PUBLISHES ITS FULL DIRECTORY OF ACCREDITED ORGANISATIONS BY NAME AND CITY — more than 1,140 institutions and companies in 52 countries, updated continuously, and it is the source of the animal-facility markers on this map. The process is substantive: the institution writes a PROGRAM DESCRIPTION covering policies, housing, veterinary care and facilities; AAALAC's Council on Accreditation reviews it and conducts an ON-SITE ASSESSMENT; deficiencies must be corrected within a set period. Accredited institutions must PROMPTLY REPORT ADVERSE EVENTS, INCLUDING UNEXPECTED ANIMAL DEATHS AND ALLEGATIONS OF COMPROMISED WELFARE; AAALAC investigates and can require corrective action or REVOKE ACCREDITATION. So an allegation can be made to the accreditor as well as to the regulator. THE LIMITS MATTER AS MUCH: accreditation is VOLUNTARY and private, so absence from the directory means nothing about whether a facility exists; the directory shows who holds it, not what was found; and AAALAC itself warns that institutions sometimes CLAIM ACCREDITATION THEY DO NOT HOLD — which is precisely why the directory is worth checking against a claim.

an_records.n: What the Animal Welfare Act does not cover
an_records.d: Rats, mice and birds bred for research are excluded from the US Act entirely, and they are the overwhelming majority of animals used. A complaint about them has nowhere to go, and the published inspection figures do not count them. Worth knowing before writing.

an_records.n: Home Office — annual statistics of scientific procedures
an_records.d: The UK publishes procedure counts by species and severity every year, and names no establishment. It is the most detailed public account of animal research anywhere and it will not tell you which building.
Member states report animal use to a central database, published as totals by species and purpose. Establishment-level detail is not published anywhere in the EU.

an_records.n: Where the numbers come from, and what they leave out — CCAC, the UK count, and the countries with none
an_records.d: ONLY A HANDFUL OF COUNTRIES COUNT AT ALL, and each counts something different — which is why global totals in this field should be read as estimates. CANADA'S CCAC publishes an annual ANIMAL DATA REPORT with DOWNLOADABLE SORTABLE SPREADSHEETS breaking down species, purpose and INVASIVENESS CATEGORY — the most usable open dataset of its kind. BRITAIN counts every regulated procedure on a protected animal under the ANIMALS (SCIENTIFIC PROCEDURES) ACT 1986, covering all vertebrates AND CEPHALOPODS, published annually by the Home Office, with NORTHERN IRELAND counting separately. THE EXCLUSIONS ARE THE POINT. Canada's CCAC covers only CERTIFIED INSTITUTIONS — typically universities — so most private laboratories and companies are absent unless government-funded, and the CCAC sets no standardised submission method. The US counts only AWA-covered mammals, excluding mice, rats and birds; official figures near 800,000 sit against unofficial estimates of 12–24 million. INVERTEBRATES SUCH AS FRUIT FLIES AND WORMS ARE NOT PROTECTED AND NOT COUNTED ANYWHERE. And JAPAN PUBLISHES NO OFFICIAL GOVERNMENT DATA at all — the only figures come from a professional association survey to which a third of facilities did not respond. Where a country publishes nothing, an estimate is all that exists.

fe_register.d: The UK publishes success rates, inspection ratings and enforcement history clinic by clinic. It is the most detailed public fertility register in the world, and the model for what a register can be rather than what most are.

US clinics report annually and the data is published clinic by clinic. Read the denominators before the percentages: a clinic that treats easier cases will report better outcomes without doing anything better.

fe_register.n: Checking a clinic where no register exists
fe_register.d: Most of the world publishes nothing clinic by clinic. Where there is no register, ask the clinic directly for its own figures, for which body licenses it, and for its last inspection — and treat a refusal as information.

fe_register.n: ICMART and the regional ART registries — where a country has no clinic-by-clinic register
fe_register.d: Most countries publish nothing clinic by clinic, but almost every region has a REGISTRY THAT COLLECTS THE CYCLES ANYWAY, and ICMART aggregates them into an annual WORLD REPORT. The regional bodies are worth naming because they are who to ask: ANARA for Africa (contributing countries have included Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Ivory Coast, Kenya, Libya, Mali, Mauritius, Nigeria, South Africa, Sudan, Togo, Tunisia, Uganda and Zimbabwe); ESHRE's EUROPEAN IVF MONITORING CONSORTIUM (EIM) for Europe; REDLARA for Latin America; ANZARD for Australia and New Zealand; CARTR Plus for Canada; SART for the US; JSOG and JSRM for Japan; MEFS for the Middle East; ASPIRE for Asia-Pacific. EIM collects IVF, ICSI, frozen embryo transfer, EGG DONATION, in-vitro maturation, FROZEN OOCYTE REPLACEMENT and pooled data on PREIMPLANTATION GENETIC TESTING. TWO LIMITS TO CARRY: the legal obligation on a clinic to report to its national authority VARIES WIDELY BY COUNTRY and participation changes every year, so the totals are a floor rather than a count; and ICMART is funded partly by UNRESTRICTED GRANTS FROM ABBOTT AND FERRING PHARMACEUTICALS alongside the professional societies.

fe_complain.d: A voluntary registry through which donor-conceived people and donors find each other, independent of any clinic. It exists because clinic records are frequently destroyed, sold or lost, and because several countries permitted anonymous donation and then reversed it without retroactive effect.

fe_complain.n: Your fertility regulator or health ministry
fe_complain.d: Complaints about a clinic go to whichever body licenses it — a dedicated regulator where one exists, otherwise the health ministry. Where the clinic is private and unlicensed, consumer protection may be the only route.

fe_complain.n: Statutory donor registers and the right to know — where the law gives one
fe_complain.d: THE QUESTION HERE IS OFTEN NOT A COMPLAINT BUT ACCESS TO A RECORD, and in a minority of jurisdictions the law creates one. SWEDEN WAS FIRST, ABOLISHING ANONYMOUS SPERM DONATION IN 1985, with people born after 1 March 1985 entitled to identifying information; the UK and FINLAND have also banned anonymous gamete donation, and in AUSTRALIA anonymous donation is not possible. VICTORIA is the fullest model and worth knowing in detail because it shows what a register can do: a CENTRAL REGISTER holding identifying information on all parties to a donor procedure that resulted in a birth, and a VOLUNTARY REGISTER through which people including DONOR SIBLINGS can record their own details; donor-conceived people and their DESCENDANTS may apply at 18 for the donor's name, date of birth and donor code; DONORS MAY ALSO APPLY for information about their offspring; 2017 amendments REMOVED THE REQUIREMENT FOR DONOR CONSENT, replacing it with CONTACT PREFERENCES; donors are limited to ten recipient women; and from 1 January 2010 the fact of donor conception is recorded on the birth register, with an addendum issued to the person themselves — not to parents — from 1 January 2028. NOTE THE CHANGE: VARTA ceased operations on 31 December 2024 and the registers passed to the DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH's Donor Conception Registrar. Only three Australian states have such registers, and most of the world has none — where none exists, the Donor Sibling Registry in this box is the alternative.

cl_find.n: ClinicalTrials.gov — finding a trial near you
cl_find.d: The largest trial registry, searchable by condition, intervention and location, and it lists trials worldwide rather than only US ones. The record names the sponsor, the sites, the eligibility criteria and the contact.
The European register, which publishes the protocol and the summary results, not only the listing.

cl_find.n: WHO ICTRP — the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform
cl_find.d: Ten country rows in this file send a reader to the ICTRP and it was not itself listed. It is a SEARCH PORTAL across the national and regional registries rather than a register in its own right: one query reaches ClinicalTrials.gov, the EU register, the Chinese, Indian, Iranian, Japanese, Korean, Cuban, Peruvian, Thai, Dutch, Brazilian, Australian-New Zealand and other primary registries at once. Two limits worth knowing: it only shows what a primary registry has published, so a trial registered nowhere is invisible here too; and records are supplied by those registries, so the detail and the update frequency vary by source. Where a country's own register is thin, unpublished or restricted, this is the way in. Searches every national registry at once, which matters because trials in China, India, Iran and Japan are often registered nationally and not in the US registry.

cl_find.n: The WHO network of primary registries — the register that covers your region
cl_find.d: ICTRP SEARCHES THESE; THIS PAGE NAMES THEM, which matters when you want to search in your own language or register a trial locally. Around SEVENTEEN PRIMARY REGISTRIES feed the platform: ISRCTN (the first, from 2000), the EU Clinical Trials Register, DRKS (Germany), the Netherlands NTR, ANZCTR (Australia and New Zealand), ChiCTR (China), the JAPAN REGISTRY OF CLINICAL TRIALS, CRiS (Republic of Korea), TCTR (Thailand), CTRI (India), SLCTR (Sri Lanka), IRCT (Iran), ReBec (Brazil), RPCEC (Cuba), REPEC (Peru), the LEBANESE registry (LBCTR, the most recent, from September 2019), an International Traditional Medicine registry, and PACTR. PACTR IS THE ONE TO KNOW FOR AFRICA: managed by Cochrane South Africa at the Medical Research Council, begun 2007 as the AIDS, TB and Malaria registry, widened in 2009 to all conditions, and IT IS THE ONLY AFRICAN PRIMARY REGISTRY IN THE WHO NETWORK — so a trial anywhere on the continent should be there, and South Africa additionally runs SANCTR. THE HONEST LIMITS: registry scale is wildly uneven, from a few hundred trials in Cuba to tens of thousands in the EU register; completeness of records differs sharply between registries; and ICTRP's own search interface is frequently slow or unavailable, so going direct to the regional registry is often faster.

cl_report.d: A patient, relative or carer can report directly, without a doctor and without permission. It matters more for gene and cell therapies than for ordinary medicines, because so few people have received any one of them that a single well-described report is a measurable fraction of what is known.
The UK route, open to patients directly.
The European adverse reaction database, searchable by medicine.

cl_report.n: Reporting where there is no national scheme
cl_report.d: Report to the trial's ethics committee and to the sponsor in writing, and keep the correspondence. Ethics committees must include lay members and will accept correspondence about a study they approved.

cl_report.n: WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring — find your national centre
cl_report.d: More than 150 countries run a national pharmacovigilance centre reporting into the same global database, and most accept reports from patients directly rather than only from doctors. If your country is not named separately here, it almost certainly has one, and this is the list. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

lab_oversight.d: Holds the notification for every UK laboratory working with engineered organisms and investigates complaints about containment. One of very few places anywhere where contained use is reportable by the public at all.
US federally funded work is overseen by an institutional biosafety committee, whose minutes are obtainable and which is required to include members from outside the institution.

In most countries laboratory work is notified rather than licensed, notifications are not published, and there is no public complaint route. The honest first question is which body holds the notifications — ask the Cartagena focal point.

lab_oversight.n: Institutional biosafety committees — the tier that exists even where there is no national register
lab_oversight.d: In most countries contained laboratory work is NOTIFIED rather than licensed and no public register is created — which is why 184 of the country boxes in this file carry no national entry here. A second tier usually does exist. Under the CARTAGENA PROTOCOL, LMOs destined for CONTAINED USE fall under ARTICLE 6 and are EXEMPT FROM THE ADVANCE INFORMED AGREEMENT PROCEDURE — contained work is deliberately outside the route that generates public records — though the handling and labelling duties in Article 18 still apply and a Party MAY REQUIRE NOTIFICATION BEFORE TRANSIT. What national biosafety frameworks create instead is an INSTITUTIONAL BIOSAFETY COMMITTEE inside every organisation doing the work, usually with a named BIOSAFETY OFFICER and PRINCIPAL INVESTIGATOR, CERTIFIED BY AND REPORTING TO the national biosafety committee. Ghana's Biosafety (Management of Biotechnology) Regulations 2007 set this out explicitly, as do India's Rules 1989. THE PRACTICAL POINT: where no national register exists, the record of what a laboratory is doing sits with that institution's own biosafety committee, and the national focal point listed on the Biosafety Clearing-House is who can be asked whether one has been certified.

complain.n: The Cartagena focal point, when nothing else is named
complain.d: Every party to the Cartagena Protocol names a national focal point, and the Clearing-House publishes the current office. Where this map does not name the body that takes a complaint in a country, that office is the one obliged to answer a question about a living modified organism, and it can say which national authority handles the rest. It is the fallback of last resort rather than the right first stop: a focal point is a correspondence address, not an inspectorate.

complain.n: IPPC national plant protection organisation contacts
complain.d: Every IPPC contracting party maintains a national plant protection organisation, and its contact details are published country by country. This is the body that handles a plant pest or a quarantine question, and in most countries it is also the body with inspectors who can actually enter a field. Where a national complaint row here is empty, this is usually the office it would have named. Two limits, both found repeatedly while checking the rows that link here: the record is updated BY THE COUNTRY, so institutional names lag — several checked in this file named ministries and departments that had since merged, been renamed or been replaced — and the convention covers PLANT HEALTH, so a food-on-the-shelf or an animal question belongs elsewhere. Treat the named person and the telephone number as the useful part.

complain.n: Codex Alimentarius contact points
complain.d: Each Codex member names a national contact point for food standards. It does not take complaints itself, but it is the office that knows which national food authority does — useful in a country whose food safety functions are split across several ministries, which is most of them.

complain.n: Consumers International — member organisations by country
complain.d: The worldwide federation of consumer organisations, with a searchable member list by country. Worth knowing as a route because a consumer organisation can do two things a state inspectorate often will not: commission an independent laboratory test on a product it has simply bought, and publish the result. Tunisia's Institut National de la Consommation runs comparative tests on request through accredited laboratories and publishes them; several members elsewhere do the same. Where this map names no national complaint route, a member organisation is often the shortest path to a test somebody else pays for. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

complain.n: Rotterdam Convention — designated national authorities for pesticides
complain.d: Every party to the Rotterdam Convention names a Designated National Authority for pesticides, and the register of them is public. It is worth knowing because it is a different lever from a complaint: the convention operates PRIOR INFORMED CONSENT on listed hazardous chemicals in international trade, so the DNA is the office through which a country can refuse import of a listed pesticide, and through which other countries are told of that refusal. In several states the DNA is the same person as the head of the plant protection organisation — in Nepal it is the chief of the Plant Quarantine and Pesticide Management Centre — so this can also be the fastest way to find who really holds pesticide policy.

decides.d: Authorises releases and publishes the permit and notification files daily, searchable by state, crop and organism. It gives the states a release is authorised in and never the coordinates.
A plant engineered to make its own insecticide is regulated as a pesticide, not as a crop. Registration documents state what the grower is obliged to do around it, which the release permit does not.

complain.n: Your state department of agriculture
complain.d: The state employs the inspectors, can enter a field and issues the penalties. Sending an account to Washington first is the commonest reason it goes nowhere. Quote the permit number. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

complain.n: EPA pesticide incident reporting
complain.d: Drift reports go first to the state lead agency, which inspects and can fine; the EPA holds the national record. Report while residue is still detectable. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

complain.n: OSHA — exposure at work
complain.d: A worker exposed while applying or working around these chemicals can file, anonymously if they choose, and retaliation for filing is separately unlawful.

notice.n: Regulations.gov — file a comment, read the response
notice.d: Where a US comment is submitted and where every other comment on the docket can be read, including the agency's published response to them.

notice.n: USDA APHIS — permits, notifications and petitions
notice.d: The searchable register itself, updated each business day, with the applicant, the crop, the trait and the states covered.

certify.d: Search any certified operation and find its certifier. Certifiers must investigate complaints about operations they certify, and can suspend certification without a court or a regulator.

test.d: Most states run an official seed testing laboratory. Charges are modest, and an enforcement body is likelier to act on a result from a laboratory it already recognises.

records.d: Clinic-by-clinic reporting for every US fertility clinic that files, with cycle counts and outcomes.

Search a licensed facility and read its inspection reports, including the failures found. Rats, mice and birds bred for research are excluded from the Act, so a search returns nothing about most laboratory animals. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

cl_find.n: ClinicalTrials.gov — the registry and the results database
cl_find.d: US law requires most trials to be registered and results posted within a year of completion. Compliance is imperfect and the registry publishes which sponsors have not posted, which is itself worth reading.

decides.d: Decides releases on advice from ACRE, and holds the public register of applications and consents.

complain.n: HSE — GMO contained use
complain.d: Holds notifications for every laboratory in Britain working with engineered organisms and investigates complaints about containment — one of very few places where contained use is reportable by the public at all.

complain.n: Wildlife Incident Investigation Scheme
complain.d: Report a dead animal, pet or bee colony you believe was poisoned by pesticide and the state collects the carcass and pays for the analysis. Results are published and feed into whether an approval is kept. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

complain.n: Food Standards Agency
complain.d: Handles GM food labelling and authorisation complaints, separately from DEFRA on releases. A change a reader should know about before assuming what is registered. The Genetic Technology (Precision Breeding) Act 2023 came into force on 13 November 2025, after its secondary legislation was finalised in May: gene-edited plants that could have arisen naturally or by traditional breeding are taken OUT of GMO regulation in ENGLAND and put through a two-tier route — a marketing notice from Defra, then a food and feed authorisation from the FSA, with Tier 1 a lighter assessment and Tier 2 a bespoke one. The FSA must establish and maintain a PUBLIC FOOD AND FEED REGISTER naming each authorised organism, its reference number, the authorisation-holder, the purpose of the genetic change and a safety summary — which is the thing to search. Note the limits: England only, since the Scottish and Welsh Parliaments withheld legislative consent, and the secondary legislation for ANIMALS has not been laid.

certify.d: Certifies organic production in the UK, and organic standards exclude engineered material outright. A positive test costs the grower the certification and the price premium with it.

notice.n: DEFRA — public register of GM applications
notice.d: Applications and consents, published with a consultation period.

test.d: The UK laboratories that run GMO detection for enforcement and for commercial clients.

legal.d: Makes formal submissions on DEFRA applications and on the Precision Breeding Act's secondary legislation, which is where the English rules on edited crops are actually being written.

records.d: Every licensed UK clinic, with its inspection rating, its success rates and any conditions on its licence. The most detailed public clinic record anywhere, and it exists because the HFEA licenses clinics and embryo research together.

records.n: Home Office — animals in science statistics
records.d: Annual procedure counts by species and severity. It does not name the establishment, which is the gap: you can learn what was done in Britain and not where.

an_inspect.n: Home Office — Animals in Science Regulation Unit
an_inspect.d: Licenses every establishment, project and person, and publishes its enforcement cases in an annual report — including the establishments where compliance failed, without naming them.

cl_find.d: The UK registry, alongside the HRA's published research summaries. Since 2023 UK trial results must also be posted in a public registry.

decides.d: Authorises plants with novel traits and publishes a decision document for each. Canada is one of very few registers listing edited and inserted-gene products side by side, which makes it the best place to check what an organism actually is.
Assesses anything sold as food and publishes the decisions.

complain.n: Provincial ministries and the federal PMRA — drift complaints
complain.d: Both levels take a drift complaint, and the row is worth knowing because the federal route is the documented one. Provinces and territories licence commercial applicators, vendors and growers, issue permits for certain uses, and enforce their own pest control statutes with inspections, violation tickets and prosecutions. But Health Canada's Pest Management Regulatory Agency also inspects and investigates the sale, importation and use of pesticides through regional officers across the country, and it investigates drift, misapplication and misuse directly. Its own compliance report for 2023-24 records 133 agricultural users inspected nationally, of which 43 were carried out in response to complaints involving drift, with dicamba and 2,4-D users targeted specifically because of reported drift. So a complaint made federally is counted and published in a way a provincial one generally is not, and it is worth making in both places rather than choosing.

complain.n: CFIA — food labelling complaints
complain.d: Canada has no mandatory GM labelling, so a complaint here concerns a voluntary non-GM claim that may be false — which is easier to prove than harm. Takes reports about permitted activities and publishes enforcement outcomes.

certify.d: Organic standards exclude engineered material; the CFIA lists accredited certifiers, and a positive test costs the operator the certification. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

notice.d: Where regulatory notices and comment periods are published. CFIA decision documents appear separately on the agency's own site.

legal.d: Publishes the tracking of Canadian approvals that the register itself does not summarise, and is the practical starting point for anyone reading CFIA decisions.

test.d: The agency's own laboratory network runs seed and grain analysis for enforcement.

records.d: The list of institutions certified for animal care; Canada publishes the institutions rather than the procedure counts.

fe_register.d: Regulates donation and prohibits payment for gametes and surrogacy; there is no public clinic-by-clinic outcome register.

an_inspect.n: Canadian Council on Animal Care
an_inspect.d: A peer-review body rather than a regulator: institutions volunteer for assessment and CCAC certification is required to hold federal research funding, which makes a voluntary system effectively compulsory. It names certified institutions and publishes national animal-use data.

lab_oversight.n: Public Health Agency of Canada — licensing
lab_oversight.d: Canada licenses laboratories handling human and terrestrial animal pathogens and maintains a national programme — one of very few countries with a single licensing authority for containment.

cl_report.d: Takes reports from consumers directly and publishes a searchable adverse reaction database.

cl_find.d: Lists authorised trials of drugs and biologics conducted in Canada.

decides.d: Runs the release register and publishes trial locations — in Germany down to the land parcel, which is more than most countries give.

complain.n: Länder authorities
complain.d: The states inspect and enforce; the federal office authorises. A complaint goes to the Land, not to Berlin. Most states run it in three tiers — a ministry coordinating, a regional authority supervising, and the district or city food and veterinary office doing the actual inspection — so the office that will visit a site is the district one. The link is the federal map of the sixteen state ministries.

certify.d: Certifies that livestock were fed without engineered feed — the part of the supply chain consumer labelling law does not touch, and where most of the volume is.
The largest German organic association; its standard excludes engineered material outright.

test.d: Publishes the validated detection methods German official laboratories use, which is what an enforcement body will accept.

notice.d: Germany publishes the location of every release to the land parcel, searchable by map. It is the most precise release register in the world and it is open to anyone.

legal.d: Files objections to EU applications and litigates on release decisions; it brought the German cases on coexistence and liability.

fe_register.d: A voluntary professional register publishing national outcome data. German law prohibits egg donation entirely, which is why German patients travel.

cl_find.d: The German national registry.

an_inspect.n: Länder animal welfare authorities — 26 approving bodies
an_inspect.d: Each Land licenses and inspects animal research, and the fragmentation has been counted: a European Commission report found 26 different authorities competent to approve an animal experiment in Germany and 285 competent for inspections, against a single authority in France, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland. Which body it is varies by state — often a Landesgesundheitsamt or a Regierungspräsidium — and each is advised by its own animal experiments commission under the Animal Welfare Act. There is still no federal register of establishments, and animal numbers are reported centrally only as totals. What IS federal, and is the way in, is the non-technical project summary: since the 2013 revision of the Act every approving authority must send the summary of an approved project to the federal institute within three months, and it is published about a month later, so an approved experiment can be read about in plain language nationally even though the licence sits in a Land. The federal centre for the protection of laboratory animals maintains the list of which authority covers which state.

lab_oversight.d: Contained use is notified to the Land, which approves it, inspects it and maintains the register; the federal register of genetic engineering facilities is public in outline. The Land also approves the facility itself, and for safety levels 3 and 4 must take an opinion from the central biosafety commission first. Release into the environment is not theirs — that is the federal office.

decides.d: Authorises releases; trial locations are published under the EU deliberate release directive.
Assesses risk and publishes its opinions.

complain.n: Services régionaux de l’alimentation (SRAL)
complain.d: The regional service inspects and takes drift complaints. It sits inside the regional agriculture directorate (DRAAF), of which there are 18 — 13 in metropolitan France and 5 overseas — under the authority of the regional prefect. Its inspectors have named statutory powers that matter for a drift complaint: they may inspect products stored on a holding, take copies of the movement records, invoices and delivery notes, and — the useful one — take samples from the tank, from treated plants or from treated soil for analysis. The link goes to the ministry page setting out those powers rather than to one region's office, since which DRAAF applies depends on where the field is.

certify.d: Holds the register of certified operators and the list of certifying bodies.

notice.d: Trial locations are published to the commune under the deliberate release directive.

test.d: The French official seed and variety testing laboratory, and an ENGL member; a result from here is what an enforcement body acts on.

legal.d: The farmers' union that brought the case in which the European Court held that newer mutagenesis techniques are genetically modified organisms — the ruling that governs whether editing is regulated across the EU.

fe_register.d: Licenses every French centre and publishes activity and outcome data centre by centre, alongside the national registers for donation and embryo research.

an_inspect.n: Ministère de la Recherche — autorisations de projet
an_inspect.d: Authorises projects and publishes non-technical summaries of each one, which is the most detailed public account of what French animal research is for. No project using animals may proceed without a specific authorisation from the research ministry, given on the favourable opinion of the ethics committee the establishment belongs to. The non-technical summary is published as soon as the authorisation is issued, must be written in plain language for the general public, and must state the objectives, the expected harms and benefits, the species, the number of animals and how the project meets the 3Rs. Where a non-animal method exists that gives the same level of information, use of animals is not permitted — a written test, not a principle. Note where to look: summaries are on this ministry page up to 2021, and after that on the European Commission's ALURES database.

lab_oversight.n: CEUCO — Comité d’expertise des utilisations confinées d’OGM (ministère de la Recherche)
lab_oversight.d: THE BODY THIS ROW NAMED NO LONGER EXISTS. The Haut Conseil des biotechnologies was dissolved by ordonnance no. 2021-1325 of 13 October 2021, its work split from 1 January 2022: ANSES took risk assessment for deliberate release, the CESE societal questions, the CCNE ethical ones — and contained use, which is what this row is about, went to CEUCO, a committee of experts sitting with the research ministry. The same reform replaced ‘agrément’ with ‘autorisation’ in the environment code, introduced an authorisation for every installation where contained use takes place, and simplified the procedure for class 1 work of null or negligible risk. For clinical trials of medicines made wholly or partly of GMOs the competent authority is now the ANSM, and since 1 January 2022 the trial sponsor declares the contained uses for the whole trial rather than each hospital site doing so.

cl_find.d: The European register. Since 2023 every trial run in the EU must be recorded here, and the protocol and summary results are published rather than only the listing — which is more than most registers give. Trials that began earlier sit in the older EudraCT register.

decides.d: Authorises on advice from the Comisión Nacional de Bioseguridad. Spain grows more engineered maize than the rest of the EU combined, so this is the one member state where cultivation is the live question.

complain.n: Autonomous community agriculture departments
complain.d: Aragón and Catalonia hold most of the area, and the community inspects rather than Madrid: Article 4 of Ley 9/2003 gives the autonomous communities the authorisation of confined use and of voluntary release for any purpose other than marketing, together with surveillance, control and the imposition of sanctions. The State keeps marketing authorisations, import and export, and anything intended for human or veterinary medicines. The point of entry is dated: under Article 25.4 of Real Decreto 178/2004 the competent authority must put the summary of a voluntary release application out to public information for 30 days, preferably before the 90-day limit for answering it expires, and the comments received must be taken into account in the report. Several communities have passed their own OMG decrees naming their competent bodies and, in Andalucía's case, creating a standing control committee.

certify.d: One of the largest organic certifiers in Spain.

notice.d: The central register of authorised organisms and cultivation notifications, which matters here because Spain is the one EU state growing at scale.

test.d: The Spanish official food and agriculture laboratory, which runs GMO detection for enforcement.

legal.d: Publishes the Spanish cultivation and contamination data that the official register does not summarise.

The smallholder farmers' union, which represents growers on coexistence in the EU's largest engineered maize area. Founded 1977 as Spain's first state-level professional farmers' organisation, it serves more than 150,000 farmers through some 220 offices and a permanent delegation in Brussels. The agriculture ministry recognises it as the most representative farmers' organisation, which puts it on the Comité Asesor Agrario, and it belongs to both COPA-COGECA and the European Coordination Via Campesina. A grower who wants the coexistence rules argued sits inside the body the ministry has to consult.

fe_register.n: Registro Nacional de Actividad — Reproducción Asistida
fe_register.d: Spain runs the largest assisted reproduction sector in Europe and publishes national activity data by centre. Egg donation is anonymous and paid here, which is why much of Europe's donor treatment happens in Spain.

cl_find.d: The European register. Since 2023 every trial run in the EU must be recorded here, and the protocol and summary results are published rather than only the listing — which is more than most registers give. Trials that began earlier sit in the older EudraCT register.

decides.n: Office of the Gene Technology Regulator
decides.d: Licenses every dealing with an engineered organism, and publishes the licence, the risk assessment and the approved field sites — which few regulators do before a decision.

complain.n: State and territory governments — statutory consultees
complain.d: On a licence application for environmental release the Gene Technology Regulator must consult the states and territories on the risk assessment and risk management plan, alongside relevant local councils, other Commonwealth agencies and the public — a statutory point of entry before the decision is made rather than after. Monitoring, compliance and enforcement under the Gene Technology Act 2000 sit with the Regulator, not with the state, so a breach is reported federally; the OGTR compliance line on this card is that route. The scheme is cooperative, underpinned by the Intergovernmental Gene Technology Agreement and corresponding state and territory legislation, and the states also sit on the Gene Technology Standing Committee and the Legislative and Governance Forum that oversee it.

complain.n: OGTR compliance
complain.d: Inspects licensed sites and publishes monitoring reports.

complain.n: FSANZ / state health departments
complain.d: Food Standards Australia New Zealand sets the labelling rules; state health departments enforce them and take complaints.

certify.d: Certifies to a standard excluding engineered material.

notice.d: Each application, its risk assessment plan and the proposed field sites, open for comment for around thirty days.

test.d: Australia's reference laboratory for GMO analysis, and the source of the methods used in enforcement.

legal.d: Files submissions on OGTR applications and publishes the analysis of them.

records.d: The Australian and New Zealand trial register, which feeds the WHO platform.

fe_register.d: Australian and New Zealand clinics report to a common registry; Victoria additionally maintains donor registers giving donor-conceived people a legal right to identifying information, applied retroactively.

cl_find.d: The Australian and New Zealand registry, covering trials at sites in both countries.

an_inspect.n: NHMRC Code / state animal ethics committees
an_inspect.d: Institutions run animal ethics committees under the national code, and each committee must include a person independent of the institution and one nominated by an animal welfare organisation.

lab_oversight.d: The OGTR certifies physical containment facilities and publishes the list, which is unusual: most countries hold notifications without publishing them.

cl_report.n: TGA — Database of Adverse Event Notifications
cl_report.d: Consumers can report directly and the database is public and searchable.

decides.d: Decides releases under the environment ministry and publishes its meeting minutes, which is where an approval first becomes visible. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

complain.n: SBCC and District Level Committees — the sub-national monitoring tier under Rules 1989 (India)
complain.d: Have authority over releases in their state and are closer than Delhi. THIS IS THE TIER TO USE, and it is the one most readers do not know exists. Under the RULES 1989 made under the ENVIRONMENT (PROTECTION) ACT 1986, six competent authorities govern GMOs; RDAC is advisory, IBSC/RCGM/GEAC regulate and approve, and THE STATE BIOTECHNOLOGY COORDINATION COMMITTEE AND THE DISTRICT LEVEL COMMITTEE MONITOR AND INSPECT AT STATE AND DISTRICT LEVEL. The DLC's stated duties are concrete: VISIT INSTALLATIONS engaged in activity involving GE organisms, FORMULATE AN INFORMATION CHART, IDENTIFY THE HAZARDS AND RISKS OF EACH INSTALLATION, coordinate for emergencies, and PREPARE AN OFF-SITE EMERGENCY PLAN FOR FIELD TRIALS — then REPORT REGULARLY TO THE SBCC AND GEAC. The SBCC has powers to INSPECT, INVESTIGATE AND TAKE PUNITIVE ACTION under the Environment (Protection) Act for violations. So a district committee should hold a hazard chart and an emergency plan for any trial in its district, and both are things a resident can ask for. Two candid points: the BRAI Bill for a unified regulator LAPSED IN 2014 and has not been reintroduced; and enforcement is weak — HT-Bt cotton is illegal but widely grown.

complain.n: FSSAI
complain.d: The food safety authority handles labelling and imported food complaints, separately from GEAC on releases.

certify.d: The national organic programme and its accredited certifiers. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

notice.d: Approvals appear first in the minutes of the committee meeting that granted them, which is the earliest a decision becomes visible. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

test.d: India accredits laboratories for GMO detection; an accredited result is what a regulator or a buyer will act on.

legal.d: Tracks GEAC decisions, files objections and publishes the minutes analysis that most Indian reporting on this subject draws from.

records.d: India's register of licensed ART clinics and banks, created under the 2021 Act after decades without one. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

fe_register.d: India registers every ART clinic and bank under the 2021 Acts, after decades in which the sector was almost entirely unregulated and a large commercial surrogacy market operated. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

cl_find.d: Registration is mandatory before enrolment; the registry publishes the protocol summary.

an_inspect.n: CPCSEA — Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals
an_inspect.d: Registers establishments and approves projects; the register of recognised establishments is public. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

lab_oversight.d: Every institution doing recombinant work must have a biosafety committee reporting to the national review committee, whose minutes are published. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

cl_report.d: Patients may report directly, including by a toll-free line.

decides.d: Issues the technical opinion that authorises a release, and publishes approvals.

complain.n: IBAMA
complain.d: Handles environmental damage and enforcement.

complain.n: Órgãos Estaduais de Meio Ambiente (OEMAs) — the state tier of SISNAMA (Brasil)
complain.d: Handle environmental damage locally, and are usually quicker to inspect than the federal body. THE POINT WORTH KNOWING: under LEI 6.938/81 the state environment bodies are ÓRGÃOS SECCIONAIS of SISNAMA, and their powers include CREATING COMPLEMENTARY LAWS AND NORMS THAT MAY BE MORE RESTRICTIVE THAN THE FEDERAL ONES, alongside licensing and inspection of works affecting two or more municipalities. The same applies downward to municipal bodies. So a stricter rule can be made at state or municipal level — the same route Japan's prefectures took. INVESTIGATION OF DENÚNCIAS is a function of IBAMA AND THE LOCAL ENVIRONMENT BODIES, not of CONAMA, which is normative only — so a complaint goes to the state or municipal agency, or IBAMA, and a request for a NEW RULE goes to CONAMA, where the seats include the productive sector AND CIVIL SOCIETY, environmental professionals and COMMUNITY LEADERS. There are 27 state bodies, one per federal unit, each named differently — the Ministry of Environment publishes the current list. Lei Complementar 140/2011 created NATIONAL AND STATE TRIPARTITE COMMISSIONS to settle which level licenses what.

complain.n: ANVISA
complain.d: Handles food safety and labelling, separately from IBAMA on environmental damage.

notice.d: Where approvals and hearings are announced.
The opinion that authorises a release is published in full, with the reasoning.

certify.d: Holds the register of certifying bodies.

test.d: The official laboratory network for seed and grain analysis.

legal.d: A public interest law organisation that has litigated on seed law, pesticide regulation and CTNBio decisions.

records.d: Annual reporting from every Brazilian embryo bank, published as a public report.

fe_register.d: Brazilian clinics must report embryo numbers and outcomes annually to ANVISA, which publishes the national report.

fe_register.n: REDLARA — Red Latinoamericana de Reproducción Asistida
fe_register.d: The Latin American assisted reproduction network: it accredits clinics across the region, runs the continental registry of treatment cycles and outcomes, and publishes an annual report. Across most of Latin America there is no statutory fertility regulator at all, so an accreditation held or withdrawn here is the only external check on a clinic — and the accredited list is public. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

cl_find.n: ReBEC — Registro Brasileiro de Ensaios Clínicos
cl_find.d: The Brazilian registry, published in Portuguese and English.

an_inspect.n: CONCEA — Conselho Nacional de Controle de Experimentação Animal
an_inspect.d: Accredits institutions and publishes the list; Brazil requires an institutional ethics committee for any animal research.

lab_oversight.d: Institutions require a Certificate of Quality in Biosafety before any contained work, and the list of certified institutions is published.

cl_report.d: Takes reports from patients and health professionals.

decides.d: Advises on releases and publishes its advice.
The ministry authorises.

complain.n: NVWA
complain.d: Inspects and takes complaints on food and plant safety.

certify.d: The Dutch organic certifier; tell them if certified land is affected. It is the body the Dutch state charges with supervising the organic market, not a competing certifier — and it is also the foundation that entered the 2002 joint venture which became Control Union Certifications, the commercial certifier now operating in 70 to 80 countries. The supervisor of a national organic market helped found a global certification business.

notice.d: Applications and permits are published with a consultation period.

test.d: The Dutch seed inspection service, which tests lots for engineered content.

legal.d: The Dutch organic chain organisation, which files on coexistence and contamination questions because its members carry the loss.

fe_register.d: The Dutch donor data foundation holds donor records and gives donor-conceived people access at 16 — the Netherlands abolished anonymous donation in 2004.

cl_find.n: Overview of Medical Research in the Netherlands (OMON)
cl_find.d: The national register, run by the Central Committee on Research Involving Human Subjects. It was the Nederlands Trial Register, then the Landelijk Trial Register from December 2022, and has been OMON since March 2024 — a reader following an older citation will not find the name. It now carries the studies from the former National Trial Register and those reviewed by the committee and published on ToetsingOnline, so one search covers both, and it holds results as well as protocols. WHO accepted it as an official data provider, which is what makes a study registered here count as prospectively registered for journal editors.

an_inspect.n: Centrale Commissie Dierproeven
an_inspect.d: Licenses projects and publishes its decisions and the non-technical summaries.

lab_oversight.d: Holds the contained use permits and publishes decisions, including for clinical gene therapy sites.

decides.d: Authorises releases.
Handles cultivation and coexistence.

complain.n: Landbrugsstyrelsen — coexistence
complain.d: Also administers the compensation fund that pays a grower whose crop loses its non-GM or organic status because of a neighbour, financed by a levy on engineered cultivation. Very few countries have one.

certify.d: The Danish organic association.

notice.d: Decisions and applications are published with a consultation period.

test.d: Runs the official GMO analysis, and Denmark tests seed lots systematically rather than only on complaint.

legal.d: Represents organic growers in the coexistence rules and the compensation fund that pays when a crop loses its status.

fe_register.d: Denmark hosts the largest sperm banks in the world, exporting to more than 100 countries, which makes its donor rules consequential far beyond Denmark. Reporting is compulsory: every public and private clinic, tissue centre and specialist gynaecologist holding a tissue-centre permit must report each IVF and IUI treatment to the health data authority, and the return was designed with the Danish Fertility Society. The register covers treatment courses from 1994 onward and includes DANISH AND FOREIGN women alike, which is what makes it usable for a map like this one — in 2015, 34% of IVF/ICSI at private clinics and 41% of private insemination activity was performed on women from abroad. Preimplantation genetic testing is reported on the same footing as infertility treatment. In 2023 around 11% of children born in Denmark, one in nine, came after assisted reproduction; the year's 37,000 treatments were down from 39,800.

cl_find.d: The European register. Since 2023 every trial run in the EU must be recorded here, and the protocol and summary results are published rather than only the listing — which is more than most registers give. Trials that began earlier sit in the older EudraCT register.

decides.d: Authorises agricultural releases.
Shares responsibility for environmental release.

notice.d: Japan's national node, which publishes approvals in English as well as Japanese. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

certify.d: The Japanese organic standard and its registered certifiers. The standard is the government's; the certifying is done by registered certifying bodies, Japanese and foreign, which the agriculture ministry lists. A reader checking a JAS mark should look for the certifier's name beside it and confirm that body is still registered, rather than treating the mark alone as the check.

complain.n: Prefectural ordinances and guidelines on open-air GM cultivation (Japan)
complain.d: Japan's prefectures inspect and enforce; the ministries authorise. A complaint about a site or a crop goes to the prefecture. THIS IS THE LAYER TO USE IN JAPAN. At least TEN OF THE 47 PREFECTURES have their own ordinances or guidelines on OPEN-AIR CULTIVATION of GM plants, explicitly to prevent cross-pollination with related crops in the region — among them HOKKAIDO, NIIGATA, CHIBA, KYOTO, IBARAKI, SHIGA, IWATE, HYOGO and TOKYO, with municipal guidelines spreading too (Tsukuba). THE NUMBERS ARE THE POINT: Hokkaido sets minimum isolation distances of AT LEAST 300 METRES FOR RICE, 1.2 KM FOR CORN AND 2 KM FOR SUGAR BEET — about TWICE the distances the agriculture ministry sets for its own research entities. Niigata's ordinance OBLIGES FARMERS TO OBTAIN PERMISSION to grow GM crops and requires research institutes to FILE REPORTS on open-air experiments, with penalties for violation. For anyone seeking a workable separation distance or a local permission regime, these are drafted, adopted and in force. Nationally, MAFF, the Ministry of the Environment and NIES run an ANNUAL SURVEY of escaped imported GM canola and soy AROUND MAJOR PORTS AND ROADS under the Cartagena Act — published monitoring of volunteer GM plants, reported to the Cartagena Protocol meetings.

complain.n: Consumer Affairs Agency (消費者庁) — food labelling
complain.d: Japan requires labelling of specified engineered foods, and this is the body that takes a complaint about one. Japan is a large importer and a very small grower, so labelling is where most disputes here actually arise. Japan labels specified engineered foods; this is where a complaint about one goes. What is actually labelled, and what changed on 1 April 2023: mandatory GM labelling covers nine agricultural products — soybeans, corn, potatoes, rapeseed, cottonseed, alfalfa, sugar beet, papaya and mustard greens — and processed foods made from them WHERE THE MODIFIED DNA OR PROTEIN IS STILL DETECTABLE after processing, monitored across 33 product categories. The voluntary side tightened: previously a product with up to 5% unintentional presence could be called 'not genetically modified'; since April 2023 only 'not detected' may carry that claim, and 5% or less is labelled as separately managed in production and sale.
