High-oleic soybeans were dropped from mandatory labelling because the trait can be produced by conventional breeding — the same detectability logic that puts gene-edited products outside labelling in several countries on this map.

legal.d: Has run the labelling campaigns that produced Japan's disclosure rules, which is where most Japanese disputes on this subject arise.

test.d: The national agriculture research organisation runs GMO detection and publishes the official methods.

records.d: The obstetrics society registers and publishes ART facilities; Japan regulates this through professional self-governance rather than statute.

fe_register.n: Japan Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology registry
fe_register.d: Clinics register with the professional society rather than a statutory regulator, and the society publishes national totals. Japan performs more IVF cycles than any other country.

cl_find.d: Japan's registry network, and the route to trials not listed elsewhere.

an_inspect.n: Science Council of Japan — institutional guidelines
an_inspect.d: Animal research is self-regulated through institutional committees under national guidelines; there is no licensing authority and no register of establishments. The structure is deliberate and stated as such. After the education and health ministries each issued basic policies on animal experiments in institutions, they asked the Science Council of Japan to write model guidelines each institution could build its own rules from — published 2006. The Council's own text argues that self-management outside legislation is sometimes called the North American model and that Japan should build a system rooted in its own ground. So there is no licence to inspect against: oversight is the institution's own committee, working to a guideline. External verification exists but is run by a scientific society, not a regulator.

lab_oversight.d: Contained use is approved by the education and science ministry; approvals are not published facility by facility. Japan's Cartagena Law splits use in two. Type 1 use is use WITHOUT containment measures, and requires the user to set out a usage plan and obtain ministerial approval in advance. Type 2 use is use WITH containment — laboratory work, storage and transport — and here containment must be applied to every recombinant experiment regardless of level; where the ministerial ordinance does not prescribe the measures for a given case, the minister's confirmation must be obtained each time. Six ministries share the implementing rules. Organisms produced by genome editing are assessed against whether they fall within the law's definition of a living modified organism, which is where the boundary is drawn.

cl_report.d: Patients may report directly through a dedicated route.

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs
decides.d: Issues biosafety certificates and publishes lists of approved events. China approved its first domestic maize and soy for planting in 2023 after more than a decade in which food-crop approvals were effectively frozen, so the list is worth checking rather than assumed.

complain.n: Provincial agricultural administrative departments
complain.d: The province is not only the enforcement level, it holds approval power: under the GMO Regulations anyone producing or processing agricultural GMOs needs approval from the Ministry of Agriculture OR a provincial agricultural administrative department. Provinces have acted. Hainan's department checked Sanya, Lingshui and Ledong over five days in December 2013, examined 107 crop samples and destroyed nine unauthorised maize and cotton trials; roughly 73 hectares of unapproved maize were destroyed nationally across several areas in 2015; after state television found unapproved rice being grown at Wuhan the ministry ordered the local government to investigate and about eleven mu were burned. The limits show in the same record. Testing in Liaoning found 93 per cent of maize sampled from fields carried engineered material after a decade of unregulated planting, and researchers there expected the provincial government to play the finding down. And when Heilongjiang, which grows a tenth of the country's staple crops, wrote a ban on planting engineered maize, rice and soya into its provincial food safety regulations in 2016, it was the first provincial ban in China; central officials pressed it to fall into line and it lifted the ban six months later, revising the regulations to prohibit only illegal production and processing of edible engineered produce. A province can act against a planting; a province cannot hold a line the centre has not drawn.

complain.n: SAMR — State Administration for Market Regulation (国家市场监督管理总局)
complain.d: Handles food labelling enforcement; China requires labelling of approved engineered ingredients. Established 2018, and the primary authority for food safety supervision, quality control, and the regulation of labelling, packaging and advertising. But the GMO decision is not made here: the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs regulates agricultural GMOs and runs their safety evaluation, issuing processing licences and the two kinds of safety certificate. Seven certificates exist for domestic production — insect-resistant cotton, virus-resistant papaya, insect-resistant rice, high-phytase corn, colour-altered petunia, disease-resistant sweet pepper, and a disease-resistant maturity-delayed tomato — of which only cotton and papaya are commercially grown; and import certificates cover soybean, corn, rapeseed, cotton and sugar beet, approved for processing as raw material rather than for planting. A labelling complaint comes to SAMR; a question about what may be grown goes to the ministry.

certify.d: The national organic standard excludes engineered material; certification is issued through accredited bodies under CNCA. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

notice.d: Biosafety certificates are published as periodic lists of approved events. There is no general public comment stage.

test.d: Testing is done through provincially designated centres; strip tests are widely used in the grain trade.

records.d: The national list of licensed fertility institutions, published province by province.

fe_register.n: National Health Commission — approved ART institutions
fe_register.d: The NHC publishes the list of institutions permitted to perform assisted reproduction; anything not on it is operating unlawfully, which is the useful thing the list does.

cl_find.d: China's national registry. Many Chinese trials appear here and not in the US registry, which is why a search of one is not a search of the field.

an_inspect.n: Provincial departments of science and technology — laboratory animal licences
an_inspect.d: A facility needs a laboratory animal licence and it is issued by the provincial department of science and technology, not by a national body: under the State Council statute of 1988 and the ministry regulations that followed, oversight sits with the national science and technology ministry, the provincial departments, and each institution's own animal care and use committee. Provinces implemented it through their own laws from 1996 onwards, beginning with Beijing, and those provincial rules cover licensing for both production and use of laboratory animals as well as quarantine, import and export, animal quality, staff training and biosafety. The consequence for anyone counting is that the licence lists are provincial rather than national: a total for China has to be assembled province by province, and what is published varies — Guangdong's monitoring institute publishes its own licence figures and rankings, most provinces publish nothing comparable. There is no national register of licensed facilities to read instead. Oversight rests with the Ministry of Science and Technology and, in practice, with provincial bureaus of science and technology, under the 1988 Regulations for the Administration of Affairs Concerning Experimental Animals. Most provinces, municipalities and autonomous regions have issued their own regulations on top, so the applicable rule depends on where the facility is. The system rests on licensing plus third-party certification, with institutions running their own management committees and ethical review; one survey put national laboratory animal licences at 1,448 as of 2017, with 89% of responding units having established a management committee. The link goes to a published account of the structure because there is no single national register a reader can consult.

lab_oversight.n: Ministry of Science and Technology — pathogen laboratory approval
lab_oversight.d: High-containment laboratories require national approval; the approval lists are not comprehensively published.

cl_report.d: Runs the national reporting system through provincial centres.

decides.d: Authorises on advice from the interministerial commission. Italy has used the EU cultivation opt-out, so the live questions here concern imports and feed rather than fields.

complain.n: Regional phytosanitary services
complain.d: The regions inspect and take drift complaints. One caution about this source: the IPPC contact record is updated by the country itself and can lag — records checked here carried ministry names that had since changed. The named person, address and telephone are the useful part; treat the institutional name as a starting point and check it against the ministry's own site.

certify.d: The Italian organic association, and the body ICEA grew out of — so the association that represents organic growers and the certifier that inspects them share an origin. That is common in this sector and rarely stated: the movement built the certifier before the law required one.

certify.n: ICEA — Istituto per la Certificazione Etica e Ambientale
certify.d: A non-profit consortium of institutions, associations, companies and civil society organisations, with around 20 offices in Italy and abroad and some 17,000 certified companies. It grew out of AIAB, the Italian organic association — which is the row above this one, so the association and the certifier in this country are not separate lineages. The Greek certifier DIO is a shareholder in ICEA and a founder of the Croatian AgriBioCert, which DIO also part-owns: three national certifiers in this category, in three countries, with ownership running between them.

notice.d: Authorisations and notices appear in the official gazette.

test.d: The national agricultural research council runs the official testing.

legal.d: Publishes legal and scientific analysis of Italian and EU biosafety decisions. A research and communication body on biotechnology based in Rome, which publishes legal and scientific analysis rather than campaigning. In a category otherwise made of farmers' unions and seed networks, it is the one that produces documents a lawyer can cite. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

fe_register.d: The national institute of health holds the register and publishes centre-level activity.

cl_find.d: The European register. Since 2023 every trial run in the EU must be recorded here, and the protocol and summary results are published rather than only the listing — which is more than most registers give. Trials that began earlier sit in the older EudraCT register.

decides.d: Authorises releases. National law prohibits the cultivation of engineered crops, so a release here would be a contained or research matter rather than a field.

complain.n: PIORiN — plant health and seed inspection
complain.d: Inspects seed and plant health, and is the body that would act on unauthorised planting.

certify.d: A Polish certification body operating since 1993, accredited by the Polish Accreditation Centre and authorised by the agriculture ministry — the first to be so authorised, which is why it holds identifier PL-EKO-01. Poland has fourteen accredited organic certifiers, so this is one route rather than the route. Two things a grower should know: certification is the condition of selling anything labelled organic at all, and there is an appeal — a producer may appeal any certification decision within 14 days, and must file separately within 7 days to contest a laboratory analysis. That second deadline is the shorter one and the easier to miss.

notice.d: The national register; cultivation is prohibited, so entries here concern contained use and imports.

legal.d: The coalition behind the national cultivation prohibition. Its route has been the legislature and then the EU institutions: it petitioned the Senate marshal in 2014 to reject a GMO bill outright, arguing the amendment was inconsistent with the constitution and with Poland's own 2009 framework position, and in September 2025 it complained to the European Ombudsman over the new genomic techniques regulation, asking for the legislative procedure to be suspended. It is a coalition and has lost members over method — the Social Ecological Institute left in 2013 citing irreconcilable differences on how it works.

Litigated and campaigned on the national cultivation prohibition. Based in Łódź, it ran the labelling campaign “Wolne od GMO? Chcę wiedzieć!” — GM-free? I want to know — and its president belongs to the Polish Legislation Society. That combination is rare in this category: an organisation that campaigns on the right to know what is in food and also has someone inside the professional body for drafting law.

test.n: IHAR — Plant Breeding and Acclimatization Institute
test.d: Runs the official GMO detection in a country that prohibits cultivation, so testing here is mostly of imports.

cl_find.d: The European register. Since 2023 every trial run in the EU must be recorded here, and the protocol and summary results are published rather than only the listing — which is more than most registers give. Trials that began earlier sit in the older EudraCT register.

decides.d: Authorises releases of engineered plants and publishes the applications.

complain.n: County administrative boards
complain.d: The county board inspects locally and takes complaints.

certify.d: The Swedish organic standard, stricter than the EU organic baseline and dominant in Swedish retail.

notice.d: Field trial applications and locations are published.

test.d: Runs GMO detection for enforcement.

legal.d: Files on Swedish and EU applications and publishes the analysis.

fe_register.d: Sweden was the first country in the world to abolish anonymous donation, in 1985; the board holds the register.

an_inspect.n: Jordbruksverket — animal experiment ethics committees
an_inspect.d: Regional ethics committees approve projects and include lay members appointed by local authorities — an unusual degree of public membership.

cl_find.d: The European register. Since 2023 every trial run in the EU must be recorded here, and the protocol and summary results are published rather than only the listing — which is more than most registers give. Trials that began earlier sit in the older EudraCT register.

decides.d: Authorises releases. Austria invoked the safeguard clause against an EU-approved variety and defended it for years — that fight is why the EU cultivation opt-out exists at all.

complain.n: Länder authorities — Gentechnik-Vorsorgegesetze
complain.d: Every one of the nine states has a Gentechnik-Vorsorgegesetz in force, or regulates planting under other state law, and these are the instrument the row refers to. They work in one of two ways: either an intended planting needs the state authority's permission, or it must be notified and the authority may forbid it. The stated purpose in both cases is coexistence — protecting organic and GM-free growing from contamination — rather than a prohibition in principle, which is how the state laws sit alongside EU rules. Cultivation measures are a state competence; the federal level splits GM work across three ministries, with the social affairs and consumer protection ministry leading and holding release and marketing applications. Upper Austria was one of the two founding regions of the European Network of GMO-free Regions in November 2003. Worth knowing for what comes next: the ministry's own analysis is that under the proposed EU regulation on new genomic techniques a blanket cultivation ban would no longer be possible and national measures would be limited to compulsory coexistence rules for category 2 plants — which in Austria would fall to these same state authorities.

certify.d: The largest Austrian certifier; the organic share of farmland here is among the highest in Europe, which is itself a coexistence constraint.

test.d: The Austrian agency for health and food safety runs GMO analysis and publishes its methods.

legal.d: The organisation behind Austria's long opposition and the safeguard clause fight that produced the EU cultivation opt-out.

cl_find.d: The European register. Since 2023 every trial run in the EU must be recorded here, and the protocol and summary results are published rather than only the listing — which is more than most registers give. Trials that began earlier sit in the older EudraCT register.

decides.d: Authorises releases. Switzerland has extended its moratorium on growing engineered crops repeatedly since 2005 while continuing to import engineered feed and to host some of the largest agricultural biotechnology companies in the world.

complain.n: BAFU — Kontaktstelle Biotechnologie des Bundes
complain.d: The federal biotechnology contact point, and the address for this subject. Gene technology is one of the few fields the Confederation executes directly instead of leaving execution to the cantons, so unlike most Swiss environmental matters a complaint does not start at cantonal level. Release trials are authorised by the Federal Office for the Environment's biotechnology section, which also supervises them; cantonal specialist offices are consulted on an application and sit on the monitoring group, but they are not where it is decided. Questions where the risk is to people go to the Federal Office of Public Health instead, and agriculture-relevant gene technology law is overseen by the Federal Office for Agriculture. Cultivation of GMOs is prohibited in Switzerland under a moratorium that also covers products of new genomic techniques.

complain.n: Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office
complain.d: Handles labelling; Switzerland labels engineered food while prohibiting cultivation.

certify.d: The Swiss organic label; its standard excludes engineered material and it covers most Swiss organic production.

notice.d: Applications and decisions are published, with the moratorium on cultivation extended repeatedly since 2005.

test.d: The federal agricultural research station runs detection and method development.

legal.d: The alliance behind the repeated extensions of the Swiss cultivation moratorium.

an_inspect.n: Cantonal veterinary offices / animal experimentation database
an_inspect.d: Switzerland publishes a searchable database of authorised animal experiments, by canton, purpose and severity — more detail than most countries release.

cl_report.d: The national centre for adverse event reporting, part of the WHO programme. Reports from patients are accepted in most member countries.

cl_find.d: Publishes every trial authorised in Switzerland, in four languages.

decides.d: Authorises under the Gene Technology Act, which is unusual in requiring an applicant to show benefit to the community and sustainability, not only safety.

complain.n: Mattilsynet — Norwegian Food Safety Authority
complain.d: Inspects food, feed and aquaculture, and takes reports. Handles food and feed labelling complaints. Established 1 January 2004 by merging four state agencies — the State Animal Health Authority, the State Food Control Authority, the State Agricultural Inspection Service and the seafood control division of the Directorate of Fisheries — together with municipal food control. So citations to any of those predate it. It answers to three ministries at once: Agriculture and Food, Health and Care Services, and Trade, Industry and Fisheries. It also carries out the functions of Norway's national plant protection organisation, including phytosanitary certificates. A concrete precedent for this map: in 2013 Mattilsynet found GM CORN ILLEGALLY IMPORTED AND DISTRIBUTED AS POPCORN, having previously stopped the sale of popcorn containing GMOs — so it does act on unauthorised engineered material in food. Deliberate release itself is governed by the Gene Technology Act of 2 April 1993 and sits with the environment authorities.

certify.d: The Norwegian organic certifier.

notice.d: Consultations are published, and Norwegian law uniquely requires an applicant to show community benefit and sustainability.

test.d: Runs GMO analysis for the food authority.

legal.d: A statutory public body that publishes independent assessments and takes public input — unusual in being official and yet genuinely open. An independent statutory body under the health and care ministry, its members appointed by the government and serving fixed terms; its mandate is to assess the social and ethical consequences of modern biotechnology and to inform and create public debate, and it issues formal opinions and consultation responses. Two things for a reader: it ADVISES, it does not decide — no permit or objection is filed here — and it is small, running about 7 full-time equivalents. It was tasked with evaluating the Biotechnology Act through 2024 into 2025, and responded to the official inquiry on the Gene Technology Act, so its published opinions are where Norwegian reasoning on gene technology is set out at length.

Norway's biosafety research centre, which produced much of the independent risk assessment literature cited internationally and trained regulators from developing countries. An independent foundation sited alongside the Arctic University of Norway, it merged into NORCE, one of Norway's largest independent research institutes, as a research group on gene technology, environment and society. A national biosafety centre becoming a department inside a general research institute is worth noting: the standing capacity to produce independent risk assessment stops being an institution with its own name.

cl_report.d: The national centre for adverse event reporting, part of the WHO programme. Reports from patients are accepted in most member countries.

cl_find.d: Regional ethics committees publish their approvals, which is the route to a Norwegian trial not otherwise registered. The link goes to the WHO ICTRP search portal, which aggregates this registry rather than being it; the national registry's own site has not been verified here.

decides.d: Decides applications under the HSNO Act and publishes them with a public submission period. New Zealand has permitted almost no outdoor release, so most of the register is contained laboratory work.

complain.n: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) — Manatū Ahu Matua
complain.d: Handles biosecurity and unauthorised organisms, including material arriving in imported seed. Formed 30 April 2012 by merging the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, the Ministry of Fisheries and the New Zealand Food Safety Authority, so citations to MAF or the NZFSA predate it. The useful part is that the business unit matters more than the ministry: complaints go to one of Agriculture and Investment Services, Biosecurity New Zealand, Fisheries New Zealand, New Zealand Food Safety, or Te Uru Rākau. NZFS is the controlling authority for food imports and exports and runs at foodsafety.govt.nz. MPI also publishes a route for reporting serious wrongdoing in an industry it regulates, which is a different thing from a consumer complaint and rarely named elsewhere in this file.

complain.n: New Zealand Food Safety
complain.d: Handles labelling complaints under the joint FSANZ standard.

certify.d: The main New Zealand organic certifier.

notice.d: Every application under the HSNO Act, with a public submission period; anyone may make a submission and be heard.

legal.d: Makes submissions on EPA applications, which in New Zealand carries a right to be heard rather than only to write in.

test.d: The primary industries ministry runs border and seed testing.

an_inspect.n: MPI — animal welfare and NAEAC
an_inspect.d: Publishes annual statistics of animal use by species, purpose and impact grade, and lists code-holding institutions.

cl_report.n: CARM — Centre for Adverse Reactions Monitoring
cl_report.d: Takes consumer reports; New Zealand's centre is run by a university rather than the regulator.

decides.n: Department of Agriculture — GMO Act registrar
decides.d: Authorises releases under the GMO Act. South Africa is the only country in Africa where engineered maize is a staple eaten directly rather than fed to animals, which makes the food-crop question live rather than hypothetical here. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

complain.n: Registrar and inspectors under the GMO Act (national)
complain.d: Compliance for engineered organisms is national, not provincial. The GMO Act is administered by a Registrar seated in the national agriculture department, and it is inspectors appointed under the Act who check that permit conditions are being kept to; complaints under the agricultural inputs legislation are likewise addressed to the Registrar rather than to a province. Provinces run their own agriculture departments and matter for extension and land use, but a reader with an unapproved planting who starts at provincial level starts at the wrong door. The real weakness is stated by the national inspection service itself: it does not have permanent officials in every province, which is why it asks industry and farming communities to report through a structured complaints procedure rather than relying on its own presence. Two name changes sit on top of this. The department was the Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries until 2019, then the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development, and after the 2024 general election that department was split again into a Department of Agriculture and a Department of Land Reform and Rural Development — so DALRRD-era documents, forms and e-mail addresses name a body that no longer exists in that form.

complain.n: Department of Health — food control
complain.d: South Africa requires GM labelling; food control handles those complaints, separately from the GMO Act registrar.

certify.n: SAOSO — South African Organic Sector Organisation
certify.d: Holds the national organic standard. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

notice.d: GMO Act decisions and applications are notified in the Gazette, which is the statutory venue. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

test.d: Runs GMO detection for the regulator and for commercial clients.
The national accreditation system lists laboratories whose GMO results are accepted for enforcement.

legal.d: Researches and litigates on seed law, biosafety and corporate concentration across southern and eastern Africa, and files formal objections to South African applications — the only organisation in the region doing that consistently.

fe_register.n: Regulations Relating to Artificial Fertilisation of Persons (GN R175, GG 35099, 2 March 2012)
fe_register.d: Licenses centres under the National Health Act; South Africa permits altruistic surrogacy with court approval. The regulations under section 68 of the National Health Act are the instrument, and they are readable in the gazette. Three provisions matter here. A cap of SIX children born alive from one donor's gametes, after which the clinic must note it in the donor file, report it to the Central Data Bank, and destroy that donor's remaining gametes. A prohibition on any preimplantation or prenatal test used to select the sex of a child except for medical reasons — which makes non-medical use of PGT-A or NIPT for sex selection unlawful, and was challenged as unconstitutional in Surrogacy Advisory Group v Minister of Health. And the register itself: the South African Law Reform Commission records that the STATE HAS FAILED TO SET UP AND MAINTAIN the database the regulations require, and that reporting to the voluntary SARA register by individual centres is exactly that — voluntary. A cap that depends on a data bank nobody built is a cap on paper.

The regional federation, which sets standards and runs training where no statutory regulator exists. Most African fertility care is private and unlicensed, so a professional body is often the only body holding standards. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

fe_register.n: ANARA — African Network and Registry for ART
fe_register.d: Collects cycle-by-cycle data from the ART centres that choose to submit it and publishes procedure counts, pregnancy and delivery rates and centre numbers by country. Reporting is voluntary and centre-led, so a country showing nothing may have clinics that have never submitted rather than no clinics. It does not license a clinic, inspect one, or take a complaint about one. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

cl_find.n: South African National Clinical Trial Register
cl_find.d: Registration is required for trials conducted in South Africa.

cl_find.n: SAHPRA / Pan African Clinical Trials Registry
cl_find.d: PACTR is the WHO-recognised registry for the whole African region, run from South Africa, and is where African trials appear when they appear anywhere.

an_inspect.n: SANS 10386 / institutional ethics committees
an_inspect.d: Animal research follows a national standard through institutional committees; there is no central register. SANS 10386, second edition November 2021, produced by the South African Bureau of Standards, sets the minimum standards and applies to any institution or entity using animals for scientific purposes — research, teaching, training, field trials, product testing, diagnostics, production of biological substances, conservation and wildlife studies, and the breeding, creation or genetic alteration of animals for those purposes. That last clause matters here: creating a genetically altered animal is inside the standard's scope. Note it is a purchased standard, not a free public document. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

lab_oversight.n: Contained use — GMO Act registration, plus the health and labour regulations
lab_oversight.d: Three instruments apply at once and a reader needs to know which. Under the GMO Act every activity with a GMO requires a permit UNLESS the organisms are contained in a REGISTERED FACILITY — registration of the facility is what replaces a per-activity permit, and the Registrar must keep a register of all contained-use facilities and trial sites with the names and addresses of the people involved. Separately, the Regulations for Hazardous Biological Agents under the occupational health and safety law define hazardous biological agents to INCLUDE micro-organisms that have been genetically modified, and set containment levels by risk group; and the National Health Act regulations, Notice R178 of 2 March 2012, require registration of microbiological laboratories handling human pathogens. The link is to the compliance page that gathers the forms and fee schedules for all of it.

cl_report.d: Takes reports from patients and professionals.

decides.d: The advisory commission that wrote Resolution 173/2015, which decided an edited organism carrying no foreign DNA is not a GMO and needs no biosafety approval. Chile, Brazil, Colombia, Paraguay and Honduras all adopted versions of it — more countries follow this text than any other on the subject. fe_register.d: Argentina requires clinics to register and mandates insurance coverage of treatment, which is unusual.

fe_register.n: REDLARA — Red Latinoamericana de Reproducción Asistida
fe_register.d: The Latin American assisted reproduction network: it accredits clinics across the region, runs the continental registry of treatment cycles and outcomes, and publishes an annual report. Across most of Latin America there is no statutory fertility regulator at all, so an accreditation held or withdrawn here is the only external check on a clinic — and the accredited list is public. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

cl_find.n: ReNIS — Registro Nacional de Investigaciones en Salud
cl_find.d: The national health research register, created by Ministry of Health Resolution 1480/11. Registration is compulsory for clinical pharmacology studies authorised by ANMAT, the sponsor carrying the duty, and for research the ministry or its agencies fund, the investigator carrying it. It records not only the studies but the ethics committees, the sites, the investigators and the sponsors, and it has a public contact tab for the lead doctor or centre — so a reader can reach the people running a study rather than only read about it. Note that several Argentine provinces run their own registers alongside it, so a study absent here may be recorded at provincial level.

complain.n: KEPHIS — Plant Health Inspectorate
complain.d: Inspects seed and plant health and is the body that acts on unauthorised material. First established under the State Corporations Act in 1996 and re-established by the Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service Act 2012, with a stated mission of assuring plant health and the quality of agricultural INPUTS as well as produce. Two of its systems are directly usable: seed certification and plant variety protection run online, and there is a web-based pest reporting and management database. Phytosanitary certificates for export are issued electronically. So for anything to do with seed identity, unauthorised planting material or a pest, this is the address — the Bureau of Standards handles the product at the port.

complain.n: KEBS — Kenya Bureau of Standards
complain.d: Handles labelling standards and complaints on imported food. Established under the Standards Act, Cap 496, operating since July 1974, with Nairobi headquarters and six regional offices. Its relevant functions are standards preparation, product certification and QUALITY INSPECTION OF IMPORTS AT PORTS OF ENTRY — that last one is the reach that matters for imported grain. For seed, planting material and agricultural inputs generally, KEPHIS, the Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service, is the regulator under the Plant Protection Act Cap 324, and it is the better address for anything in a field rather than at a port. It does enforce, and the basis is specific. Market surveillance rests on ARTICLE 46(1) OF THE CONSTITUTION — the consumer right to protection from harmful goods — with inspection powers under sections 9, 10, 12, 13 and 14 of the STANDARDS ACT CAP 496 and Legal Notice No. 78 of 2005; the Act itself provides for powers of inspectors, ORDERS THAT GOODS BE DESTROYED, conditional release, and an appeal TRIBUNAL. KEBS states that complaints about substandard products are acknowledged, reviewed and acted upon, and that detection leads to SEIZURES, REWORKING AND PROSECUTIONS. It has a dedicated market surveillance site, ms.kebs.go.ke, which is the address for a complaint. Two live changes: the STANDARDS BILL 2025 would repeal Cap 496 — KEBS's own council calls the 1974 Act outdated and puts the cost of substandard goods at Sh200 billion a year — and draft Standards (Product Certification) Regulations 2026 went to consultation with comments due 5 June 2026. Both would widen these powers. Field and seed questions remain KEPHIS.

cl_find.n: Clinical Trials Registry — Pharmacy and Poisons Board
cl_find.d: Kenya's national medicines regulatory authority, established under the Pharmacy and Poisons Act, regulates every clinical trial in the country and runs its own online registry. The system was built in Kenya and upgraded under the HATUA project with European development partnership funding — worth noting in a category where several African entries point at a regional or global aggregator instead. Sponsors submit an annual approval checklist for every ongoing trial, so a trial that has lapsed is visible as such. The board also runs a separate electronic pharmacovigilance reporting system, which is where an adverse reaction goes.

decides.d: The federal biosafety portal, which publishes applications, advice and the register. Authority is split between the federal level and the three regions, which is why a Belgian answer usually has two halves.

complain.n: Regional agencies — Flanders, Wallonia, Brussels
complain.d: The regions inspect and enforce; the federal level authorises.

certify.d: One of the main Belgian organic certifiers.

legal.d: The Walloon and Flemish organic associations, which respond to federal biosafety consultations. The Walloon and Flemish organic associations, which make submissions on federal biosafety advice. An association OF PRODUCERS AND CONSUMERS TOGETHER, based at Jambes, represented across Brussels and Wallonia by 21 LOCAL GROUPS in four regional groupings — so there is a group near most people rather than a single office. Three things make it usable. It publishes an ANNUAIRE DES PRODUCTEURS BIO, a directory of certified producers, so a reader can find growers directly. Its MENTION NATURE & PROGRÈS is a private standard sitting above the EU organic label with additional social and environmental criteria — and the French parent association operates it as a PARTICIPATORY GUARANTEE SYSTEM, one of the oldest in the world, active since 1972, certifying through PEER REVIEW by farmers, consumers, agronomists and technicians rather than a paid certifier, with 15 production standards recognised in the IFOAM Family of Standards. For a reader who cannot afford third-party certification, peer review is the alternative model. It has campaigned on HIDDEN GMOs since the late 1990s, and publishes the review Valériane. Velt is the Flemish-language counterpart.

fe_register.d: Collects cycle-level data from every Belgian centre and publishes national reports.

complain.d: Inspects and enforces on seed and crops.

decides.n: DGAV — Direcção-Geral de Alimentação e Veterinária
decides.d: Authorises and holds the cultivation register. Portugal is one of only two EU states with commercial engineered maize, so its coexistence rules are among the few actually in use.

complain.n: DGAV — coexistence and neighbour notification
complain.d: Portuguese coexistence rules require a grower to notify neighbours before planting, and to keep isolation distances. That notification is the document to ask for.

certify.d: A Portuguese organic certifier.

notice.d: Portugal requires notification of intended plantings and publishes them, which is what makes its coexistence rules enforceable.

test.d: The reference laboratory, and the relevant one because Portugal is one of two EU states with commercial engineered maize.

legal.d: Tracks Portuguese plantings and the coexistence notifications, in one of two EU states growing commercially. A volunteer structure rather than a staffed organisation, backed by eleven Portuguese environment and agriculture bodies including the national farmers' confederation, Quercus, LPN, GEOTA and ZERO. It works alongside Friends of the Earth Europe, and reports more than ten thousand Portuguese citizens having registered written opposition. A reader looking for who to join here is looking at a coalition of existing associations, not a membership list.

fe_register.n: Conselho Nacional de Procriação Medicamente Assistida
fe_register.d: Licenses centres and holds the donor register; Portugal's constitutional court struck down donor anonymity in 2018. Created by Law 32/2006 as the regulator of the practice, it sits at the Assembleia da República rather than inside the health ministry — a fertility regulator answering to the legislature, and it publishes the authorised centres by region.

decides.n: Ministry of Rural Development and Food
decides.d: Authorises. Greece has used the EU cultivation opt-out, so the questions here concern imports and feed.

complain.n: Regional plant protection services
complain.d: The region inspects and enforces; the ministry authorises. One caution about this source: the IPPC contact record is updated by the country itself and can lag — records checked here carried ministry names that had since changed. The named person, address and telephone are the useful part; treat the institutional name as a starting point and check it against the ministry's own site.

certify.n: DIO — Inspection and Certification Organization of Organic Products
certify.d: Greece's first accredited inspection and certification body and the only non-profit one, working for around 25 years with roughly 6,000 operators certified, through a central office in Athens and seven regional offices. Worth following the ownership: it is a founding member and shareholder of the Croatian certifier AGRIBIOCERT and a shareholder of the Italian body ICEA. So the Greek and Croatian rows in this category are not independent of each other — a grower choosing between certifiers in the region may be choosing between bodies with a common stakeholder.

test.d: The Greek reference laboratory for plant protection and GMO analysis.

legal.d: A seed-saving network that maintains Greek landraces and works on the seed law that governs them. Its work is collecting, conserving, distributing and rescuing traditional seed varieties. That is a different route to the same end as a legal challenge: a landrace kept in circulation is not dependent on any approval decision, and cannot be withdrawn from the market by whoever owns it.

fe_register.n: National Authority of Medically Assisted Reproduction
fe_register.d: Licenses centres; Greece permits donation and surrogacy under court approval, and receives substantial cross-border treatment. Under law 3305/2005 it keeps a register of the licences it grants and, since a 2024 amendment, of the results of the preimplantation genetic tests carried out by the units it licenses — so the screening done on embryos is recorded by the regulator and not only by the clinic. It publishes its own decisions, including its 2025 rules on egg donors and its instructions for applicants aged 50 to 54.

cl_find.d: The European register. Since 2023 every trial run in the EU must be recorded here, and the protocol and summary results are published rather than only the listing — which is more than most registers give. Trials that began earlier sit in the older EudraCT register.

decides.d: Authorises releases and keeps the register.

complain.n: ÚKZÚZ — Ústřední kontrolní a zkušební ústav zemědělský
complain.d: Inspects seed and crops and runs the official testing laboratories. Established by Act No. 147/2002 Sb. as a specialised organ of state administration under the agriculture ministry, based in Brno with offices across the country. Its remit covers exactly the inputs this map follows: variety testing, feed, agrochemistry, soil and plant nutrition, SEED AND PLANTING MATERIAL, permanent crops, protection against harmful organisms, and plant protection products. Since 1 January 2010 it is also the ministry's designated control body for official organic controls, and grants the derogations allowing conventional seed to be used in organic production. Note the domain moved to ukzuz.gov.cz; older citations use ukzuz.cz. Food on sale is a different body, the SZPI.

certify.d: The largest Czech organic certifier.

notice.d: The national register of authorised organisms and release sites.

test.d: The central testing institute runs the official seed and crop analysis.

fe_register.n: Národní registr asistované reprodukce — Ministry of Health (mzd.gov.cz)
fe_register.d: Licenses centres; the Czech Republic is a major destination for cross-border egg donation. Note the ministry's address changed to mzd.gov.cz; older citations use mzcr.cz. Every clinic must be certified by the ministry and must report every IVF and insemination treatment, donor programmes included, to the National Assisted Reproduction Register, with annual reporting of outcomes — pregnancy result, complications and any fetal abnormalities. Inspection is by the State Institute for Drug Control, ordinarily at two-year intervals and immediately where something unexpected happens. Two limits set in law: an anonymous egg donor must be over 18 and under 35, and the female partner's age limit is 48 years and 364 days. Surrogacy is neither legalised nor prohibited, which is why agencies pair Czech treatment with a surrogate elsewhere.

Where this file usually offers a contact, that report offers the LANDSCAPE: who is working on this in Hungary and how they connect. Full text is hosted by Agroecology Europe.

complain.n: Ruokavirasto — Finnish Food Authority
complain.d: Inspects food, feed and seed, and runs the official testing. Began operating 1 January 2019, merging the Finnish Food Safety Authority (Evira), the Agency for Rural Affairs and part of the National Land Survey's IT services — so any citation to Evira or evira.fi predates it. Its remit names the whole input chain: food safety and quality, animal health and welfare, plant health, fertilisers, feed, plant protection products, soil conditioners, PLANT PROPAGATION MATERIAL and raw materials used in agricultural and forestry production. Head office in Seinäjoki, not Helsinki. Restaurants and food service are supervised by MUNICIPAL authorities, which is where a complaint about a premises goes.

complain.n: БАБХ — Bulgarian Food Safety Agency (BFSA)
complain.d: Inspects and enforces. Created by its own Act in January 2011 and operating from mid-February that year, as a specialised body under the agriculture ministry — note the ministry was renamed from Agriculture, Food and Forestry to simply Agriculture in 2022, so older citations differ. It is an INTEGRATED controller across the whole chain: food and feed safety and quality, additives and drinks, veterinary medicine and animal welfare, PLANT PROTECTION AND FERTILISERS, phytosanitary control and border inspection. That breadth is why it is the right address for almost any question here. Practically: Bulgaria is divided into 28 regions and each has a Regional Food Safety Directorate carrying out the official controls, so a complaint is handled regionally. Two addresses circulate, bfsa.bg and bfsa.egov.bg; the first answers.

complain.n: Državni inspektorat — State Inspectorate (Croatia)
complain.d: Responsible for inspection and official controls across many areas including food safety and sanitary and phytosanitary inspection. Its history is worth knowing before relying on an older citation: a State Inspectorate was created in 1997 to bring numerous separate inspectorates under one umbrella, ABOLISHED in 2014 with functions returned to separate authorities including the agriculture ministry, then RE-ESTABLISHED by a 2018 reform, the current institution starting work in April 2019. A reader following guidance written between 2014 and 2019 will be sent to the ministry instead.

Its founders include the Greek certifier DIO, which is also a shareholder — so this body and the Greek one in this category share ownership across a border.

decides.n: Your Cartagena focal point — the current office
decides.d: The named biosafety contact for this country, kept current by the Secretariat. Where a department has been renamed or merged, this is the list that says which office holds it now. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: Роспотребнадзор — Rospotrebnadzor
complain.d: Handles food labelling complaints; Russia requires labelling and prohibits cultivation. Handles food safety and consumer complaints. It answers the enforcement question emphatically. Created 12 March 2004 by Presidential Decree No. 314, merging the State Service for Sanitary and Epidemiological Surveillance with the State Inspectorate for Consumer Rights Protection, and since May 2012 it reports DIRECTLY TO THE GOVERNMENT rather than through the health ministry. It is Russia's national public health agency as well as its consumer regulator: it drafts and enforces consumer-rights policy, carries out federal state sanitary-epidemiological surveillance covering environmental hazards, food quality and disease outbreaks, licenses activities affecting human health, issues sanitary certification under Customs Union requirements, and conducts epidemiological investigations into foodborne outbreaks. Worth knowing for this map: the VECTOR Institute falls under Rospotrebnadzor, so the same federal service holds a high-containment research centre and the consumer complaint line.

certify.d: The national organic standard and its register of certified producers. The link goes to the IFOAM certifiers directory, searchable by country, rather than to this certifier's own site, which has not been verified here. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

notice.n: Federal registration portal — registration without a comment stage
notice.d: Feed and food approvals are registered rather than consulted on; there is no public comment stage. That is the finding for this row rather than a gap in it: a register records what was decided, a consultation invites an objection before it is, and Russia's arrangement offers the first without the second. Where an approval has been made, the Clearing-House country profile is where to read it. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.
notice.conf: No national notice venue — this describes where decisions surface, not a page that announces them in advance. Check the country's Clearing-House record.

legal.n: Союз органического земледелия — Union of Organic Agriculture (Russia)
legal.d: Represents certified producers; Russia prohibits cultivation and import for planting, so the live questions concern feed and food. Registered in Moscow in September 2013, a voluntary membership association of individuals and legal entities, and the largest Russian independent movement for organic agriculture. Note what it is and is not: it describes itself as politically unaligned and is an OFFICIAL PARTNER OF THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE, a member of the ministry's PUBLIC COUNCIL, and a partner of Rosselkhoztsentr, Roskachestvo and the plant protection research institute — so it works inside the state's own consultative structures rather than against them, which is how this subject is carried in Russia. Its practical value to a reader is its ARCHIVE: over 20,000 tagged articles and 600-plus event announcements over nine years, read in 52 Russian regions and 27 countries. It covers certification, producers and regional programmes, and is the route to finding who is doing this work in a given oblast.

cl_report.d: The national centre for adverse event reporting, part of the WHO programme. Reports from patients are accepted in most member countries.

cl_find.n: State Register of Medicines — clinical trials
cl_find.d: The health ministry register lists authorised trials; Russian trials are largely absent from Western registries.

an_inspect.n: Institutional bioethics committees, under GOST standards and Federal Law 498-FZ
an_inspect.d: There is no special legislation on the keeping and use of laboratory animals in Russia; a 2025 review in a Russian law journal says so directly and calls for one. What exists instead: Federal Law 498-FZ of 2018 prohibits procedures causing pain or suffering without scientific justification and requires oversight by institutional research ethics committees; and a set of interstate GOST standards — 33044-2014 on good laboratory practice, 33215-2014 on rodents and rabbits, 33218-2014 on non-human primates — which were drawn up by a non-commercial association of laboratory-animal specialists and apply across CIS member states. The practical expert work is done regionally. Note the lineage: the founding document is a Soviet health ministry order of 12 August 1977. The link goes to the legal review because there is no register or regulator page to send a reader to.

decides.d: Authorises. Ukraine's registration system has long lagged actual planting, which is documented rather than alleged — surveys have repeatedly found unregistered engineered soy in the field.

complain.n: Держпродспоживслужба — State Service on Food Safety and Consumer Protection
complain.d: Inspects and enforces on food, feed and seed. Handles food labelling complaints; Ukraine requires GM labelling. A central executive body under the Cabinet of Ministers, directed through the agrarian policy minister, and it holds an unusually wide brief: food safety, veterinary medicine and veterinary practice licensing, consumer protection, and metrological supervision — including of the measuring instruments used in trade. It publishes an annual report on its own activities. Two things to expect: martial law has altered the inspection regime, and its recent published work is heavily oriented to aligning controls with EU standards, which is where the substantive rule increasingly comes from.

certify.d: The main Ukrainian certifier, and the relevant one because Ukraine's registration system has lagged actual planting.

notice.d: Registration decisions are published by the ministry, though the register has long lagged actual planting.

legal.n: Organic Ukraine — public union of certified operators
legal.d: Represents growers in a country where the register has long lagged actual planting. It admits certified operators only, which makes it a business association rather than a campaign: it represents producers, processors, distributors and input makers who already hold certification. Ukraine's organic law bans the words organic, biodynamic, biological, ecological and the bio- prefix on anything not produced to the standard, so a member's interest in enforcement is commercial before it is anything else. Sector bodies reported after February 2022 that micro, small and medium organic businesses might cease operating. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

fe_register.n: Order No. 787 of 09.09.2013 — Procedure for the use of ART in Ukraine
fe_register.d: Ukraine permitted commercial surrogacy for foreign couples at scale, which the 2022 invasion turned into an acute and widely reported problem. The instrument itself is the useful thing here, and it is readable in the state legal register. Its conditions decide who may take part: surrogacy is open only to married heterosexual couples, at least one spouse must be genetically related to the child and the surrogate must not be, and foreigners may take part on the same footing as citizens. Commercial surrogacy is permitted with no ceiling on the surrogate's remuneration and no separate authority's permission. Under Family Code article 123(2) the commissioning couple are the parents from the moment of transfer, and article 139(2) bars any contest of maternity — so the surrogate cannot change her mind after birth. Preimplantation genetic diagnosis is among the permitted additional technologies.

cl_find.d: Authorises and lists trials; Ukraine hosted a substantial trial sector before 2022. The link goes to the WHO ICTRP search portal, which aggregates this registry rather than being it; the national registry's own site has not been verified here.

decides.d: Authorises releases and publishes decisions. Nigeria approved Bt cowpea in 2019 — the first engineered food crop released in sub-Saharan Africa, and one of very few anywhere developed by a public institute for a staple its own country eats.

complain.d: Food and drug control; takes complaints on labelling and food safety.

certify.d: Holds the participatory guarantee scheme used by most Nigerian organic producers. notice.d: The agency publishes applications and invites comment, which is how the Bt cowpea decision was notified.

legal.d: Files objections to NBMA applications and publishes the analysis of them — the most consistent objector in West Africa.

test.d: The agency runs its own detection laboratory, which is unusual in the region. The agency runs its own detection laboratory, unusual in the region.

fe_register.n: AFRH — Association for Fertility and Reproductive Health (Nigeria)
fe_register.d: Nigeria has the largest fertility sector in West Africa with no statutory regulator; the professional association is the only body holding standards. A non-governmental professional association, not a regulator, and it says so: it brings together clinicians, embryologists, nurses, counsellors, researchers and policymakers, and among its stated aims is developing and maintaining the AFRH Data Registry. In a country with no statutory ART regulation, the register is a professional body's project rather than a legal requirement. Its own officers describe reverse medical tourism — patients arriving from abroad because a cycle costing about $20,000 in the United States can be done here for around $6,000 including travel and accommodation, one practitioner reporting 40% of his patients came from outside the country in 2024.

The regional federation, which sets standards and runs training where no statutory regulator exists. Most African fertility care is private and unlicensed, so a professional body is often the only body holding standards. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

fe_register.n: ANARA — African Network and Registry for ART
fe_register.d: Collects cycle-by-cycle data from the ART centres that choose to submit it and publishes procedure counts, pregnancy and delivery rates and centre numbers by country. Reporting is voluntary and centre-led, so a country showing nothing may have clinics that have never submitted rather than no clinics. It does not license a clinic, inspect one, or take a complaint about one. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

cl_find.d: Authorises trials; the Pan African Clinical Trials Registry also covers Nigerian studies.

decides.d: Authorises releases and runs the public consultation. Ghana approved Bt cowpea after Nigeria, following the same public-institute route.

complain.n: PPRSD — Plant Protection and Regulatory Services Directorate (MOFA)
complain.d: Inspects seed and plant health. One caution about this source: the IPPC contact record is updated by the country itself and can lag — records checked here carried ministry names that had since changed. The named person, address and telephone are the useful part; treat the institutional name as a starting point and check it against the ministry's own site. Established 1965 under the Prevention and Control of Pests and Diseases of Plants Act 307, now replaced by the PLANTS AND FERTILIZER ACT, 2010 (Act 803) — cite the 2010 Act, not the 1965 one. The relevant part for this map is inside it: the Ghana Seed Inspection and Certification Division, constituted by Part II of that Act, does field inspection, laboratory analysis of seed samples, monitoring of seed quality and seed certification, including foundation and certified seed and planting materials. So the seed question and the plant health question reach the same directorate. Ghana's national plant protection policy is Integrated Pest Management, adopted 1992.

complain.n: Ghana FDA — Food and Drugs Authority
complain.d: Handles food labelling complaints. Established 1997 as the Food and Drugs Board under PNDC Law 305B and now drawing its mandate from Parts 6, 7 and 8 of the Public Health Act, 2012 (Act 851). Its published function list is the useful page, and two entries on it matter here: it INVESTIGATES CONSUMER COMPLAINTS for the products it regulates, and it TESTS all regulated products for conformance — so the complaint and the analysis sit in the same body. It also monitors products at all ports of entry and carries out market surveillance. Enforcement is real: its Enforcement Directorate works with Ghana Police officers seconded to the FDA and liaises with the judiciary to secure prosecutions, and conducts market raids. WHO listed it as a Level Three regulatory authority in May 2020. Crops in the field are the plant protection directorate's, not this body's.

complain.n: EAA — Ethiopian Agricultural Authority
complain.d: It now has a page of its own, which the earlier note said it did not. The EAA is a federal agricultural REGULATORY authority, an autonomous body with its own legal personality, established under Article 45 of Proclamation No. 1263/2021 with its powers set out in Council of Ministers Regulation No. 509/2022. It was created expressly to strengthen a weak regulatory system by BRINGING TOGETHER SCATTERED REGULATORY BODIES — the rights and obligations of the Veterinary Drug and Feed Administration and Control Authority transferred to it, and its Veterinary Drug and Animal Feed Directorate now sets standards including maximum residue limits, using Codex as the basis. Its remit covers agricultural TECHNOLOGIES, INPUTS, PRODUCTS AND SERVICES: ensuring they are standardised, registered and handled by certified persons, and inspecting for compliance with efficacy, quality, health and safety standards. Registrations run five years and are renewable. Food and drugs on the market are the separate EFDA; seed is governed by the Seed Proclamation 1288/2023.

complain.n: Ethiopian Food and Drug Authority
complain.d: Handles food labelling and safety complaints. A federal regulatory body established under Proclamation No. 1263/2021 with its mandate set by Regulation No. 531/2023, covering the safety and quality of food alongside medicines, medical devices and cosmetics. Note the narrowing: before those two instruments it regulated products, professionals, premises and practices; since them its mandate is limited to regulated products. A complaint about a premises or a practice now goes somewhere else.

certify.d: Certification is mostly for export coffee and sesame. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.d: Works on farmer seed systems and the biosafety proclamation that was relaxed in 2015. Founded 2002 to continue the SEEDS OF SURVIVAL programme begun at the ETHIOPIAN NATIONAL GENE BANK, and it has kept a working partnership with the Ethiopian Biodiversity Institute for over a decade — so it sits between farmers and the national genetic resource system rather than outside it. What it actually runs is the useful part: COMMUNITY SEED BANKS, on a documented model — a seed reserve holding farmer varieties alongside research-centre varieties, lent to members who must RE-DEPOSIT MORE THAN THEY BORROWED after harvest, with stock keeping about five years without serious loss of viability, and the bank doubling as a grain reserve against crop failure. It has published a manual on establishing one. It holds a Slow Food International award for recovering Ethiopian indigenous crop varieties through IN SITU conservation. For anyone building seed autonomy rather than contesting a release, this is the practical model. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

legal.n: Institute for Sustainable Development (ISD) — and the Shella Mella organic cotton cooperative
legal.d: Represents growers following the 2015 relaxation of what had been one of Africa's strictest biosafety laws. There is no single national organic movement to name; two concrete bodies are more useful. The INSTITUTE FOR SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT, founded 1996, works with communities across Ethiopia on the exchange of traditional and modern knowledge and supports indigenous farming methods. And the SHELLA MELLA COTTON COOPERATIVE in Gamo Zone, established 2013, is the documented working case: it moved its 200 members from conventional to ORGANIC COTTON with support from PESTICIDE ACTION NETWORK, was CERTIFIED ORGANIC IN 2017, and — the part that matters here — IT SELECTS AND DISTRIBUTES ORGANIC COTTON SEED TO ITS MEMBERS ITSELF. Plant protection relies exclusively on biological control agents and plant extracts including neem. An IPM pilot from 2006 reached more than 3,000 farmers in 14 villages through FARMER FIELD SCHOOLS, women now 30% of participants, and the cooperative sells directly to textile factories under contract. Cotton is where engineered varieties enter African farming — compare Benin's OBEPAB and Burkina Faso's Bt cotton record.

test.n: KEPHIS — Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service
test.d: Kenya's plant health regulator and designated National Plant Protection Organization, whose plant quarantine section is the regional reference laboratory for COMESA and a centre of excellence for germplasm exchange, so it accepts samples from neighbouring states. Its laboratories cover molecular diagnosis by conventional and real-time PCR and LAMP, bacteriology, virology, analytical chemistry and seed testing, and it takes samples from farmers directly as well as from its own inspectors; the bacteriology laboratory is ISO/IEC 17025 accredited. It analyses and inspects: it does not authorise a GMO. Importing one is approved by Kenya's National Biosafety Authority, and KEPHIS issues the permit only after that approval. nearest capable laboratory is in another country and access runs through the regional body.

decides.d: Handles applications. Egypt is the largest wheat importer in the world, and its state tender specifications on engineered content set terms for exporters across several continents — a buyer decision that functions as regulation. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: CAPQ — Central Administration of Plant Quarantine (Egypt)
complain.d: Inspects imports and enforces at the border. One caution about this source: the IPPC contact record is updated by the country itself and can lag — records checked here carried ministry names that had since changed. The named person, address and telephone are the useful part; treat the institutional name as a starting point and check it against the ministry's own site. Egypt's national plant protection organisation and its representative to the IPPC and NEPPO, under the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation. Ministerial Decree No. 562/2019 REESTABLISHED it as the agency responsible for GRAINS AND OILSEEDS inspections, reversing Prime Ministerial Decree 2992/2016 which had stopped government teams travelling and given grain import inspection to the export and import control organisation. Mandatory pre-shipment inspection of grain at the port of LOADING is back, carried out by Egyptian officials abroad — an unusual reach, and directly relevant to a country importing engineered maize and soy at scale. The division with the National Food Safety Authority is still moving: NFSA, established 2017 as an independent body under the Prime Minister, now handles contaminants and residues in IMPORTS, while CAPQ remains the authority for EXPORTS and their residue levels until NFSA takes that over too. Dokki, Giza.

complain.n: National Food Safety Authority
complain.d: Handles food safety and labelling complaints on imports. Established by Law No. 1 of 2017 as an independent body under the prime minister's office, consolidating food safety functions previously spread across over fifteen separate government entities, and responsible for inspection, licensing and certification for domestic production, imports and exports. A caveat reported by Egyptian business-climate monitors and worth knowing before relying on it: the authority is treated as an ordinary public agency for expenditure purposes despite the powers the law grants it, and has been described as unable to secure resources as basic as vehicles for its inspectors. A mandate and a budget are different things. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

test.n: Central Laboratory for Agricultural Climate / AGERI
test.d: National laboratories run detection; testing of imported grain is the practical use. Founded 1990 at Giza within the Agricultural Research Centre, and described as the vehicle for transferring and applying genetic engineering technology in Egyptian agriculture. Note what that means for a reader wanting a test: the institute that develops engineered crops is also the one that would identify them. The link goes to the Agricultural Research Centre's institute listing rather than a laboratory page, because AGERI is a research institute rather than a testing service.

legal.n: ECESR — Egyptian Center for Economic and Social Rights
legal.d: Litigates on food and agriculture policy, including import specifications. A LEGAL institution founded 2009 that works through LITIGATION as well as research and campaigning — which is what distinguishes it from a campaigning group. Its declared domain includes FREE TRADE agreements, investment, privatisation and corruption alongside labour, health and housing, so a seed or import rule arriving through a trade agreement is within its subject matter. Its record shows it litigates and wins on environmental questions: it has pursued the government's continued neglect of a COURT RULING BANNING NILE POLLUTION, and has brought cases on expropriation and on privatisation deals. For anyone needing a court rather than a regulator in Egypt, this is the body with the practice.

decides.d: Authorises. Bangladesh released Bt brinjal in 2013 — the first engineered food crop grown by smallholders in South Asia, and the most studied case of one.

complain.n: Department of Agricultural Extension
complain.d: The extension service is the practical contact for a grower. Formed 1982 by merging six bodies including the Plant Protection Directorate, and the largest agency in the country's extension system, with staff down to sub-district level — which is why it is the practical first contact even though its remit is advisory rather than regulatory. Two things to expect: extension is described as top-down with limited links to research, and it operates separately from the livestock and fisheries departments, so a complaint about an engineered animal goes elsewhere.

complain.n: BFSA — Bangladesh Food Safety Authority
complain.d: Handles food safety and labelling complaints. An autonomous statutory regulator formed February 2015 under the Food Safety Act 2013 (Act No. 43 of 2013), under the Ministry of Food, governed by a five-member body and explicitly modelled on the US FDA. Two things a reader should know. The Act's own definitions cover PESTICIDE RESIDUE in detail, including residues contaminated from the environment — so drift onto a crop is inside its subject matter, not outside it. And the authority operates its OWN MOBILE COURT which can fine and sentence for food adulteration, which is an enforcement power almost nothing else in this category has. Consumer complaints about goods and services generally go to a different body, the Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection under the commerce ministry, which is quasi-judicial and has offices in every divisional city.

certify.d: Mostly export-facing. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.d: Runs the Nayakrishi Andolon farmer seed network and documented the Bt brinjal releases from the growers' side.

notice.d: Approvals are gazetted; the Bt brinjal releases were notified this way.

test.d: Ran the Bt brinjal trials and the associated testing. An autonomous institute under the agriculture ministry at Joydebpur, Gazipur, working on all crops except rice, jute, sugarcane and tea, which have their own institutes — so a question about engineered rice goes to the rice institute, not here. It runs 6 to 8 regional stations, 7 crop research centres and 28 sub-stations, and conducts validation and farmers' field trials through 9 farming-system sites and 80 multilocation testing sites. Note what that means: the institute that developed and trialled Bt brinjal is also the analytical capacity a reader would be sent to, and it is a research institute rather than a testing service.
