complain.n: Administration des services techniques de l’agriculture
complain.d: Inspects and enforces. Set up 1967, with origins in an 1883 law, and reorganised by the law of 30 November 1976. Two of its statutory tasks are the ones that matter here: carrying out analyses of the composition and quality of agricultural products and means of production, and ensuring compliance with the rules on agricultural products, means of production, plant protection and the protection of plant products. So the same administration analyses and enforces — a sample and a complaint go to one address, which is rare on this map. A CORRECTION and a specific: since the LAW OF 8 SEPTEMBER 2022, official controls across the food chain are split between ASTA and a NEW body, the Administration luxembourgeoise vétérinaire et alimentaire (ALVA), which absorbed the veterinary services administration, the health directorate's food safety division and ASTA's own animal feed control service. ALVA is now the single administration for official controls on food chain safety and conformity, on the market and at import and export, and it takes food samples for PESTICIDE RESIDUE analysis and runs multiannual control plans specifically covering pesticides, contaminants AND GMOs. ASTA keeps primary production of plant-origin food, organic production and labelling, and quality schemes. The part that matters most here: ASTA's SEED AND PLANT CERTIFICATION SERVICE is the competent authority for the CONTROL OF GMOs IN SEED and vegetative propagating material intended for food and feed production, and issues NON-GMO CERTIFICATES for seed, seed potatoes, plants and products of animal origin. Its plant protection service handles plant health, import control from third countries and phytosanitary passports.

decides.d: Authorises. Iceland has permitted contained barley production for pharmaceutical proteins — molecular farming in greenhouses rather than fields, which is the form this takes where outdoor release is impractical.

complain.n: Matvælastofnun (MAST) — Icelandic Food and Veterinary Authority
complain.d: Established by Act No. 167 of 21 December 2007 and the competent authority for food safety, animal health and welfare, CONTROL OF FEED, SEED AND FERTILISERS, plant health and water for human consumption — one body for the whole chain, which is unusual and is the reason it is the right address for almost any question here. Seed control sitting inside it matters for this map. Note the legal basis: Iceland is party to the EEA Agreement and has implemented EU legislation on veterinary matters, foodstuffs and feed, so the substantive rule is usually an adopted EU one. Selfoss, not Reykjavík: Austurvegur 64, IS-800. A CORRECTION to the single-address claim: MAST IS THE COMPETENT AUTHORITY FOR GM FOOD AND FEED, BUT THE ENVIRONMENT AGENCY OF ICELAND IS THE COMPETENT AUTHORITY FOR GM ORGANISMS — contained use, deliberate release, cultivation and marketing. So a labelling question comes here and a release question does not. MAST's own remit is still wide: food safety, animal health and welfare, control of FEED, SEED AND FERTILISERS, plant health and water for human consumption, under Act No. 30 of 7 May 2018 (the authority was established by Act No. 167 of 2007). The GM labelling rules are Reglugerd nr. 1237/2014, and MAST publishes both the regulation and how the control of genetically modified food is organised. Practically, its CONTACT FORM expressly invites notifications about FOOD LABELLING and illegal operations, and states that all messages are processed — a rare published commitment. Note local health committees carry out food surveillance in their regions under MAST's supervision, so the inspector is often local.

certify.d: Founded 1994, a non-governmental body that inspects and certifies every organic unit in Iceland — farms and processors alike — under its own standards, published in Icelandic and English and written within the EU framework. It also operates on a small scale in the Faroe Islands. It needs both a permit from the industries ministry and accreditation from the Icelandic Service for Accreditation. One body certifying an entire country is the opposite of the fourteen-certifier market in Poland, and worth knowing: there is no second opinion available domestically.

complain.n: MCCAA — Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority
complain.d: Handles food labelling complaints. Formed 23 May 2011 by amalgamating the Malta Standards Authority, the Consumer and Competition Department and the Malta National Laboratory — so it holds functions many member states split across separate bodies. It houses the Standards and Metrology Institute, Malta's national standards body and a CEN/CENELEC member, runs market surveillance and product testing, and is the EUROPEAN FOOD SAFETY AUTHORITY'S MALTESE FOCAL POINT, which means it maintains the list of Maltese organisations competent to do food and feed risk assessment work. For a small state that concentration is the point: one address for standards, testing, consumer complaint and the EFSA interface. Import and export control is Customs.

decides.d: Authorises. Costa Rica permits engineered crops to be grown for seed export while not authorising them for domestic cultivation — so it hosts the production of a crop its own farmers may not plant. Several cantons have declared themselves GM-free.

complain.n: Servicio Fitosanitario del Estado (SFE) — Ley 7664
complain.d: Created in 1997 by Ley 7664, attached to the agriculture ministry but with its own instrumental legal personality — which is why it acts in its own name rather than the ministry's. Its stated mission is to act as NATIONAL AUTHORITY protecting agricultural resources from pests and contributing to the protection of human health and the environment, by setting phytosanitary and sanitary measures. It issues export phytosanitary certificates and publishes an online consultation to verify one. Animal feed sits elsewhere: SENASA, the national animal health service, runs the feed control office.

complain.n: Ministerio de Salud — denuncias sobre productos de interés sanitario
complain.d: Handles food registration and labelling. A denuncia about a producto de interés sanitario — anything whose composition or use can affect health, including food, pesticides and natural products — can be lodged in person, by telephone, by email or through the ministry's website, and an in-person complaint may be made orally or in sign language, recorded onto a form by the official. That range of channels is unusual and worth knowing: most rows on this map assume a written complaint. Every processed food sold in Costa Rica must hold a current registro sanitario, granted through the Regístrelo platform; selling without one can mean withdrawal from the market or closure of the business. There is a DEDICATED DENUNCIA FORM for productos de interés sanitario, and four ways to lodge one: in person, by telephone, by e-mail or through the ministry's website — in person at an ÁREA RECTORA, regional or central office, and the ministry accepts the account verbally, in writing OR IN SIGN LANGUAGE. Its denuncia remit covers environmental matters, products, and the operation of establishments. Before complaining, a reader can check the product themselves: registrations are searchable on the REGÍSTRELO platform, and the LEY GENERAL DE SALUD N° 5395 prohibits the manufacture, trade and use of unregistered, adulterated or falsified products. The ministry issues public ADVERTENCIAS SANITARIAS naming specific products, and has decomisado goods found on sale unregistered, with illegible labels or labels in a language other than Spanish, or in damaged and opened packaging — so mislabelled product is actively pursued here. Fees are waived for people in poverty and reduced for micro-enterprises.

certify.d: One of the organic certifiers operating in Costa Rica; the other commonly named is Kiwa BCS, the local arm of the Dutch group that appears elsewhere on this map. The link goes to the Ente Costarricense de Acreditación's searchable register of accredited conformity assessment bodies rather than to the certifier's own site, because the register is what shows whether an accreditation is current.

legal.d: Brought the cases and the canton declarations that made much of Costa Rica GM-free. Worth knowing why it is the address: the RCB and FECON hold THE TWO ECOLOGIST SEATS ON THE COMISIÓN NACIONAL TÉCNICA EN BIOSEGURIDAD (CNTBio), the body that decides on releases in Costa Rica, and are recorded as the members who have maintained reasoned opposition to new events. So this is not an outside campaign but a participant inside the deciding commission — which means it holds the papers, and can be asked what was argued. It works with the Bloque Verde network. Costa Rica's authorised events have been largely SEED MULTIPLICATION FOR EXPORT by transnational companies rather than production for domestic consumption, which is the distinctive fact about the country's record. It arose in 1997 out of the debate on what became Costa Rica's LEY DE BIODIVERSIDAD, and is a space of articulation between ecologist, peasant and indigenous organisations and individuals. IT LITIGATES, and the case is the thing to know: a CONTENCIOSO-ADMINISTRATIVO PROCESS RUNNING MORE THAN TEN YEARS over the release of STACKED TRANSGENIC COTTON, reaching its final stage in June 2025, with the agricultural scientists Fabián Pacheco and Jaime García as principal witnesses. The arguments are worth carrying: COSTA RICA FORMS PART OF THE CENTRE OF ORIGIN OF COTTON, so release risks the country's own biodiversity; and the release proceeded DESPITE A REQUEST FOR TECHNICAL INFORMATION NEEDED BY CTNBio MEMBERS TO CAST A REASONED VOTE — a procedural objection any commission member elsewhere could make. They accuse the Servicio Fitosanitario del Estado of being lax and permissive toward the transnationals planting in a country holding 5% of world biodiversity. It publishes a Revista costarricense de agroecología campesina. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

notice.d: Where authorisations appear. Costa Rica permits growing for seed export without authorising domestic cultivation.

fe_register.n: REDLARA — Red Latinoamericana de Reproducción Asistida
fe_register.d: The Latin American assisted reproduction network: it accredits clinics across the region, runs the continental registry of treatment cycles and outcomes, and publishes an annual report. Across most of Latin America there is no statutory fertility regulator at all, so an accreditation held or withdrawn here is the only external check on a clinic — and the accredited list is public. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

fe_register.n: Artavia Murillo v. Costa Rica — the IVF ruling
fe_register.d: Costa Rica prohibited IVF entirely in 2000 on the ground that an embryo is a person. In 2012 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights held the ban violated the right to private and family life and ordered it lifted — the only case anywhere of an international court compelling a state to permit assisted reproduction.

decides.d: Authorises. Cuba develops its own engineered crops through state institutes rather than importing them, which is a route no other country in the region takes. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: Ministerio de la Agricultura (MINAG), Cuba
complain.d: Inspects and enforces. Its Dirección General de Agricultura holds the two directorates that matter here in one place: Sanidad Vegetal, and Semillas y Recursos Fitogenéticos — plant health, and seed and plant genetic resources. It also has delegations in every province and almost every municipality, which is where a complaint actually starts. Among its statutory functions is protecting the national territory from the introduction and spread of pests and diseases. Its published functions name the two powers that matter: protecting the national territory from the introduction and spread of plant pests and diseases WHILE EXERCISING THE REGISTRATION AND CONTROL OF THE USE OF CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL AND NATURAL PESTICIDES, and directing the policy on prospecting, conservation, introduction, maintenance, documentation and use of PLANT GENETIC RESOURCES AND SEED. So the pesticide register and the seed policy are both here. Practically, the Dirección de Sanidad Vegetal in Havana issues phytosanitary import, export and transit permits — collection Tuesdays and Thursdays, mornings only — and PROVINCIAL PLANT HEALTH DEPARTMENTS sit in each MINAG delegation with plant protection and plant quarantine specialists, reachable outside hours through the alert system of the Territorial Plant Protection Stations for an emergent abnormal situation. That last route is the one to use for something appearing in a field. Laboratory work is the Unidad de Laboratorios Centrales de Sanidad Agropecuaria.

complain.n: Oficina Nacional de Normalización
complain.d: Handles labelling standards. The national standards office, which develops and enforces standards across sectors including food, audits against them and certifies producers who comply. Cuba splits the field four ways: this office for standards, MINAG for agriculture and plant health, the public health ministry for food safety, and the food industry ministry for processing. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

certify.d: Largely state-run and domestic rather than export-certified. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.n: ACTAF — Asociación Cubana de Técnicos Agrícolas y Forestales
legal.d: Runs the participatory plant breeding programme, in a country developing its own engineered crops through state institutes. A non-governmental organisation founded 2 February 1987 that groups PROFESSIONALS — agricultural and forestry technicians — rather than farmers, which makes it a different kind of ally: it can argue on technical ground. It funds and promotes projects to generalise environmentally compatible technologies, including water use, VITROPLANTAS (tissue-cultured plants), recovery and management of forest areas and development of NEW VARIETIES, and it runs International Encounters on Organic Agriculture. It has a national headquarters in Playa, Havana, WITH PROVINCIAL BRANCHES AND MUNICIPAL BASE ORGANS — so there is a technical contact near most producers, which matters given that Cuba's plant health alert system, named in this country's other entry, also runs provincially. It coordinates the Grupo de Jóvenes Agroecólogos within the Latin American agroecology society, and applies the agriculture system's gender strategy. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

notice.n: Gaceta Oficial de la República de Cuba
notice.d: Where decisions appear, in a country developing its own engineered crops through state institutes.

cl_find.n: Registro Público Cubano de Ensayos Clínicos
cl_find.d: Cuba runs its own registry and develops therapies through state institutes. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

cl_report.d: The national centre for adverse event reporting, part of the WHO programme. Reports from patients are accepted in most member countries.

fe_register.n: REDLARA — Red Latinoamericana de Reproducción Asistida
fe_register.d: The Latin American assisted reproduction network: it accredits clinics across the region, runs the continental registry of treatment cycles and outcomes, and publishes an annual report. Across most of Latin America there is no statutory fertility regulator at all, so an accreditation held or withdrawn here is the only external check on a clinic — and the accredited list is public. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

decides.d: Venezuela's seed law prohibits engineered seed outright and was written with substantial public participation — one of the few seed laws anywhere drafted that way. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: INSAI — Instituto Nacional de Salud Agrícola Integral
complain.d: The agricultural health institute; inspects and enforces. Created by the Ley de Salud Agrícola Integral and attached to the agriculture and lands ministry, it is the governing body for plant health in Venezuela. Two things from its internal regulation are directly useful: it is required to receive, process and resolve DENUNCIAS, complaints, claims, suggestions and petitions from citizens on agricultural health, and it coordinates the issue of registrations, permits, certifications and authorisations for activities in that field. So the body that authorises is the body that takes the complaint. Operators must also register in RUNSAI, the national agricultural health register, and are obliged to notify INSAI of suspected or present pests.

certify.d: Participatory rather than third-party certification. Participatory guarantee has its own global register, run by IFOAM with FAO, searchable by country and by product — the equivalent for this kind of certification of the certifiers' directory used elsewhere in this category. From the 2022 survey it counted at least 323 initiatives worldwide, 62 of them still under development, involving around 1.4 million producers. A PGS certifies through the active participation of producers, consumers and other stakeholders in setting the standard, running the procedure and making the decision, which is why it is cheap enough for a smallholder and why no third-party auditor appears in it.

legal.d: The network behind the seed law drafted with public participation. A CAUTION ON THE NAME, because it is easy to reach the wrong organisation: RED DE SEMILLAS LIBRES IS A SHARED NAME ACROSS LATIN AMERICA, not a single body. The best-documented is COLOMBIA'S, formed against Resolution ICA 970 of 2010 — which required all seed in Colombia to be registered and certified — and Law 1518 of 2012 approving UPOV 1991, WHICH COLOMBIA'S CONSTITUTIONAL COURT STRUCK DOWN AS INEXEQUIBLE. That ruling is the precedent worth knowing: a seed law implementing UPOV 91 was held unconstitutional. A regional gathering, 'Sembrando Vida en América', was first held in Peru. When searching, name the country — and expect the Colombian material, including Grupo Semillas' work and the documentary on Resolution 970, to be the fullest source even for a reader elsewhere.

legal.n: Movimiento Semillas del Pueblo and the Campaña Venezuela Libre de Transgénicos
legal.d: Participated in drafting the seed law that prohibits engineered seed — one of few seed laws written with substantial public participation. The movement to name is SEMILLAS DEL PUEBLO, active since 2013 alongside the Campaña Venezuela Libre de Transgénicos and the Red Nacional de Guardianes de Semilla — urban grower collectives, small producer organisations from west, centre and east, researchers and seed and bioinput producers. Drafting of the LEY DE SEMILLAS began October 2013 with peasant movements and ecological organisations participating, and it was approved in 2015: it PROHIBITS TRANSGENICS AND PATENTS ON SEED, resting on articles 127 and 305 of the Constitution. Its distinctive machinery is the CONSEJO POPULAR DE RESGUARDO Y PROTECCIÓN DE LA SEMILLA (arts. 48–50), a Poder Popular body with BINDING power to intervene in the formulation and execution of public policy on local, peasant, indigenous and afrodescendant seed. In practice the movement runs a pilot for CONSERVATION AND MULTIPLICATION of those seeds toward a Plan Popular de Semillas, with collective ensemillamiento agreements under which participating organisations commit to multiply and safeguard what they receive — for instance the MFE peasant maize variety in Anzoátegui.

fe_register.n: REDLARA — Red Latinoamericana de Reproducción Asistida
fe_register.d: The Latin American assisted reproduction network: it accredits clinics across the region, runs the continental registry of treatment cycles and outcomes, and publishes an annual report. Across most of Latin America there is no statutory fertility regulator at all, so an accreditation held or withdrawn here is the only external check on a clinic — and the accredited list is public. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

decides.n: National Biosafety Focal Point — Ministry of Environment
decides.d: Handles biosafety. Sri Lanka attempted a nationwide switch to organic farming in 2021 by banning agrochemical imports outright; the resulting yield collapse and reversal is the most cited case anywhere of what happens when input systems change without transition. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: Department of Agriculture (Sri Lanka)
complain.d: Inspects seed and crops. Its regulatory services run under four named acts — the Plant Protection Act, the Soil Conservation Act, the Control of Pesticides Act and the Seed Act — and it holds a Seed Certification and Plant Protection Centre. That combination is the relevant one: seed certification and plant protection in the same centre means a question about seed identity and one about a plant health problem reach the same people. Headquarters at Peradeniya, with institutes across the agro-ecological regions.

complain.n: SLSI — Sri Lanka Standards Institution
complain.d: Handles food labelling standards and complaints. Established 1964 as the Bureau of Ceylon Standards, now under the Sri Lanka Standards Institution Act No. 6 of 1984, governed by a Council appointed by the minister. It does enforce, at the border: the COMPULSORY IMPORT INSPECTION SCHEME covers 122 items gazetted on national health and safety grounds under Gazette No. 2064/34 of 29 March 2018, and SLSI recommends to Customs whether a consignment is released. Consignments without an acceptable certificate of conformity are SAMPLED AND TESTED, and all are subject to random checking. It also registers fish and fishery products and runs pre-export inspection. Note the ministry has moved more than once — Science and Technology, then Science, Technology and Research — so cite the Act rather than the parent.

certify.d: Largely export-facing, for tea and spices; the 2021 agrochemical ban and its reversal is the context anyone here should know. Largely for tea and spice export. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

test.d: Runs food testing including GMO detection. Its Biotechnology Section houses the national testing laboratory for detecting and identifying living modified organisms, established 2022, about 8,000 square feet laid out as a one-way laboratory to avoid cross-contamination, with procedures traceable to ISO methods. It was funded by the GEF and FAO — a national testing capability paid for by an international fund, which is how most of the laboratories in this category came to exist. Sri Lankan law requires food containing GM substances to be declared for import and sale, so there is a rule for the test to serve.

legal.n: MONLAR — Movement for Land and Agricultural Reform (Sri Lanka)
legal.d: Works on seed and land policy; the 2021 agrochemical ban and its reversal is the context here. Formed in 1990 as a NETWORK of farmer organisations, NGOs and people's organisations, and LA VÍA CAMPESINA'S MEMBER IN SRI LANKA. Its working method is the PEOPLE'S PLANNING FORUM: local forums where members meet to SHARE SKILLS AS WELL AS SEEDS and act together to protect their environment — the same farmer-to-farmer logic as Nicaragua's Campesino a Campesino, organised around a local assembly. It also runs a model ECOLOGICAL FARM jointly with the Makandura Government Farm, used as a centre for farmer training — a state farm and a peasant movement operating a demonstration site together. Two further things a reader can use: it maintains a LIBRARY at Rajagiriya on ecology and natural resource management, including post-1977 acts, cabinet papers and white papers and the writings of its founder Sarath Fernando; and it has scrutinised national land policy in detail, including the Urumaya land-titling programme launched in 2024 and discontinued in March 2025.

cl_report.d: The national centre for adverse event reporting, part of the WHO programme. Reports from patients are accepted in most member countries.

fe_register.d: The regional society, which runs training and publishes regional data where national registers do not exist. ASPIRE covers the Asia-Pacific and its data are drawn from members who choose to report, so coverage varies sharply by country. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment
decides.d: Holds biosafety. Nepal prohibits the import of engineered seed, and the practical question is what crosses the open border with India rather than what is authorised. Formed on 14 May 2026 by merging the Ministry of Forests and Environment with the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development, so both predecessor names appear on documents and both predecessor sites may still be serving.

complain.n: PQPMC — Plant Quarantine and Pesticide Management Centre (Nepal)
complain.d: Formed by restructuring the Plant Protection Directorate and the National Plant Quarantine Programme, and UPGRADED TO A CENTRAL-LEVEL ORGANISATION by government decision of 17 April 2018 under the federal structure — so citations to the Plant Protection Directorate inside the Department of Agriculture, or to npqpnepal.gov.np, predate it. It is Nepal's national plant protection organisation and IPPC contact point, and its chief also serves as the Designated National Authority for Pesticides under the ROTTERDAM CONVENTION — which matters: that is the treaty route for prior informed consent on hazardous chemicals in trade. Five sections: NPPO, plant quarantine regulation and monitoring, PESTICIDE REGISTRATION AND MANAGEMENT, pest risk analysis, and survey and surveillance. Fifteen quarantine offices — three on the China border, one at Tribhuvan International Airport, eleven along the Indian border. Hariharbhawan, Lalitpur.

complain.n: Department of Food Technology and Quality Control
complain.d: Handles food safety and labelling. Based in Babarmahal, Kathmandu, under the agriculture and livestock development ministry, acting under the Food Act and Food Rules. It inspects food industries, markets and import consignments, runs laboratory testing of samples for contaminants and adulteration, and can seize substandard food and take legal action. Nepal splits the rest across several acts and departments — pesticides sit with the Department of Agriculture, standards with the Bureau of Standards and Metrology under the industry ministry, and local governments do market monitoring.

certify.d: Participatory schemes, mostly domestic. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.d: Works on seed law and the imports crossing the open border with India. Established 1992 and working as a NETWORK between individuals and organisations rather than as a single field operator — so it is the way to find the practitioners, not the practitioner itself. For hands-on work the counterpart is the HIMALAYAN PERMACULTURE CENTRE, a farmer-led body registered at district and government level, an alliance of community groups across villages in Surkhet and Humla, whose staff and members are all farmers; it runs demonstration, training, RESOURCE PRODUCTION and research at its own centres in Kathmandu, Surkhet and Humla, and on farmers' own land — with the stated rule that on-farm research must be RISK-FREE, because a failed experiment costs a household food. That constraint is worth carrying anywhere this map suggests on-farm testing. Read alongside Nepal's PQPMC entry: the same country's pesticide registration and Rotterdam authority sit there.

Represents growers, in a country where what crosses the open border with India is the practical question. Founded 1951, LA VÍA CAMPESINA'S MEMBER IN NEPAL and the country's largest peasant federation — an alliance of 23 national producer organisations with structure in ALL 75 DISTRICTS, which is the reach that matters in a country where the regulator sits in Kathmandu. Recently active on food sovereignty, the right to food and climate justice as well as land reform. A caution: Nepal has more than one national farmer body and they are politically distinct — the Nepal Farmers Association, founded the same year, is the peasant wing of the Nepali Congress and works toward commercialisation of agriculture. Name the organisation, not just 'the farmers' federation'.

fe_register.d: The regional society, which runs training and publishes regional data where national registers do not exist. ASPIRE covers the Asia-Pacific and its data are drawn from members who choose to report, so coverage varies sharply by country. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Irrigation
decides.d: Handles approvals. Myanmar grows engineered cotton, much of it from seed that arrived without formal approval — the same adoption-before-registration pattern seen in Pakistan and Paraguay. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: Plant Protection Division — Department of Agriculture (Myanmar)
complain.d: Inspects seed and crops. One caution about this source: the IPPC contact record is updated by the country itself and can lag — records checked here carried ministry names that had since changed. The named person, address and telephone are the useful part; treat the institutional name as a starting point and check it against the ministry's own site. Read this row together with the two others for this country. The FDA under the health ministry covers food, drugs, devices and cosmetics on the market; this division covers plant health and pesticides in the field. But the finding recorded in Myanmar's legal-help entry governs both: ENGINEERED COTTON ARRIVED LARGELY WITHOUT A FORMAL APPROVAL ROUTE, so a complaint about it is not a complaint about a breach of a permit — there was no permit to breach. That changes what a reader is asking for: not enforcement of a condition, but a decision on material already planted. The IPPC country page carries the named contact.

complain.n: Food and Drug Administration Myanmar
complain.d: Handles food labelling and safety. Established 1995 as a division and upgraded to a separate department in April 2013, under the health ministry and headquartered in Nay Pyi Taw. It covers food, drugs, medical devices and cosmetics together. Agricultural questions sit elsewhere: engineered cotton in Myanmar arrived largely without a formal approval route, which is recorded in the legal-help row for this country.

certify.d: Small and export-facing. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.d: Works with smallholder growers on seed, in a country where engineered cotton preceded approval. Established 1998 and described as Myanmar's largest grassroots NGO, working initially with communities in Kachin State affected by decades of conflict and later more widely, regardless of ethnic origin or religion. Its six areas include AGRICULTURE AND FORESTRY and livelihoods, and it has worked with large numbers of farmers on TRANSITION TO ORGANIC FARMING — which is the relevant thread here, because reporting from the Ayeyarwady delta describes foreign SEED CORPORATIONS, livestock breeding operations and feed companies establishing demonstration zones and pressing for land relocation, irrigation routing and RICE SEED PURE-LINE SELECTION, alongside land acquisition from small farmers. Its projects are designed with SELF-HELP MECHANISMS intended to reach self-sufficiency within three years rather than continuing dependence on external funding. TWO CAUTIONS: its own domain has not been reliably reachable, so the link here is the Myanmar Information Management Unit's stable record; and since the 2021 coup the operating environment for civil society organisations has changed, so verify current status and take care in approaching anyone.

legal.n: Myanmar — the legal position, and why no organisation is named here
legal.d: Represent growers of engineered cotton that largely arrived without formal approval. NO ORGANISATION IS NAMED IN THIS ROW DELIBERATELY. The ORGANIZATION REGISTRATION LAW of 28 October 2022 makes registration MANDATORY FOR ALL ASSOCIATIONS regardless of size or location under criminal penalty — up to five years' imprisonment — restricts permitted activity to 'social tasks', PROHIBITS ANYTHING DIRECTLY OR INDIRECTLY RELATED TO THE POLITICAL OR ECONOMIC SECTORS, and bars service to those the authorities deem opponents. Naming a group as a contact could expose it. THE LEGAL POSITION ON ENGINEERED ORGANISMS, which a reader can use without contacting anyone: Myanmar HAS NO COMPREHENSIVE BIOSAFETY LEGISLATION. A Biosafety Law was drafted but not adopted. BT COTTON WAS APPROVED UNDER AN EARLIER VERSION OF THE SEED LAW while all other imported seed must arrive with a NON-GE CERTIFICATE, and an estimated 75% of cotton farmers were planting Bt cotton by 2017/18. There is no clear law on developing, planting, selling or importing GE food or feed, AND NO PROCESS FOR REQUESTING APPROVALS. Related laws: Pesticide Law, Plant Pest Quarantine Law, Seed Law, Animal Health and Development Law.

fe_register.d: The regional society, which runs training and publishes regional data where national registers do not exist. ASPIRE covers the Asia-Pacific and its data are drawn from members who choose to report, so coverage varies sharply by country. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

decides.d: Handles biosafety under the Cartagena Protocol; there is no commercial cultivation. What the country profile actually holds: the national focal point and competent authorities the country has notified, its national biosafety law where filed, and the decisions it has submitted under Article 20. It is a country's OWN filings, so a thin profile means the country has filed little — not that it decides little. Filing is a treaty obligation without a sanction for missing it.

complain.n: DPPSPS — Plant Protection, Sanitary and Phytosanitary Department, General Directorate of Agriculture (Cambodia)
complain.d: Inspects seed and imports. THREE BODIES SPLIT THIS WORK, and knowing which is which saves a wasted letter. The DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE LEGISLATION (DAL) is the REGULATORY AUTHORITY for pesticide registration, licensing and inspection, and is Cambodia's ROTTERDAM CONVENTION focal point, acceded May 2013 — so a prior-informed-consent question goes there. The DPPSPS is the TECHNICAL adviser: pest monitoring, forecasting, OUTBREAK WARNING, INVASIVE SPECIES CONTROL, efficacy field testing for registration, and recommendations on pesticide use. The NATIONAL AGRICULTURAL LABORATORY does the analysis. Stockholm, Montreal and Basel focal points sit in the MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT instead. Two candid findings worth carrying: Cambodia has NO PESTICIDE MANUFACTURING CAPACITY and most product is imported OFFICIALLY AND ILLEGALLY from Thailand and Vietnam; and an ADB assessment recorded that NO LABORATORY IN THE COUNTRY COULD ANALYSE FOR PESTICIDE RESIDUES although the equipment existed. A Plant Protection and Quarantine Law was in draft to replace Sub-Decree No. 15 on Phytosanitary Inspection — check whether it has passed. #54b/49F, Street 393-656, Toul Kok, Phnom Penh.

complain.n: CCF — Consumer Protection, Competition and Fraud Repression Directorate-General
complain.d: Inspects imports and enforces labelling rules, and takes consumer complaints about the quality and safety of goods on sale. Renamed from Camcontrol by Sub-decree 38 of 16 March 2020 and raised to a directorate-general under the Ministry of Commerce, with branches in the capital and 25 provinces. It acts on what is being sold; it does not authorise a release or inspect a field. Formerly CAMCONTROL, and the lineage explains its character: founded 1983 as the Cambodia Import-Export Inspection Company, an inspection business, becoming an office in 1992, a department in 1997, a directorate-general in 2008, and reconstituted under Sub-Decree No. 38 of 16 March 2020. Its Department of Consumer Protection has four offices — Investigation; Repression of Fraud and False Propaganda; CONSUMER COMPLAINT HANDLING and dissemination; and Trade Inspection — and there are 25 branches across the capital and provinces. It also runs its own Laboratory Department. So the complaint, the investigation and the analysis are all inside one directorate-general.

certify.d: Participatory schemes for rice and pepper. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.n: CEDAC — Cambodian Center for Study and Development in Agriculture
legal.d: Works on seed systems and agricultural policy. Founded August 1997 with initial support from the French NGO GRET, to develop ECOLOGICALLY BASED FAMILY AGRICULTURE and a cooperative and mutual assistance movement in rural Cambodia. It is recognised above all for FARMER-LED EXTENSION SERVICES, innovation training, support for farmer organisations and its publications — so the practical route here is training and organising rather than litigation. Its cooperatives let smallholders buy seed, fertiliser and equipment together and negotiate directly with buyers, which is the bargaining-power answer to a seed market a single farmer cannot influence, and it has organised organic rice export to Europe. ONE THING TO WEIGH: its founder, Yang Saing Koma, later became a Secretary of State in the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries and a member of the ruling party's central committee — a route into government that also means the organisation is not at arm's length from it. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

decides.n: Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment
decides.d: Handles biosafety; no commercial cultivation is authorised. What the country profile actually holds: the national focal point and competent authorities the country has notified, its national biosafety law where filed, and the decisions it has submitted under Article 20. It is a country's OWN filings, so a thin profile means the country has filed little — not that it decides little. Filing is a treaty obligation without a sanction for missing it.

complain.n: Department of Agriculture (Laos)
complain.d: Inspects seed and imports. The instrument is REGULATION No. 2860/MAF of 11 June 2010 on the Control of Pesticides, made under the Law on Agriculture, the ENVIRONMENT PROTECTION LAW and the Law on Food, and it covers production, processing, import and export, distribution, transportation, storage, use AND PROPER DISPOSAL. ALL PESTICIDES produced, imported, exported, distributed or used must be REGISTERED WITH THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE. Two exceptions are stated plainly and are worth knowing: registration is NOT required for BOTANICAL PESTICIDES THAT ARE NOT PACKED FOR SALE — which protects home-prepared plant preparations — and provisional registration may be granted for products imported for RESEARCH, TRIAL OR EXHIBITION where they are registered in the country of origin. Enforcement runs down to the DISTRICT AGRICULTURE AND FORESTRY OFFICE, with staff assigned to a pesticide inspection unit. Violators are educated, warned, fined or punished by severity. Candid note: an SPS assessment records that Lao PDR lacks a functioning SPS management system and has VERY LITTLE ABILITY TO CONTROL AGRO-CHEMICALS.

complain.n: Food and Drug Department
complain.d: Handles food labelling and safety. The FDD registers and licenses food products and establishments and inspects processing facilities, IMPORT CHECKPOINTS and retail outlets. Testing sits with the FOOD AND DRUG QUALITY CENTRE, one of two main laboratories in Vientiane analysing samples collected by food inspectors, covering physical, chemical and microbiological analysis. The FDD also hosts the permanent bureau of the national food commission, which draws members from SEVEN MINISTRIES, and is the country's CODEX CONTACT POINT — so it is the address for a standards question as well as a complaint.

certify.d: Participatory certification, largely domestic. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.n: Asian Farmers' Association for Sustainable Rural Development
legal.d: A regional federation of national farmers' organisations, covering countries where no domestic organisation works on this subject specifically.

decides.d: Handles biosafety. Papua New Guinea holds extraordinary crop and forest diversity and very little regulatory capacity, which is the combination the Cartagena Protocol was written for. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

decides.n: Your Cartagena focal point — the current office
decides.d: The named biosafety contact for this country, kept current by the Secretariat. Where a department has been renamed or merged, this is the list that says which office holds it now. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: NAQIA — National Agriculture Quarantine and Inspection Authority
complain.d: Established 1994 under the Quarantine Act, headquartered in Port Moresby, administering that Act and inspecting and testing agricultural products against quarantine and health standards. Its surveillance runs at airports, seaports and international mail exchanges — the entry points rather than the field, which is the limit of it. The stakes are stated in its own material: about 87% of the population depends on agricultural production and 26% of produce is exported, with rural populations heavily dependent on subsistence agriculture, and the country is relatively free of many pests and diseases found elsewhere. Linked through the national trade facilitation portal, which is reachable; naqia.gov.pg is the agency's own domain. A CORRECTION to the border-only reading I recorded earlier. NAQIA monitors and surveys at airports, seaports AND INTERNATIONAL MAIL EXCHANGES, and under the NAQIA ACT 1997 it may ORDER THE TREATMENT of imported animals or plants, or SOIL, COMPOST, MANURES, ORGANIC FERTILISERS, hay, straw, fodder, litter, clothing, utensils, packages or packing material used in connection with an importation — a treatment power over material already landed, not merely a power to refuse entry. The Minister may declare by NATIONAL GAZETTE notice that goods shall not enter from a specified place. Offences carry fines, and in one prosecution provision THE BURDEN OF PROVING WANT OF KNOWLEDGE falls on the defendant. Two structural points: NAQIA is a CORPORATE BODY funded both by parliamentary appropriation AND FEES FOR SERVICES, and — worth knowing before citing a statute — the Quarantine Act 1953 was never amended to remove its animal and plant components, so those functions are TECHNICALLY DUPLICATED with the Department of Agriculture and Livestock.

complain.n: NISIT — National Institute of Standards and Industrial Technology (PNG)
complain.d: Handles food labelling standards. Established under the NISIT ACT 1993 as the statutory national standards body, covering technical standards, METROLOGY, conformity assessment schemes and technical barriers to trade, and it sets quality benchmarks for FOOD PRODUCTS. Note the boundary: BIOSECURITY AND IMPORT INSPECTION ARE NAQIA'S, and food regulation is shared with the Department of Agriculture and Livestock. ONE HONEST NOTE ON ORGANIC CERTIFICATION: PNG HAS NO NATIONAL ORGANIC STANDARD. Work with DAL and NISIT to develop one was advised but did not progress, and organic production for export therefore runs on INTERNATIONAL STANDARDS — IFOAM and the EC Regulation — applied by foreign certifiers. So a PNG grower seeking certification is dealing with an overseas standard and an overseas certifier, not a national one. P.O. Box 3042.

certify.d: Mostly coffee and cocoa for export. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.n: Centre for Environmental Law and Community Rights
legal.d: Public interest environmental lawyers, and the practical route in a country with extraordinary diversity and little regulatory capacity. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

test.d: The Pacific Community runs the regional plant health and testing capacity that individual island states do not maintain. What that means in practice: a sample may have to leave the country to be analysed, with the delay and cost that implies, and the regional laboratory sets its own priorities. Where a national standards body or agriculture department can do the analysis, it is the nearer route.

notice.d: Pacific island states handle biosafety largely through regional bodies and their Clearing-House filings rather than a national notice venue, because almost everything arrives as an import rather than an application.
notice.conf: No national notice venue — this describes where decisions surface, not a page that announces them in advance. Check the country's Clearing-House record.

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture — Biosecurity Authority of Fiji
decides.d: Handles biosafety and biosecurity together, which is common across the Pacific: island states treat an engineered organism as an import question first.

decides.n: Your Cartagena focal point — the current office
decides.d: The named biosafety contact for this country, kept current by the Secretariat. Where a department has been renamed or merged, this is the list that says which office holds it now. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: BAF — Biosecurity Authority of Fiji
complain.d: Inspects imports and enforces. Established 17 December 2008 under the Biosecurity Promulgation, replacing the Quarantine and Inspection Department inside the agriculture ministry, and reassigned to the Minister for Agriculture and Waterways in 2019. Its statutory mandate reaches well past the border and is the reason to write to it: as well as protecting against entry, it must carry out SURVEILLANCE AND MONITORING of pests and diseases within Fiji, prevent the establishment and spread of regulated pests and THE RELEASE OF ORGANISMS that might adversely affect animals, plants, human beings or the environment, and eradicate, contain or control what is already present. Note its constitutional form: it is a COMMERCIAL Statutory Authority under the Public Enterprise Act 1996, funded partly by prescribed fees under the Biosecurity (Fees and Charges) Regulations 2011 — a regulator with commercial objectives, which is unusual and worth knowing. Suva headquarters at Provident Plaza I, Ellery Street.

complain.n: Food Unit — Ministry of Health and Medical Services (Fiji)
complain.d: Handles food labelling and safety complaints. The instruments are the FOOD SAFETY ACT 2003 and the FOOD SAFETY REGULATIONS 2009. The Act requires EVERY FOOD ESTABLISHMENT TO BE INSPECTED AT LEAST ONCE A YEAR, and the Food Unit may CANCEL OR REVOKE A HEALTH LICENCE on its own findings or on a municipal council's recommendation — it has closed supermarkets outright. Health inspectors are appointed AUTHORISED OFFICERS under the Act and are based EITHER IN MUNICIPAL COUNCILS OR IN HEALTH OFFICES around the country, with the CENTRAL BOARD OF HEALTH responsible for administration and enforcement — so the nearest authorised officer may sit in the town council. TWO THINGS DIRECTLY RELEVANT HERE: the Act sets MAXIMUM RESIDUE LIMITS for food AND ANIMAL FEED sold or produced locally, and the Regulations publish the PROCEDURE FOR TAKING SAMPLES for physical or chemical analysis, including DIVISION OF THE SAMPLE where possible — a divided sample is what allows an independent re-test. Pesticides are separate: the PESTICIDES ACT 1971, administered by the Ministry of Agriculture, under which an unregistered pesticide may not be used, offered or sold, with a DAILY FINE FOR A CONTINUING OFFENCE.

certify.d: A regional standard used across the Pacific islands. The Pacific Organic Standard is a REGIONAL standard rather than a national law: it is adopted by producers and organisations across the island states rather than enforced by any one government, and much certification under it is participatory rather than third-party. Whether a given initiative excludes engineered material is a question to put to that initiative.

legal.d: Works across the Pacific on trade agreements and their seed and biosafety provisions.

Where a national standards body or agriculture department can do the analysis, it is the nearer route.

decides.d: Handles biosafety.

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining
decides.d: Holds seed and crop approvals, and runs the plant quarantine service that inspects what arrives. Fisheries and mining sit in the same ministry, so an enquiry has to name the agency as well as the ministry to reach the right desk.

complain.n: Plant Quarantine / Produce Inspection Branch (PQPI)
complain.d: Operates under the Agricultural Produce Act 1926 and the Plants (Quarantine) Act 1993, with its head office at 193 Old Hope Road and export complexes at Norman Manley and Sangster international airports. Its stated mandate is imports and exports — ensuring pest-free cut flowers and fresh produce moving in and out — so like most bodies in this category it works at the border. But note the ORDER power under the Quarantine Act: a pest can be declared notifiable and an area declared infected, bringing restrictions on planting, replanting or cultivation inside that area. That is the domestic reach a border service usually lacks. The branch has been pursuing ISO/IEC 17020:2012 conformity for its export services.

complain.n: BSJ — Bureau of Standards Jamaica (and the NCRA)
complain.d: A CORRECTION. BSJ was established under the Standards Act 1969 and holds responsibility for the Processed Food Act 1959 and the Weights and Measures Act 1976. But it RESTRUCTURED IN 2018: the regulatory and enforcement functions were delegated to a separate body, the National Compliance and Regulatory Authority (NCRA), which operates independently of BSJ. So BSJ develops standards, tests, calibrates and certifies — the right address for an analysis — and the NCRA is where enforcement now sits. Same split as Rwanda's, five years earlier. BSJ remains Jamaica's WTO/TBT National Enquiry Point and FAO/WHO Codex contact point, and proposed technical regulations are published for a 30-day comment period before final publication in the Jamaica Gazette Supplement.

certify.d: National organic body. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.d: Public interest environmental organisation that files on planning and environmental decisions.

notice.d: Decisions are gazetted; imports are the practical question. Not linked here: check for a current online edition, or ask the Cartagena focal point for the issue. The gazette is authoritative in print, and in most jurisdictions a measure takes effect on the date it is published there. Not linked here: check for a current online edition, or ask the Cartagena focal point for the issue.

test.d: Caribbean testing runs through regional facilities in Trinidad and Jamaica rather than one per island. The Bureau of Standards Jamaica is named elsewhere in this country's entries and runs testing laboratories of its own; where a sample can be handled domestically that is the nearer route, and the regional reference laboratory is for what it cannot do.

decides.d: Handles biosafety under the Cartagena Protocol. What the country profile actually holds: the national focal point and competent authorities the country has notified, its national biosafety law where filed, and the decisions it has submitted under Article 20. It is a country's OWN filings, so a thin profile means the country has filed little — not that it decides little. Filing is a treaty obligation without a sanction for missing it.

complain.n: CFDD — Chemistry, Food and Drugs Division, Ministry of Health
complain.d: The body TTBS excludes. The CFDD administers the FOOD AND DRUGS ACT Chapter 30:01 AND THE PESTICIDES AND TOXIC CHEMICALS ACT Chapter 30:03 — so food and pesticides are both here, which is unusual. Its Food and Drug Inspectorate inspects and SAMPLES foods, drugs, cosmetics, chemicals and the devices used to manufacture, process or preserve them, visiting manufacturing establishments; the Chemistry, Food and Drugs Laboratory does the chemical and microbiological analysis for compliance with both Acts, so the complaint and the test are in one division. Two committees advise the Minister — a Food Advisory Committee on food standards and LABELLING, and the Pesticides and Toxic Chemicals Board which regulates pesticides. One power worth knowing: where an imported food would breach the Act, an inspector may admit it FOR RE-LABELLING OR RECONDITIONING under supervision, and if that is not satisfactorily done within three months it is forfeit. National food safety standards are adopted from Codex. Maraj Building, 92 Frederick Street, Port of Spain; cfdd@health.gov.tt.

complain.n: Plant Quarantine Service — Ministry of Agriculture, Land and Fisheries
complain.d: Works under the Plant Protection Act 13 of 1975, issuing import permits, inspecting import and export cargo and baggage at ports of entry, seizing where necessary, and executing POST-ENTRY inspections — the last of which is what takes it past the border. Suspicious material goes to the Entomology and Plant Pathology Diagnostic Laboratories for testing before conditional release or destruction, and plant material is screened in a glasshouse. Imports contravening the Act are seized and destroyed. Import permit applications are processed through the trade ministry's TTBizLink platform rather than at the service's own office at Centeno. Under the PLANT PROTECTION ACT Chap. 63:56 no person may import fruits, PLANTING MATERIAL, plant pests, PATHOGENS, plant products, SOIL or vegetables without a permit, applied for FOUR WEEKS in advance. The Regulations are strict in ways worth knowing: propagating material must be limited to the SMALLEST POSSIBLE PROPAGATIVE UNIT; plants and rooted cuttings ARE NOT ADMISSIBLE IF ESTABLISHED IN A GROWING MEDIUM OTHER THAN AGAR-BASED MEDIA — which effectively channels living plant imports through TISSUE CULTURE; anything carrying or contaminated with soil is prohibited; and restricted articles ARRIVING BY MAIL are covered through joint arrangements between the Postal and Plant Quarantine Services and Customs. The ministry has warned expressly that ONLINE PURCHASES from Amazon, eBay or similar need the same permit and a phytosanitary certificate, or the items may be seized. Suspicious material goes to the Entomology and Plant Pathology Diagnostic Laboratories or the glasshouse before conditional release or DESTRUCTION. Permits now run through the TTBizLink single window, which shows ONLY commodities the PEST RISK ANALYSIS UNIT has approved for that country of origin. Movement between Trinidad and Tobago itself can require a phytosanitary certificate.

complain.n: TTBS — Trinidad and Tobago Bureau of Standards
complain.d: A CORRECTION that matters for this map. TTBS, established 8 July 1974 and now under the Standards Act No. 18 of 1997, states its primary role as developing, promoting AND ENFORCING standards — but its mandate covers all goods EXCEPT FOOD, DRUGS AND COSMETICS. Those are the Chemistry, Food and Drug Division of the Ministry of Health. So for a food labelling or contamination question this is the wrong body, and the row previously implied otherwise. Note also the domain moved to gottbs.com; ttbs.org.tt remains the email domain. The right address is named below.

certify.d: Small, mostly cocoa. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.n: Caribbean Network for Integrated Rural Development
legal.d: Represents Caribbean smallholders on seed, land and food policy across the region. LINK REMOVED after a link check: the site no longer resolves. The body may still exist — confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, and through the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, before assuming it has gone.

decides.d: Authorises. Panama grows engineered maize on a modest scale and its position matters disproportionately because of what transits the canal. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: MIDA — Ministerio de Desarrollo Agropecuario
complain.d: Inspects and enforces. Created by Law 12 of 25 January 1973. Its directorates map onto the questions this map asks: plant health for phytosanitary surveillance and diagnosis, animal health, and agricultural quarantine covering both external and internal movement — internal quarantine being the one that matters if something has already been planted. A 2014 executive decree also gave it an environmental unit setting environmental quality standards for the sector. Regional offices and agencies are listed on the site.

complain.n: APA — Agencia Panameña de Alimentos
complain.d: Handles import, transit and transshipment paperwork for food for human and animal consumption, and replaced AUPSA under Law 206 of 30 March 2021. It processes the documents a consignment travels on; it does not authorise a release, and a complaint about a planting goes elsewhere.

certify.d: Small and export-facing. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

notice.d: Decisions are gazetted; what transits the canal gives Panama's position weight beyond its size.

fe_register.n: REDLARA — Red Latinoamericana de Reproducción Asistida
fe_register.d: The Latin American assisted reproduction network: it accredits clinics across the region, runs the continental registry of treatment cycles and outcomes, and publishes an annual report. Across most of Latin America there is no statutory fertility regulator at all, so an accreditation held or withdrawn here is the only external check on a clinic — and the accredited list is public. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

decides.d: Ecuador's constitution declares the country free of engineered seed and crops — one of only a handful of constitutions anywhere addressing this directly, alongside Hungary's.

complain.n: Agrocalidad
complain.d: The agricultural quality agency; inspects and enforces.

complain.n: ARCSA
complain.d: Handles food labelling and safety; the constitution declares the country free of engineered seed.

certify.d: The state agency accredits organic certifiers; Ecuador's constitution already declares the country free of engineered seed. Largely for banana, cacao and coffee export.

notice.d: Where decisions appear, though the constitution already declares the country free of engineered seed and crops.

decides.d: Handles approvals. Guatemala sits inside the centre of origin for maize, where wild relatives and thousands of local varieties still grow, so gene flow here is a different question from gene flow in a field in Iowa. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: VISAR — Viceministerio de Sanidad Agropecuaria y Regulaciones (MAGA, Guatemala)
complain.d: Inspects seed and imports. A CAUTION ON ITS RECENT HISTORY: VISAR WAS ABOLISHED by Acuerdo Gubernativo 217-2023 in September 2023 and RESTORED by Acuerdo Gubernativo 33-2024 on 14 February 2024, so material from that window may name a different structure. Guatemala's national plant protection organisation sits inside it as the DIRECCIÓN DE SANIDAD VEGETAL. VISAR holds PESTICIDE AND SEED REGISTRATION, plant and animal health, and phytosanitary certification — so a complaint about an unregistered input and a question about what is registered go to the same address. Its site publishes the instruments: the Ley de Sanidad Vegetal y Animal and its Reglamento (Acuerdo Gubernativo 745-99), the Reglamento para la Inocuidad de los Alimentos (969-99), the LISTADO DE PLAGAS REGLAMENTADAS (Acuerdo Ministerial 82-2021), and the procedure for authorising third parties to prepare PEST RISK ANALYSES. It runs phytosanitary diagnostic laboratories at Km. 22 and in Petén. Note that quarantine service administration has been delegated to the regional body OIRSA by Acuerdo Gubernativo 438-98.

complain.n: DRCA — Departamento de Regulación y Control de Alimentos (MSPAS, Guatemala)
complain.d: Handles food labelling, in a centre of origin for maize. One of six departments in the DIRECCIÓN GENERAL DE REGULACIÓN, VIGILANCIA Y CONTROL DE LA SALUD. It issues the LICENCIA SANITARIA for any business that manufactures, processes, packages, stores, distributes or sells food, inspects premises, grants the REGISTRO SANITARIO for products, AND SANCTIONS ESTABLISHMENTS THAT BREACH THE REGULATION. Two checks a reader can run before complaining. EVERY PACKAGED FOOD MUST CARRY A REGISTRO SANITARIO NUMBER ON ITS LABEL, and selling without one carries FINES, PRODUCT SEIZURE AND CRIMINAL LIABILITY under the Código de Salud, Decreto 90-97, arts. 216-220. And the sanitary licence is VALID FIVE YEARS under Acuerdo Gubernativo 969-99 art. 20 unless a later inspection finds serious violations. Registration follows the Central American RTCA 67.01.31:20. THE SURVEILLANCE ROUTE IS PUBLISHED AS A PROCEDURE: DRCA inspectors take food samples and send them to the LNS national laboratory for physicochemical or microbiological testing, returning a conformity evaluation report — so a sample can be taken and tested on the state's own initiative. Avenida Bolívar 28-07 Zona 8; tel 2231-2913.

certify.d: Mostly coffee and cardamom. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.
A Guatemalan certifier operating across Central America, and one of the few based in a centre of origin for maize.

legal.n: REDSAG — Red Nacional por la Defensa de la Soberanía Alimentaria en Guatemala
legal.d: Forced the repeal of the 2014 seed law, one of the clearest reversals of a UPOV-implementing act anywhere. More than 50 organisations, working through political and LEGAL advocacy, with indigenous peoples, peasant communities and fishing communities as the stated political subject. It is directly engaged on the question this map turns on: with the ALIANZA DE AUTORIDADES ANCESTRALES para la Defensa de la Biodiversidad y las Semillas Nativas it has publicly rejected the GENETIC EDITING OF MAIZE IN GUATEMALA, including CRISPR trials, on the ground that it violates food sovereignty and SEEKS TO PATENT AND PRIVATISE NATIVE AND CRIOLLO SEED — noting that most CRISPR agricultural patents sit with Corteva. The argument is made from Guatemala being a centre of maize domestication, dated in the cited study to between 9000 and 1500 BCE in Mesoamerica. That combination — ancestral authorities plus a national food sovereignty network objecting jointly to gene editing — is the clearest documented opposition to the carve-out records this map holds.

notice.d: Decisions are gazetted, in a centre of origin for maize where wild relatives and thousands of local varieties still grow.

Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

decides.d: Authorises. Honduras was the first Central American country to permit engineered maize commercially, and adopted a version of Argentina's Resolution 173 on edited organisms. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: SENASA inspection
complain.d: Inspects seed and crops. THE SPLIT IS CLEAN AND WORTH KNOWING: SENASA registers and regulates AGROCHEMICALS, FERTILISERS AND PESTICIDES; ARSA handles food, cosmetics, medicines and devices. Every product carrying a registro sanitario must SHOW THE REGISTRATION NUMBER ON ITS LABEL, issued by one or the other — so a reader can check a product before complaining, and an absent or irregular number is itself the ground for a denuncia. Read with this country's legal entry, where the Supreme Court struck down the plant variety protection law in 2021 and ANAFAE documented criollo maize contamination.

complain.n: Agencia de Regulación Sanitaria
complain.d: Handles food labelling and safety. Created by Decreto PCM-032-2017 of 28 April 2017, so it postdates older citations to the health ministry. It supervises, verifies and regulates PRODUCTS, SERVICES AND ESTABLISHMENTS affecting public health, and issues the registro sanitario for processed food under the Ley General de Salud and the Reglamento de Alimentos. Two things a reader can use. REGISTRATIONS ARE VERIFIABLE at arsateca.arsa.hn, so a label number can be checked against the register before anything else. And the registration process ITSELF INCLUDES A PLANT INSPECTION — a visit to the production plant for domestic manufacturers, or to the warehouse for importers — with registration valid FIVE YEARS and renewable, which tells a complainant roughly when the establishment was last seen. It also runs a national portal for notifying ADVERSE EVENTS AND INCIDENTS. Offices in Comayagüela (2270-6600) and Comayagua (2772-6575, WhatsApp +504 9207-1251), Mon–Fri 8:00–16:00. Candid note: practitioners report ARSA's published processing deadlines are frequently not met.

certify.d: Mostly coffee for export. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.n: CNTC and the Alianza SARA / REHCAT (Honduras)
legal.d: Work on seed systems in the first Central American country to permit engineered maize. The same organisations represent growers directly. THE COURT RULING IS THE THING TO KNOW: in NOVEMBER 2021 the Supreme Court of Justice declared the LEY DE OBTENTORES DE VEGETALES UNCONSTITUTIONAL — a plant variety protection law passed in 2012 without consultation. That is the second such judgment in this file after Colombia's, and it has been cited as an example for other countries facing seed multinationals. The organisations: the CENTRAL NACIONAL DE TRABAJADORES DEL CAMPO (CNTC), La Vía Campesina's presence, and CODIMCA work on seed and land; the ALIANZA SARA brings together COCOCH, CNTC, ACAN, the Confederación Hondureña de Mujeres Campesinas, COPINH, CEHPRODEC, REDAS and consumer bodies; and REHCAT — the Red Hondureña Contra Agrotóxicos y Transgénicos — was the first national movement, formed after GM maize and soya ENTERED AS FOOD AID AFTER HURRICANE MITCH IN 1998 with no legal framework in place. ANAFAE has documented CONTAMINATION OF CRIOLLO MAIZE, the predictable result of permitting GM maize in the valleys while banning it on hillsides, since maize is open-pollinated. CNTC also records evictions and prosecutions of campesinos, so approach with care.

notice.d: Where SENASA resolutions appear, in the first Central American country to permit engineered maize commercially.

fe_register.d: The Latin American assisted reproduction network: it accredits clinics across the region, runs the continental registry of treatment cycles and outcomes, and publishes an annual report. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. decides.n: Ministry of Environment — National Biosafety Committee
decides.d: Handles approvals. Cameroon's agricultural research institute holds germplasm collections for crops grown across central Africa that exist nowhere else, which is what benefit-sharing arrangements are written about. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: MINADER — Direction de la Réglementation et du Contrôle de Qualité and its regional delegations (Cameroun)
complain.d: Inspects seed and imports. The DRCQ is the address, and its published remit is wide: drafting regulation on agricultural inputs and products AND ON ORGANIC AGRICULTURE; REGIONAL AND SUB-REGIONAL HARMONISATION of input rules; following the international conventions Cameroon has ratified on inputs and on PLANT GENETIC RESOURCES FOR FOOD AND AGRICULTURE; organising SEED AND PLANT CERTIFICATION; quality control of inputs and products; PHYTOSANITARY CONTROL AT THE BORDERS; HOMOLOGATION OF PESTICIDES for agricultural use; and HOMOLOGATION OF SPECIES AND VARIETIES. It contains a Sub-Directorate for Pesticides, Fertilisers and Treatment Equipment, a Sub-Directorate for SEED REGULATION AND PLANT QUARANTINE, and the NATIONAL DIAGNOSTIC LABORATORY for agricultural products and inputs. The COMMISSION NATIONALE D'HOMOLOGATION for phytosanitary products meets under the minister's chairmanship. So variety approval, seed certification, pesticide homologation and the Plant Treaty obligations all sit in one directorate.

complain.n: ANOR — Agence des Normes et de la Qualité (Cameroun)
complain.d: Handles food labelling standards. Created by Décret Présidentiel N°2009/296 of 17 September 2009, under the MINISTRY OF MINES, INDUSTRY AND TECHNOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENT — not agriculture — and it does enforce: its published mandate includes QUALITY CONTROL AND MARKET SURVEILLANCE, verifying conformity and WITHDRAWING NON-CONFORMING PRODUCTS FROM THE MARKET, alongside PRE-SHIPMENT CONFORMITY ASSESSMENT (PECAE) of imported goods. So a product already on sale can be removed by ANOR. It homologates Cameroonian standards through technical committees — Comité Technique n°48 covers FOOD TECHNOLOGY AND PRODUCTS — and is a CODEX member. Yaoundé, Bastos. Note the boundary: pesticide and seed regulation belong to MINADER's DIRECTION DE LA RÉGLEMENTATION ET DU CONTRÔLE DE QUALITÉ, which holds sub-directorates for PESTICIDES, FERTILISERS AND TREATMENT EQUIPMENT and for SEEDS AND PLANT QUARANTINE, a NATIONAL DIAGNOSTIC LABORATORY, responsibility for ORGANIC AGRICULTURE regulation and for PLANT GENETIC RESOURCES conventions, and it runs the COMMISSION NATIONALE D'HOMOLOGATION for phytosanitary products.

certify.d: Participatory certification, largely domestic. Search it by country of operation rather than by country of origin: in most places the certificate a grower actually holds is issued by a multinational certifier working locally, not by a body founded there, and the national names in this category are only part of the picture.

legal.n: RADD — Réseau des Acteurs du Développement Durable (Cameroun)
legal.d: Works on biosafety and germplasm questions in central Africa. Created 1996, based in Yaoundé, and its seed work is the reason to name it. It runs the FOIRE DES SEMENCES PAYSANNES DU CAMEROUN (FOSPAC), an annual three-day event held just before sowing — late February to early March — where farmers exhibit, exchange AND SELL THEIR OWN SEED, with thematic workshops, organised with the agriculture ministry MINADER, GIZ and local administrative authorities including the préfet, sous-préfet and mayor. A peasant seed fair convened WITH the administration rather than against it is a distinct model. It has drafted the DÉCLARATION D'ESSE, a roughly twenty-page advocacy instrument setting out what peasant-seed actors expect of government in honouring its international commitments to recognise peasant seed systems, and what those actors commit to themselves — then taken it round partner sites in CAUSERIES PAYSANNES to be discussed and enriched. It works explicitly on UNDROP, the UN Declaration on the Rights of Peasants, which Cameroon has adhered to, and on FARMERS' RIGHTS OVER SEED.
