legal.d: Biosafety and seed work in Central Africa runs through national farmer organisations and regional environmental networks rather than one coalition. No single regional body has been identified for this; the work runs through national organisations, and the Cartagena focal point is the route to whoever is currently active.

decides.n: Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development
decides.d: Handles biosafety. Madagascar's endemic biodiversity is among the highest on Earth and largely found nowhere else, which makes any deliberate release a different order of question here. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: Direction de la Protection des Végétaux (DPV)
complain.d: The competent authority for plant health and phytosanitary matters across the whole territory, inside the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock. It contains three services and the one that inspects arriving material is the Service de l'Inspection et de la Quarantaine Végétale, so an enquiry has to name it. It also registers agropharmaceutical products. Formerly the Service de la Protection des Végétaux under the 1986 law, a title that now belongs to a sub-unit rather than to the authority. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.

test.n: South African approved GMO testing laboratories (DALRRD / SANAS)
test.d: Madagascar has no national capacity to detect engineered material, so samples go to South Africa. That is a definite route rather than a vague one: the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development approves laboratories through its Directorate of Genetic Resources specifically for GMO testing of seed lots, and the South African National Accreditation System accredits them to ISO/IEC 17025, an accreditation recognised internationally through ILAC. Holders of that approval include SciCorp and GreenHill Laboratories; both are private companies, and testing is a paid service with no public route behind it. South Africa is the only country on the continent growing engineered crops commercially, which is why the detection capacity sits there. nearest capable laboratory is in another country and access runs through the regional body.

complain.n: Direction de la Production Végétale
complain.d: Inspects seed and crops. The unit inside it is the SERVICE DE LA PROTECTION DES VÉGÉTAUX ET DU CONTRÔLE PHYTOSANITAIRE (SPVCP), 01 BP 58, Porto-Novo, and its head is registered with the IPPC as a phytosanitary inspector expert in surveillance AND PESTICIDE MANAGEMENT. Departmentally the DPV acts THROUGH THE DIRECTIONS DÉPARTEMENTALES DE L'AGRICULTURE, DE L'ÉLEVAGE ET DE LA PÊCHE (DDAEP), which hold the SERVICE DE LA RÉGLEMENTATION ET DU CONTRÔLE — so the departmental DDAEP is the nearer office and the SRC the unit that enforces. Two other bodies to know: the COMITÉ NATIONAL DE GESTION DES PESTICIDES (CNGP) handles pesticide management including HIGHLY HAZARDOUS PESTICIDES, and the AGENCE BÉNINOISE DE L'ENVIRONNEMENT covers the environmental side. PHYTOSANITARY RISK ANALYSIS (ARP) is a named instrument here. Read with this country's legal entry — OBEPAB, which works on organic cotton and pesticide reduction.

legal.n: OBEPAB — Organisation Béninoise pour la Promotion de l’Agriculture Biologique
legal.d: Worked on the decade-long moratorium. A non-profit created 1995 and registered in 1997, founded expressly TO REDUCE PESTICIDE USE, on the stated ground that much ill health and many deaths in rural Benin are caused by pesticides. Its central work is ORGANIC COTTON — which matters directly to this map, since cotton is where engineered varieties enter West African farming. It works with producer organisations rather than for them: it hosted an exchange visit in 2022 for cotton growers from MALI, BURKINA FASO, SENEGAL AND CAMEROON through the Association des Producteurs de Coton Africains, so it is a regional teaching point, and it runs public workshops with input suppliers, the agriculture ministry, the national research institute and organic cotton producers' unions. Its coordinator's stated position is notable and quotable: conversion of everyone to organic is not required — there are practices people can adopt to improve conventional production. Related site: pabebenin.org.

test.n: Laboratoire National de Biosécurité, Ouagadougou — UEMOA reference laboratory
test.d: Designated as the reference laboratory for GMO analysis for the eight UEMOA states and as the central node of a sub-regional laboratory network. Operational since September 2019 at Kamboinsin, attached to Burkina Faso's Agence Nationale de Biosécurité, equipped for detection, identification and quantification of engineered organisms, serological and nucleic-acid analysis, and compositional analysis of food. The sub-regional network it anchors is still being formed, so this is the designated route rather than a demonstrated routine one and a sample crossing a border may have to be arranged case by case; detection capacity in the region in practice sits in Nigeria, Ghana and Burkina Faso. It analyses a sample and reports; it does not authorise a release and does not take a complaint. nearest capable laboratory is in another country and access runs through the regional body. decides.d: Handles biosafety. Nicaragua permits no commercial cultivation and its seed law protects farmer varieties, which is the position most of Central America has moved away from. The Clearing-House entry in this box explains what a country profile holds and what a thin one means.

complain.n: IPSA — Instituto de Protección y Sanidad Agropecuaria
complain.d: Inspects seed and imports. IPSA is Nicaragua's national plant protection organisation under LEY 862, its creating law, and LEY 1020, LEY DE PROTECCIÓN FITOSANITARIA — note the second is newer than most instruments in this file. Its Departamento de Semillas administers Ley No. 280 on seed production and trade within the Sistema Nacional de Semillas, so SEED CERTIFICATION, VARIETY REGISTRATION AND PLANT HEALTH SIT IN ONE INSTITUTE. Certification inspectors visit research centres, nurseries, seed sources, production fields, processing and ginning plants and storage. Kilómetro 5.5 carretera norte, Managua. Read with this country's legal entry: Ley 693 gives civil society a standing role through the COTESSAN technical councils.

complain.n: ANRS / Dirección de Alimentos — MINSA (Nicaragua)
complain.d: Handles food registration and labelling. THE DIVIDING LINE WITH IPSA IS THE DEGREE OF PROCESSING, which is unusually clean: MINSA, through the AUTORIDAD NACIONAL DE REGULACIÓN SANITARIA (ANRS) and its Dirección de Alimentos, controls PROCESSED AND SEMI-PROCESSED FOODS, pre-packaged drinks, cosmetics, hygiene products, medicines and devices; IPSA covers UNPROCESSED agricultural raw materials of plant or animal origin AND ANIMAL FEED INPUTS. So a packaged product goes to MINSA, a field or feed question to IPSA. MINSA issues the REGISTRO SANITARIO DE ALIMENTO and licences for food and drink establishments, with an online pre-solicitud. Its authority rests on LEY N° 423, Ley General de Salud, alongside the Central American technical regulations, and it publishes resolutions, circulars and forms by date.

legal.n: The seed and food sovereignty law framework (Nicaragua) — and where to take it
legal.d: Works on the seed law that protects farmer varieties. NAME THE LAWS RATHER THAN A GROUP, because the small promotion groups here have no durable web presence and a reader is better served by the instruments. Seed is governed by LEY No. 280, Ley de Producción y Comercio de Semillas (1997), administered by IPSA's Departamento de Semillas as part of the Sistema Nacional de Semillas, with Central American technical regulations and Nicaraguan certification norms beneath it; certification inspectors visit research centres, nurseries, SEED SOURCES, production fields, processing and ginning plants and storage. Pesticides sit under LEY No. 274. The lever is LEY No. 693, LEY DE SOBERANÍA Y SEGURIDAD ALIMENTARIA Y NUTRICIONAL, which defines FOOD SOVEREIGNTY as the right of peoples to define their own policies, and builds in a role for CIVIL SOCIETY defined expressly to include producer guilds, ethnic, women's and youth associations, community groups and unions — with sectoral technical councils (COTESSAN) advising the executive secretariat. For a citizen the practical route is that council structure. Read with UNAG and its Campesino a Campesino programme.

legal.n: UNAG — Unión Nacional de Agricultores y Ganaderos (Nicaragua)
legal.d: The national growers' union; Nicaraguan seed law protects farmer varieties. A GREMIAL organisation of agricultural and livestock producers — a membership body of farmers rather than an NGO speaking for them, which is the distinction that matters when a government asks who is represented. Its stated purpose is improving members' quality of life while promoting sustainability and socioeconomic competitiveness in harmony with the environment. THE PART THAT TRANSFERS: it runs the PROGRAMA CAMPESINO A CAMPESINO (PCAC) — farmer-to-farmer extension, in which practices spread by peasants teaching peasants rather than by state extension officers. That method originated in Central America and has been adopted worldwide; for a reader wanting seed and agroecological knowledge to move without depending on an extension service, this is the documented model. Note UNAG's own web presence is thin; the profile linked here is a stable directory record. A separate national body, UNAPA, represents associated producers.

fe_register.n: REDLARA — Red Latinoamericana de Reproducción Asistida
fe_register.d: The Latin American assisted reproduction network: it accredits clinics across the region, runs the continental registry of treatment cycles and outcomes, and publishes an annual report. Across most of Latin America there is no statutory fertility regulator at all, so an accreditation held or withdrawn here is the only external check on a clinic — and the accredited list is public. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.

complain.n: DGSVA — Dirección General de Sanidad Vegetal y Animal (MAG, El Salvador)
complain.d: Inspects seed and crops. ITS PUBLISHED SERVICE LIST NAMES THE COMPLAINT ROUTE FIRST: 'ATENCIÓN A DENUNCIA DE PROBLEMAS CON PLAGAS EN VEGETALES' — attending to complaints about pest problems in plants — alongside training for producers and the general public on phytosanitary matters, and TAKING SAMPLES OF VEGETABLES TO MONITOR FOR PESTICIDES. It also inspects, in the country of origin, the plants and production units of agricultural products to be imported, and SELLS BENEFICIAL ORGANISMS for fruit fly control (Diachasmimorpha longicaudata), which is an unusual public service. The instrument is the LEY DE SANIDAD VEGETAL Y ANIMAL, Decreto 524, and the enforcing arm for pesticides is MAG's Inspection and Registration Division: NO PESTICIDE MAY BE MANUFACTURED, FORMULATED, IMPORTED OR DISTRIBUTED WITHOUT REGISTRATION, and registration requires the scientific and commercial name, the quantitative and qualitative formula, structural chemistry, and the name and address of the manufacturer, importer or distributor. Note the Central American regional pesticide registration system: registration in one country of the region can carry into the others. Santa Tecla, La Libertad; IPPC contact registered June 2024.

complain.n: Departamento de Sanidad Vegetal
complain.d: Inspects imports and seed. It holds pesticide registration and oversight of the import, manufacture and distribution of plaguicidas as well as plant health, so both questions go here. THE SERVICE TO ASK FOR IS DIAGNÓSTICO FITOSANITARIO, and the procedure is published step by step: a written request to the Encargado del Departamento de Sanidad Vegetal OR THE DIRECTOR OF YOUR REGIONAL OFFICE; the department then contacts you to arrange A VISIT TO THE PLACE WHERE THE CASE APPEARS, takes data on site, TAKES A SAMPLE AND SENDS IT TO A LABORATORY, and issues a report with the results. That is a free on-site investigation with laboratory analysis, requestable by an ordinary grower — rare in this file. Its División de Cuarentena Vegetal runs 25 quarantine stations across 9 airports, 12 seaports and 4 land crossings, with diagnostic laboratories at Las Américas airport and Haina Oriental offering phytopathology, nematology and weed analysis. Two cautions: a law creating a consolidated SENASIA has been drafted, which would move these functions; and domestic reporting describes inspector numbers and field resources as severely reduced. Tel. 809 547-3888. Mon–Fri 8:00–16:00.

complain.n: DIGEMAPS — Dirección General de Medicamentos, Alimentos y Productos Sanitarios (República Dominicana)
complain.d: Handles food labelling and safety. DIGEMAPS holds the REGISTRO SANITARIO for pre-packaged food and drink under the Reglamento Sanitario de Alimentos, and runs a VIGILANCIA SANITARIA service. THE CHECK WORTH KNOWING: the register of food and beverage sanitary registrations IS PUBLISHED AS AN OPEN DATASET on datos.gob.do covering 2018 onward, so a reader can look up whether a specific product is registered rather than asking. Imports are gated: THE CUSTOMS DIRECTORATE MAY NOT RELEASE COMMERCIAL FOOD IMPORTS WITHOUT PRIOR AUTHORISATION FROM THE MINISTRY OF SALUD PÚBLICA. A foreign-origin product made locally additionally requires a certificate from the competent authority of the country of origin, LEGALISED OR APOSTILLED, confirming the producer is authorised there. Labels must meet NORDOM 53. Av. Tiradentes, Ens. La Fe, Santo Domingo; (809) 541-3121.

test.n: No regional GMO testing laboratory — Caribbean
test.d: The Dominican Republic is not a CARICOM member, so testing runs through national food laboratories or commercial services rather than through any regional route. There is no regional detection laboratory to fall back on either: CARICOM's own Regional Biotechnology and Biosafety Policy treats the testing requirement as outstanding work, stating that laboratory facilities still need to be ESTABLISHED in the region and certified to international standards before member states can recognise each other's results. Regional institutes do related work — CARIRI in Trinidad and Tobago on food safety and microbiology, CARDI on agricultural research — but none is a designated detection laboratory for engineered material, so a sample goes to an accredited commercial laboratory, in practice outside the region. nearest capable laboratory is in another country and access runs through the regional body.

The unit is the plant protection service (DSPV) inside the Ministério da Agricultura e Desenvolvimento Rural, with a head of phytosanitary control; correspondence works in Portuguese, French or English. The governing instrument is DECRETO LEI Nº 04/99 on plant quarantine, published in the Boletim Oficial of 18 August 1999, which sets the phytosanitary measures intended to prevent the introduction into the country of organisms harmful to plants or plant products — so import controls have a named legal basis here even though the service is small. Capacity is being built rather than assumed: in March 2024 thirty-eight phytosanitary officials and field technicians were trained in detection, surveillance and diagnosis under the IPPC's plant health programme, with the agriculture minister publicly backing it. As a CILSS member state, what may lawfully be sold as a pesticide is set regionally by the Comité Sahélien des Pesticides, and GMO testing for the region runs through Burkina Faso's biosafety laboratory — both named elsewhere in this box. Registration of the IPPC contact dates from 2005.

complain.n: Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security
complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. Arriving seed, plant material and cargo are inspected here, which is where an organism never approved for release would turn up. No website is published in that source, so this names the office without linking it. It is a plant health body: it does not authorise a release, and it is not the biosafety regulator. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. The unit to name is the CROP PROTECTION UNIT within the ministry at Youyi Building, Brookfields, Freetown, which also holds the pesticide importation records. The instrument is the CONTROL OF PESTICIDES ACT 1989 — old, and the country's own agriculture plan says these Acts may need review. The ministry has renamed more than once: Agriculture, FORESTRY and Food Security in older citations, now Agriculture and Food Security, with the domain moving from maffs.gov.sl to maf.gov.sl. Two other bodies matter: the ENVIRONMENT PROTECTION AGENCY enforces environmental law over food production and runs environmental impact assessments for food industry projects, and the Sierra Leone Standards Bureau does market surveillance. Worth knowing that pesticide importation data is routinely collected by the ministry and has been published in peer-reviewed analysis covering 2010–2021 — so a documented import record exists for anyone examining what has entered the country. Sierra Leone adopted the Africa Phytosanitary Programme in June 2024, with the minister committing to assign phytosanitary staff.

complain.n: PAQS — Plant & Animal Quarantine Services, Ministry of Agriculture (Liberia)
complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. Arriving seed, plant material and cargo are inspected here, which is where an organism never approved for release would turn up. No website is published in that source, so this names the office without linking it. It is a plant health body: it does not authorise a release, and it is not the biosafety regulator. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. A regulatory service under the ministry's Department of Technical Service, covering PLANTS AND ANIMALS TOGETHER, and it undertakes EMERGENCY PROTOCOL to control an invasive species incursion or epidemic outbreak with other stakeholders — so it is the address for something already established, not only for something at the border. It works to IPPC, WOAH, WTO/SPS and CITES standards. Two other bodies to know: the LIBERIA AGRICULTURE COMMODITY REGULATORY AUTHORITY regulates agricultural commodities nationally, and a PLANT PESTICIDE REGULATORY SERVICES BUREAU has its own Act, alongside a Fertilizer Regulatory Division Act. Expect fragmentation and say so: an SPS assessment found food safety responsibilities spread across the health, agriculture and commerce ministries and Monrovia City Corporation WITH OFTEN OVERLAPPING FUNCTIONS, and most biosecurity agencies concentrated at the seaport and in the capital rather than at land borders. Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Ministerial Complex, Monrovia.

complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. Based at Yundum Agricultural Station rather than Banjul, which is where a caller should look. Pesticide management in the Gambia runs through THREE bodies working together, not one: the NATIONAL ENVIRONMENT AGENCY (NEA), the agriculture department's AGRICULTURAL PEST MANAGEMENT UNIT (APMU), and the National Agricultural Research Institute (NARI) — so a pesticide question may belong to the environment agency rather than to plant protection. The stated policy objectives are to protect crops, SEED and stored produce, to prevent the entry and spread of quarantine pests, and to ensure imports and exports meet the phytosanitary regulation in force. The Gambia adopted integrated pest management, PEST RISK ANALYSIS and good agricultural practices as its crop protection and quarantine strategy in 2002, at the Inter-African Phytosanitary Commission assembly — so a pest risk analysis is a recognised instrument to ask for here.

complain.n: Direction de la Protection des Végétaux — Ministère de l’Agriculture et de la Souveraineté alimentaire
complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. Arriving seed, plant material and cargo are inspected here, which is where an organism never approved for release would turn up. No website is published in that source, so this names the office without linking it. It is a plant health body: it does not authorise a release, and it is not the biosafety regulator. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. The instruments are LOI N° 2000-042 of 26 July 2000 on plant protection and its Décret n° 2002-062, plus LOI N° 96-025 on the production, control and marketing of CERTIFIED SEED. Under Article 26 a pesticide may only be marketed or used once homologated by the agriculture minister after the opinion of the CONSEIL CONSULTATIF DE LA PROTECTION DES VÉGÉTAUX — and, as a founding CILSS member, also under the Sahelian committee's common registration rules; the law expressly says the article ceases to apply if that committee is dissolved. ADVERTISING of unhomologated products, INCLUDING FREE SAMPLES, is prohibited, and advertising of homologated ones may state nothing beyond the registration decision. Note the ministry renamed to include Souveraineté alimentaire. And the honest position from the country's own pest management plan: pesticides are sold freely in an informal market, and THE LIST OF HOMOLOGATED PRODUCTS IS UNKNOWN TO SELLERS AND USERS ALIKE — so the rules above are real but weakly known on the ground.

complain.n: Direction de la Protection des Végétaux et du Conditionnement, Ministère de l'Agriculture
complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. Arriving seed, plant material and cargo are inspected here, which is where an organism never approved for release would turn up. No website is published in that source, so this names the office without linking it. It is a plant health body: it does not authorise a release, and it is not the biosafety regulator. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. Organised by Arrêté N°122/MA/DG/282/DPVC/2000 under the agriculture ministry, with phytosanitary protection governed by LOI 14/PR/95 of 13 July 1995 on plant protection. Two central divisions in N'Djamena — Legislation and Phytosanitary Control, and Surveillance, Interventions and Logistics — and, more usefully for a reader outside the capital, ELEVEN PHYTOSANITARY BASES AND OBSERVATION POSTS spread across the national territory. Its listed duties include liaison with FARMERS' ORGANISATIONS AND NGOs, and training of farmers for their own self-organisation, which is unusual to find written into a directorate's founding instrument. On chemicals: every product used in the country must be homologated before import, A LIST OF AUTHORISED PRODUCTS EXISTS and every import must refer to it, with DPVC carrying out that control; maximum residue limits are imposed via national or international standards including Codex and EU norms. A Commission Nationale de Contrôle des Pesticides à Usages Agricole sits alongside, with environment, finance, health and territorial administration ministries.

complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. The specific bodies to name, from the country's own pest management framework: within the agriculture ministry (MADR), the DIRECTION DE LA PROTECTION DES VÉGÉTAUX (DPV) does the plant protection work; the COMITÉ NATIONAL DE GESTION DES PESTICIDES (CNGP) governs the pesticide framework and is charged with PRE- AND POST-REGISTRATION CONTROL; and the Agence Centrafricaine de Développement Agricole (ACDA) and the research institute ICRA sit alongside. Control of distributors and applicators — ensuring ONLY REGISTERED PRODUCTS ARE SOLD AND USED — is shared between those MADR bodies, the environment ministry's DGEES and the health ministry's vector control unit. Everyday monitoring is done by the REGIONAL DIRECTORATES OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT together with health services and community health structures, which is the nearest thing to a local address here. The Chambre d'Agriculture, producer organisations and local NGOs are named in the same framework as participants. Note two ministry domains circulate, agriculture.gouv.cf and madr-gouv.com.

complain.n: Directorate of Plant Protection /Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security. Ministries Complex. Parliament Road Juba/ South Sudan
complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. Arriving seed, plant material and cargo are inspected here, which is where an organism never approved for release would turn up. No website is published in that source, so this names the office without linking it. It is a plant health body: it does not authorise a release, and it is not the biosafety regulator. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. It has its own page and its published duties name the thing this map cares about first: INSPECTION OF IMPORT AND EXPORT SEEDS and agricultural products entering the country, and checking import, export and other permits. It establishes plant quarantine CHECK POINTS at border entry points and Juba Airport, issues phytosanitary certificates, surveys existing pests, and GATHERS AGRICULTURAL STATISTICS INCLUDING ON PESTS AND PESTICIDES. It also coordinates with the quarantine authorities of NEIGHBOURING COUNTRIES to build a working mechanism under the IPPC — which matters for a landlocked state whose material arrives overland. The legal position is developing rather than settled: the PLANT PROTECTION ACT 2017 is in place, and a draft SOUTH SUDAN PHYTOSANITARY REGULATION 2024 together with a National Plant Protection Policy went to a validation workshop in Juba on 12 June 2024, built on the African Union SPS policy framework. Until that regulation is approved the Act lacks its implementing detail. Ministries Complex, Parliament Road, Juba; IPPC contact registered October 2024.

complain.n: Ministry of Agriculture, Regulatory Services Department
complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. Arriving seed, plant material and cargo are inspected here, which is where an organism never approved for release would turn up. No website is published in that source, so this names the office without linking it. It is a plant health body: it does not authorise a release, and it is not the biosafety regulator. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. The instrument is PLANT QUARANTINE PROCLAMATION No. 156/2006, in force, and the Regulatory Services Department runs four quarantine stations — ASMARA INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT, MASSAWA SEAPORT, ASSAB SEAPORT AND TESENEY — which are the official entry points where imported plants and plant products are inspected. Two things put this department at the centre of the seed question: it CERTIFIES AND MULTIPLIES seed varieties introduced at research centres, with multiplied improved seed reported rising from 700 to 50,000 over a decade; and with other institutions it has built a NATIONAL INFORMATION SYSTEM DOCUMENTING OVER 4,500 SEED VARIETIES. It also controls chemical pesticides — over 300 tonnes of expired product were disposed of in a national campaign between 2007 and 2017 — and has acted on production-stage contamination, citing control of pesticide-contaminated tomatoes from Gash-Barka sold in Asmara markets. The National Agricultural Research Institute, established 2003, develops the varieties. Note the IPPC contact registration dates from 2006.

complain.n: Plant Protection Directorate — Ministry of Agriculture and Agrarian Reform (Syria)
complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. Arriving seed, plant material and cargo are inspected here, which is where an organism never approved for release would turn up. No website is published in that source, so this names the office without linking it. It is a plant health body: it does not authorise a release, and it is not the biosafety regulator. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. The unit is the PLANT PROTECTION DIRECTORATE, which acts as the national organisation under Article IV of the IPPC and holds quarantine, PESTICIDE REGULATION and pest control. Its instrument is LAW 26 OF 2007 with Resolution No. 23/C, which is drafted widely: the material subject to regulation includes any plant, plant product, storing place, filling material, means of conveyance, container, SOIL, ANY OTHER LIVING ORGANISM or anything that may host pests, and such material may be held in phytosanitary quarantine for a specified period under the Directorate's technicians. It defines BENEFICIAL ORGANISMS to include fungi, bacteria, VIRUSES OR WHATEVER IS SIMILAR and invertebrates declared beneficial by the Ministry. On engineered organisms specifically: Syria prepared a national biosafety framework in 2006 naming SEVEN national authorities and ONE REFERENCE LABORATORY, and enacted a national biosafety law as LAW No. 24 OF 2012; this ministry follows up implementation for GMOs and their products for human consumption and agricultural use, plant and animal, veterinary and feed, with the economy and trade ministry handling related legislation. Note the framework's GEF implementation funding was never released after 2011.

complain.n: GDPP — General Directorate of Plant Protection, Ministry of Agriculture and Irrigation (Yemen)
complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. Arriving seed, plant material and cargo are inspected here, which is where an organism never approved for release would turn up. No website is published in that source, so this names the office without linking it. It is a plant health body: it does not authorise a release, and it is not the biosafety regulator. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. IT HAS ITS OWN SITE, plant-protection-yem.org, in Arabic and English. Three instruments: LAW No. 25 of 1999 on the handling and trade of agricultural pesticides — seven chapters, 36 articles, with stated penalties — LAW No. 7 of 2011 on Plant Quarantine, and LAW No. 20 of 1998 on SEEDS AND AGRICULTURAL FERTILISERS. Under the 1999 Law no pesticide may enter without prior licence from the ministry, the product must be registered, and the ministry must approve the type and quantity in advance; a Pesticide-Registration Committee handles registration, and the government built a PESTICIDES FORMULATION LABORATORY to check the quality of imports. Enforcement reaches beyond the ministry to Customs, ports of entry, the industry and trade ministry, security and armed forces AND POST OFFICES. The directorate is to coordinate with the Environmental Protection Authority. Evidence it acts: an October 2018 inspection campaign on pesticide stores and shops, with the minister reporting the SEIZURE OF 125 TONNES of banned and prohibited pesticides.

complain.n: PPQD — Plant Protection and Quarantine Directorate, MAIL
complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. Arriving seed, plant material and cargo are inspected here, which is where an organism never approved for release would turn up. No website is published in that source, so this names the office without linking it. It is a plant health body: it does not authorise a release, and it is not the biosafety regulator. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. It sits in the Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock, and the specific unit for chemicals is its PESTICIDES DIVISION: it maintains the PESTICIDE REGISTRY, receives and prepares registration applications and submits them for approval, working with the public health ministry. Decisions are taken by a PESTICIDE COMMITTEE chaired by MAIL's technical deputy minister with the head of PPQD as deputy chair, plus representatives of commerce and industry, public health and the Agricultural Research Institute — so a pesticide question is decided by a cross-ministry committee, not by the directorate alone. The governing texts are the Plants Protection and Quarantine Law and, for seed, the SEED LAW No. 149 of 2009; there is also a Regulation on Laboratory Analysis of Products of Plant Origin. Expect very little biological alternative to be registered: as of the most recent published account only one parasitoid and three microbial products were registered or pending. The IPPC contact for this directorate was registered in 2019, before the change of government, so verify the named person before relying on it.

complain.n: Plant and Animal Quarantine Unit — Ministry of Fisheries, Agriculture and Ocean Resources (Maldives)
complain.d: The office this country has designated as its official contact point under Article VIII.2 of the International Plant Protection Convention, as published by the IPPC Secretariat. Arriving seed, plant material and cargo are inspected here, which is where an organism never approved for release would turn up. No website is published in that source, so this names the office without linking it. It is a plant health body: it does not authorise a release, and it is not the biosafety regulator. The IPPC country page is the link here; the IPPC contacts entry in this box explains what that record gives and where it lags. THE MINISTRY HAS MOVED TWICE IN THREE YEARS: a Ministry of Agriculture and Animal Welfare was formed 17 November 2023 and DISSOLVED 14 APRIL 2026, merged into the Ministry of Fisheries, Agriculture and Ocean Resources — so agriculture.gov.mv and any 2023–26 citation names a ministry that no longer exists separately. The working body is the PLANT AND ANIMAL QUARANTINE UNIT, under the Plant Protection Act No. 12/2011, the Plant Quarantine Regulation and the Agricultural Pesticides Control Regulations No. 2021/R-12. The Regulation gives the Unit real holds: imported planting material may be KEPT IN QUARANTINE FOR SIX TO TWELVE MONTHS, its APPROVAL IS REQUIRED BEFORE SUCH MATERIAL IS USED COMMERCIALLY OR PASSED TO ANOTHER PARTY, and it may TAKE SAMPLES for checking and research at its discretion. Plants may only be imported by entities REGISTERED with the Unit, and notice must be given 48 hours before inspection. Where a regulated pest is found it can prohibit movement of affected plants and announce the information publicly.

subnational._note: Matched on the location string of whatever the reader has open, so a record in Iowa shows Iowa's inspector rather than the national one. This is the level that employs the people who can enter a field, and almost every national entry on this map points down to it without naming it.

_generic.d: Employs the inspectors, can enter a field and issues the penalties. Find yours in the directory; sending a report to Washington first is the commonest reason it goes nowhere.

Iowa.n: Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship
Iowa.d: Pesticide Bureau takes drift complaints and inspects. Iowa plants more engineered maize and soy than any other state, so this is the busiest such office in the country.

Illinois.d: Bureau of Environmental Programs handles pesticide misuse complaints and licensing.

Nebraska.d: Pesticide programme takes drift reports and inspects applicators.

Minnesota.d: Runs an incident response programme for pesticide drift and spills, and publishes its enforcement actions.

Indiana.d: Unusually, Indiana's pesticide regulator sits at Purdue rather than in a department, and it publishes case outcomes.

Kansas.d: Pesticide and fertilizer programme takes complaints and inspects.

Missouri.d: Bureau of Pesticide Control. Missouri was the centre of the dicamba drift complaints, which ran to thousands of reports in a single season.

Arkansas.d: The board that restricted dicamba use after a season of drift complaints, and the clearest case of a state body acting against a federally registered product.

California.d: Runs its own registration regime alongside the federal one and publishes a full pesticide use report — the most detailed public record of what is sprayed anywhere in the United States.

Texas.d: Handles pesticide complaints and applicator licensing.

North Dakota.d: Pesticide programme; North Dakota grows most of the US canola and a large share of the soy.

South Dakota.n: South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources

Wisconsin.n: Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection
Wisconsin.d: Agricultural resource management division takes drift complaints.

Michigan.n: Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development
Michigan.d: Pesticide and plant pest management division.

Oregon.d: Handles pesticide complaints, and holds the record of the creeping bentgrass escape — engineered grass found outside its trial site and still being managed two decades later.

Washington.d: Pesticide management division takes drift complaints.

Hawaii.d: Hawaii hosts most US seed-corn winter nurseries, so more engineered field trials happen here per acre than anywhere else in the country, and county-level restrictions have repeatedly been litigated.

Puerto Rico.d: Puerto Rico is the other major winter nursery site for seed corn, and is a US territory rather than a state, so federal rules apply with no state legislature above the department.

_generic.d: The federal office authorises; the Land inspects and enforces. A complaint goes to the Land, not to Berlin.

Bavaria.n: Bayerisches Landesamt für Gesundheit und Lebensmittelsicherheit
Bavaria.d: Bavaria declared itself GM-free and was the state where the Bablok honey case arose.

Baden-Württemberg.d: The regional councils inspect and enforce.

Lower Saxony.d: Lower Saxony holds much of Germany's arable land and its seed industry.

Saxony-Anhalt.d: Saxony-Anhalt was where most German engineered maize trials took place before cultivation ended.

_generic.d: The community inspects and enforces, not Madrid.

Aragón.n: Departamento de Agricultura, Ganadería y Medio Ambiente de Aragón
Aragón.d: Aragón plants more engineered maize than any other region in the European Union.

Catalonia.n: Departament d’Acció Climàtica, Alimentació i Agenda Rural
Catalonia.d: Catalonia is the second largest area of engineered maize in the EU.

Andalucía.n: Consejería de Agricultura, Pesca, Agua y Desarrollo Rural
Andalucía.d: Andalucía holds the largest organic area in Spain, which makes coexistence the live question here.

_generic.d: State committees have authority over releases in their state under the 1989 rules, and are closer than Delhi. Several states have refused trials the GEAC approved.

Maharashtra.d: Maharashtra grows the largest area of Bt cotton in India and has seen unapproved herbicide-tolerant cotton planted at scale.

Telangana.d: Much of India's cotton seed production happens here, so seed rather than crop is the question.

Kerala.d: Kerala declared itself an organic state and has refused engineered crop trials outright.

_generic.d: CTNBio authorises nationally; the state agency inspects and handles environmental damage. IBAMA acts where a state does not.

Mato Grosso.d: Mato Grosso grows more soy than any other state in Brazil, which makes this the busiest agricultural inspectorate in the country.

Paraná.d: Paraná attempted to ban engineered crops and lost in court to federal authority — the clearest Brazilian test of whether a state can decide this.

Rio Grande do Sul.d: Where engineered soy first entered Brazil, smuggled across the Argentine border and planted before it was legal.

Goiás.d: Inspects seed and crops in a major soy and maize state.

Bahia.d: Inspects in the western Bahia cotton and soy frontier.

Pará.d: Amazonian state where the agricultural frontier and forest law intersect.

_generic.d: The CFIA authorises; the province licenses applicators and takes drift complaints.

Saskatchewan.d: Saskatchewan grows most of Canada's canola, which is the crop the Schmeiser case was about and where volunteer plants are most common.

Alberta.d: Handles pesticide licensing and drift complaints.

Manitoba.d: Inspects and takes complaints; Manitoba is a major canola and soy province.

Ontario.d: Handles crop complaints; Ontario grows most of Canada's engineered maize.

Quebec.d: Quebec regulates pesticide use more tightly than other provinces and requires prescriptions for some treated seed.

British Columbia.n: BC Ministry of Agriculture and Food
British Columbia.d: Handles complaints; several BC municipalities have passed GM-free resolutions.

_generic.d: The OGTR licenses nationally; the state inspects, licenses applicators and takes drift complaints.

Western Australia.d: Where the Marsh v Baxter case arose — an organic grower who lost certification after engineered canola blew onto his land, and lost the case. It is the reference for what a neighbour can and cannot recover in Australia.

South Australia.d: South Australia maintained a moratorium on engineered cultivation until 2020, retained on Kangaroo Island.

Victoria.d: Handles crop and chemical use complaints.

Queensland.n: Queensland Department of Agriculture and Fisheries
Queensland.d: Handles complaints; Queensland grows most Australian engineered cotton.

Tasmania.d: Tasmania has maintained a moratorium on engineered cultivation since 2001 and markets itself on it — the longest state-level prohibition in Australia.

_generic.d: CONABIA advises nationally and SENASA enforces; the province inspects and sets fumigation distances from schools and houses, which is where most Argentine disputes are.

Buenos Aires.n: Ministerio de Desarrollo Agrario — Buenos Aires
Buenos Aires.d: The largest agricultural province; municipal fumigation-distance ordinances here have been repeatedly litigated.

Córdoba.d: Where the Barrio Ituzaingó case was tried — the first criminal conviction anywhere for spraying near homes.

Santa Fe.d: Major soy province with contested municipal spraying limits.

Entre Ríos.d: Where a court ordered minimum spraying distances around rural schools, later contested.

Chaco.d: Where health surveys near sprayed areas prompted provincial restrictions.

_generic.d: MARA issues the biosafety certificate; the province enforces. Provincial departments are the level at which unapproved planting has actually been acted on, including crop destruction.

Heilongjiang.d: China's largest soy province, and the one that prohibited engineered planting within its own borders while the country imports engineered soy at scale.

Xinjiang.d: Where most Chinese cotton is grown, and where engineered cotton has been planted longest.

Hainan.d: The winter breeding base: seed companies from across China grow generations here each off-season, which makes it the country's densest concentration of trial material.

Jilin.d: Major maize province, and among the first permitted to plant engineered maize commercially after 2023.

Henan.d: China's largest wheat province; wheat is not engineered commercially anywhere, which makes Henan a reference point rather than a site.

_generic.d: SENASICA authorises nationally; the state inspects. PROFEPA takes citizen complaints about environmental damage and is obliged to respond.

Sinaloa.d: Mexico's largest maize-producing state by volume, and the centre of the commercial planting argument.

Chiapas.d: Where engineered sequences were reported in local maize landraces in 2001 — the finding that started the centre of origin debate and was contested for years.

Oaxaca.d: Holds more maize landrace diversity than almost anywhere on Earth, maintained by smallholders rather than a genebank.

Yucatán.d: Where Maya beekeepers won a court ruling suspending engineered soy permits, on the ground that they had not been consulted — free, prior and informed consent enforced by a court.

_generic.d: The GMO Act registrar authorises nationally; the province inspects and takes complaints.

Free State.d: South Africa's largest maize province, and the country grows engineered maize as a staple eaten directly rather than as feed.

Western Cape.d: Holds most of the country's organic and export horticulture, which makes coexistence the live question here rather than cultivation.

_generic.d: NBMA authorises nationally; the state ministry and NAFDAC handle enforcement and labelling.

Kano.d: Where Bt cowpea was first distributed to farmers — the first engineered food crop released in sub-Saharan Africa.

Lagos.d: The port and the market: most imported food enters here, so labelling and import questions land in Lagos rather than in a field.

_generic.d: The health ministry authorises; the region inspects. Italy has used the EU cultivation opt-out, so most regional work concerns imports and coexistence.

Friuli.d: Where a farmer planted engineered maize in 2010 in open defiance of the national ban, was prosecuted, and the crop destroyed — the only such case in Italy.

Tuscany.d: Tuscany was among the first European regions to declare itself GM-free, and led the network that others joined.

Sardinia.d: An island, which is a coexistence argument in itself: the EU opt-out names geography as a ground in its own right.

_generic.n: Your SRAL — regional plant protection service
_generic.d: The ministry authorises; the SRAL inspects and takes drift complaints. Trial locations are published to the commune.

Occitanie.d: Where most French maize trials were sited before cultivation ended, and where the faucheurs volontaires crop destructions took place.

Nouvelle-Aquitaine.d: France's largest maize region, and the centre of the seed multiplication industry.

Brittany.d: Most French livestock is here, so imported engineered feed rather than cultivation is the question.

_generic.d: The ministry authorises; the province and the quarantine agency inspect.

Java.d: Most Indonesian rice and maize is grown here, on smallholdings averaging under a hectare.

Sumatra.d: Where the oil palm estates are, and where engineered palm has been proposed rather than planted.

_generic.n: Your Department of Agriculture regional field office
_generic.d: The Bureau of Plant Industry authorises; the regional field office inspects. Local government units have also passed their own restrictions.

Central Luzon.d: The rice bowl, and where the Golden Rice trials were sited — the approvals a court revoked in 2024.

Mindanao.d: Most Philippine maize is grown here, much of it engineered, and several local government units have declared restrictions of their own.
